the pasnuaao, starvation in manacles, and sucn- like persuasive institutions, are in full swing, under the noses of the European Legations—with their sanction, in one thumbscrew case not yet a year old, and in bastinado cases every day—within sight of Gibraltar, which, as you know, is more British than Brixton." "Yes. And what now ? " "Well, Abdullah and everyone else knows who killed Cassim. I told iron the Riffs had no laws. Wog s,aop paiunq u tram OSJOM 914 ppm& enj pue qamnoo IMO siq ltspl aaAan WOO OH *latipat ammo ,UITSBIIO st 111:11.InPclV •auo OAIRII if-th-e-Mogador Tice-Consul were not very shortly done to death. Further, he would be damned through all eternity—Abdullah, I mean. That law is just as fixed as this old wall we're sitting on." "And so now, Abdullah is-" "Yes. But there are complications. But let's go up for dinner. It's getting late." "No. Tell me those complications, Kerr." "-Well, to begin with Abdullah is what we Westerners would call engaged to be married,' to a very beautiful girl. Her mother happens to have been a Spaniard, which means that Abdullah's relation to her, up till now, has been something very different to a Moor's ordinary attitude towards an ordinary Moorish girl whom he is about to marry. Abdullah, in this case, has seen his future wife and talked with her. More, I believe they know each other well, and are passionately in love. As you know, that is not a feature of ordinary Mohammedan matrimonial affairs. Secondly: Three months ago, Abdullah, who is a man of apparently fine physique—you saw that— broke a blood-vessel. The English doctor here declared that any great and sudden shock was liable, at any time, to cause Abdullah's death, by stoppage of the heart's action. Thirdly: Abdullah is devotedly attached to Baron Dremhon, the brother of the German Consul here." "And for these reasons, I suppose, clings to his life ? " "He told me yesterday, with tears in his eyes," replied Kerr calmly, "that he was dead, but was living a little while to please the Baron." "But, how—" "Well, you see, the Baron is a very ,good fellow, in his way, though little enough under- stood or appreciated here. He is a literary man who burns most of what he writes, and lives in a cottage outside the city gates, and close to his brother, the German Consul's place. He saved Abdullah's life once in a skirmish on the Red Hill, near Tangier, you know. Since then, Abdullah has never slept further away from the Baron than on the mat outside his bedroom door, or beside his horse when they're travelling. He goes out with the Consul's little son, as you saw this even- ing, because the Baron is fond of the youngster. Abdullah wouldn't trust any mere European nurse to protect the boy. Abdullah has no wife at present, and much as he worships Fatima—the half- caste I told you of—he only arranged to marry her when the Baron consented to their both living in his cottage and looking after him." "Poor devil!" I muttered. "It is hard for him to die." _ _

"Oh, it's not that," said Kerr quickly. "Kismet covers that. But, you see, when all this happened, two months ago, the Baron implored Abdullah to do nothing without his consent. The Baron's fond of Abdullah, you know, in his way. Bismillah! You can't help it, once you've looked into that Moer's face, with its brown agate eyes, and thin, biscuit-coloured cheeks. Well, the Baron put it this way. He said: Our European methods are the best, Abdullah. Trust me. The French Vice-Consul shall be shot for this murder, legally; and neither you nor anyone else be blamed for it. See, your vendetta shall be satisfied, and you shall have your wife and me, and your life as well—only trust me.' So Abdullah com- municated the news to his compatriots, and it was agreed that matters might stand in abeyance for two months. The special circumstances were taken into account, you see, and that's why that fat Algerian Vice-Consul is walking about the beach this evening and thinks himself safe. He thinks Abdullah is content to be a Christian protected dog without caste, and that the matter has in some way blown over." "Then I suppose Abdullah is safe ? " I hazarded questioningly, forgetful of a long since registered vow to never interrupt Howard Kerr in a story. "You forget," he said. "The Riff's one law is unalterable. But come along! It's getting chilly, and dinner will be waiting." So I paid the penalty of my interruption, and turned to walk up the stony yard-wide street of the port to the city gate, and to my friend's quaint white house, inside the walls. "Yes," be continued, as we picked our way among the Jews and the Moorish beggars, "that law is fixed and unalterable. The two months is up to-morrow, but we have all known for a week and more that the Baron was powerless. His own brother, the Consul, can't help him. Remem- ber Tunis, and you'll understand that the French Legation is the biggest power here; just as it is the best hated; just as the British is the best respected. The llogador Vice-Consul has the French Legation, and many years of diplomatic and Moorish traditions on his aide. The authorities daren't stultify themselves any further. By Allah, it's the gossip of the Coast now. No, if that Mogador Vice-Consul's sense Were in pro- portion to his fat, he'd leave Casa Blanca to-night, and not bother about pack-mules either, but just ride his fastest horse. The bullying hound, he owns enough of 'em, goodness knows— and every one stolen! Then we reached Howard Kerr's house, and were greeted in the little patio by his own Moor, Achmet, who informed us that Allah's blessings would rest upon us for ever, and that dinner was waiting. So I heard no more about Abdullah the Riff, just then. But, at intervals, I thought about him, his loving nature, his physical weakness, his brown eyes, and his strange:position, till the night died away in the cool embrace of hushed purple morning. Then I fell asleep with a monotonous call to prayer from the tower of Csasa Blanca's principal mosque ringing vaguely in my ears. "Prayer," I thought. "And to a Godlof such gruesome inevitability!" But next day I concluded that.there was a certain grandeur, a certain large nobility about such implicit and all-embracing faith in any God. Kerr was always a late riser, and even in Morocco, where some judge the days's glory departed two hours before noon comes, with its silent blaze of mature splendour; even here, he was seldom astir before nine o'clock. At a few minutes after that time I rode down to the beach with him to bathe. I do not think that life, the mere living, aver seemed to me a more precious and delightful thing, than on that brilliant June morning at Casa Blanca, when sea and airs and smooth white sand alike, were warm and soft to languorousness, yet withal, seemed to combine in laughing joyously up at the fathomless blue above them—that wonderful north African sky which travelled workers, in the Quartier Latin and elsewhere, strive so hard and so unavailingly to adequately depict on canvas. As we cantered slowly up from the warm sea to the warmer town, I heard a sudden distant scream; piercing and metallic the sound was in the throb- bing stillness of that atmosphere. We both reined in our horses with a jerk, and Howard Kerr's towel fell on to the sand. "Abdullah and Fatima, by the Lord!" muttered Kerr. And then, wheeling our horses together— they were both Barb stallions, and fighters, too, as a general thing—we galloped, stirrup to stirrup, towards the wattled huts from which it seemed the scream had come.

Where the people came from I cannot say, but while we galloped those few hundred yards, the beach round about the four Moorish dwellings became thronged, crowded by a shouting, gesticu- lating mob of many coloured natives, Spaniards, half-castes, Barbary Jews, Moors of all classes and both sexes, yelping pariah dogs, and Basha's soldiers carrying gas-pipe-barrelled guns, and naked daggers. Kerr and myself were by no means late arrivals, as events proved, but the warm air reeked tragedy when we pressed our horses through ,the outskirte of the mob. What we saw was the mortal remains of the French IVice-Consul;in Mogador, Ben Mohammed An; ; an indescribably horrible object, slashed and hacked beyond recognition, huddled on the sodden white sand. Near by, on one side, a Moorish woman and two men were clinging to the half- caste girl, Fatima, whose beauty impressed me strongly, even in those circumstances. Her hyak was torn from her shapely head and shoulders, leaving bare a face and neck and breast of a kind not often seen in Morocco. She was struggling and screaming almost unceasingly. On the far side of the dead Vice-Consul, two Moors, Basha's soldiers, were biting and scratching the sand, in what seemed to be their death throes. A little further on still, stood Abdullah, Shailni, all but naked to the waist, a long gun at his feet, and an unusually large curved Fez dagger in his right hand, ~intnrw snlendirl

or a savage at bay, and fighting fok his lire. fie had killed two guards, besides the Vice-Consul, and now, his gun being empty, himself bleeding from several wounds, Abullah wss keeping a whole crowd at bay with that terrible Fez knife of his. At the moment of our arrival, three soldiers were grouped about the dead Vice-Consul, and were deliberately trying to cover his murderer with their Moorish guns. Seeing this, Abdullah fought the more furiously with those who tried to close about a eedutation to my friend, from out that reeling liamble. _ _

"Peace be on you I" he cried. And Kerr answered him: "Good be with yet" Then Ohe three soldiers who stood over the remains of Ben Mohammed An, shouted to the crowd to stand aside: "Baalak I Baalak!" And Abdullah's assailants swept back, leaving him for a moment panting, surrounded by his own blood, but apparently free. He seemed to have changed his mind about eluding the soldiers' aim, and stood now absolutely still; a statue in crimson-stained light bronze. The long guns covered him now, and one fancied one could hear the pulses of the crowd beating.

And then—an interruption. A gasp, a torn breath came from Fatima. Her kaftan remained in the hands of her friends, and, her lithe figure almost naked, she bounded, like a wounded spring-bok, across the open space, to where stood Abdullah, the Riff. . And at that moment came the tearing report of the three muzzle-loaded Moorish guns, their smoke for a few seconds throwing a veil over a scene already sufficiently dramatic, as well as horrible. Her body was over his. The aim had been sure enough, and all three charges had torn her girlish shoulders and body. Nothing had reached Abdullah, but he was quite dead when the smoke cleared away. Afterwards, the bodies of these two loving barbarians were buried together, their last embrace not being an easy one to disturb. That evening, when our nerves had steadied down again, —Morocco sunshine and Mohammedan phlegm eat up excitement—Howard Kerr said to me:
"There you are, Amigo! There's a short story made to your hand; on your second day in Morocco, too."

"A book, if you like, Kerr," I told him; "but not a short story." "And why not the story ? " "Because in a book it could be made fiction, Kerr; trimmed and served with circumstantial sauce, you know. As a short story it would necessarily be just bare fact and—so no one would believe it or be interested. "
"Oh, I don't know. Try the unadorned fact, for once, Amigo and—pass me a cigarette witl you ? "
So I have written the thing as it was. [THE END.]

A DOCUMENT FROM MOROCCO.
BY A. J. DAWSON. Author of "Bismillah," "God's Foundling," ‘"ln the Bight of Benin." &c.

In Casa Blanca there is a queer old olive-grey wall which runs right down from the Easbah gate to the white beach, where the Jews kill their consecrated cattle at sun-up, and the Europeans take their before-dinner constitutional at sun- down. The olive-grey wall is a yard thick in places, flaky and battered and lichen-grown all over; and, so the antiquarians say, it is a relic of the Roman occupation of Morocco. But I was a new arrival, and saw nothing about the wall save its general picturesqueness, its many shot4marks, and the undoubted advantages it offered as a resting-place from which to enjoy a gorgeous sunset, and the evening's welcome cool. I had landed at the curious old fortress that very afternoon, from a tramp coaster bound for Cadiz, and Howard Kerr had met me according to promise, his felucca skimminc, safely enough over the foam-flecked bar which the rickety little tub I had travelled in, dared not attempt to cross. Now we were sitting. Kerr and myself, on the end of the crumbling wall afore-mentioned, and talking of things as we found them. It was my first glimpse of Morocco, and I had not, as yet, passed the stage of thinking it very like that further off great world of nenetrating smells and up-thrusting colour, which tourists call "The East." "Traditions seem to linger here," I opined, with a nod in the direction of a cavalcade passing below us, along the broad, tide-ribbed sand. A European youngster, pale and exotic-looking, was seated on a donkey. A nurse—German, to judge by her appear- ance—walked beside, with one hand on her charge's waist, and a Moor brought up the rear; patiently, submissively, striding behind the donkey, a broken doll in one of his thin hands, the curved end cof his dagger's silver sheath shewing under a care- lessly hitched-up grey gellabia. "Yes. But apropos of what ? " asked Kerr. "The Moor walking behind that donkey. I suppose he is a Moor ? " "Very much so, and a Itiffian at that." "Well ; is he not typical of the docile servility of the coloured and subject East, under the influence of the white and dominant West. He meanders serenely along in that menial capacity, the humble servant of a child and a nurse-maid; yet under his cloak he carries a silver-sheathed scimitar, which I suppose will never be used, and which probably cost him at least three miinths' wages." ‘-dh! The youngster's the son of the German Consul here." With leisurely care, my friend and host was rollling for himself a fresh cigarette, which he prenntly lighted at the butt of a ready- made African.t. 'But you forget, Amigo," he continued, "that you are not in the coloured and subject East. You are in Morocco, which has nothing to do wig) East or West, which carefully cherishes its own barbarism, and is in a way more unassailable than is Great Britain, say, because it can at any time command the protection of all the others against any one Continental nation." "But it doesn't." "There is as yet no need." "And the natives seem humble enough." "Ah! Ask the Christians here, which of them would dare to walk unprotected through the Soko, during Moolud, or any other great festival. Morocco is not the East, my friend, not by a long way. But it's quaint you should have chosen that particular Moor to hang your deduction on. Yes, it's odd you should have hit upon Abdullah, Shá,ilni; because he, to use their own phraseo- logy, though walking abroad, is yet but a dead man—or a dog." "My dear Kerr, what in the world is the true inwardness of that ? "

"Eh? Well, wait a moment. There now, look! You see that very fat man? No, not the one in stockings and white. There, to the left of those camels, with an orange-coloured gellab." "Yes, I see. There's a strip of violet at the neck of his ,gellab." "Right. Well, that's the French Vice-Consul at Mogador. If our friend with the donkey, Abdullah the Riff, from Sheshawan, succeels shortly in killing that fat Algerian from Mogador, well and good; he, Abdullah, is practically a dead man. If he does not kill the French Vice-Consul, then is he most assuredly a dog, whose apparently human body will very soon be ripped open, by some such dagger, as that you saw him wearing, skilfully wielded by one of his country- men from the Riff."

"Oh! Well, that sounds simple enough certainly," I said. "But I don't quite realise the situation yet, all the same. It seeing that the inoffensive donkey-driver stands to lose both ways." "Yes. But remember that his belief in Kismet is on a par with your attitude towards, say, the law of gravitation. As he anticipates no pleasure in life other than what Allah and his Prophet have ages since arranged for, so he is coavinced no evil can befall hisn, save the inevitable. Fatalism, like cannibalism, bimetallism, or anything else of the sort, has its points, you know." "Well, but—why don't you enlighten me, you professor of the out-of-the-way ? " "It's difficult, while Morocco is still only part of the Orient to you. But, see! Abdullah, as I said, is a Riff. Barring the adventurers on certain China seas, I suppose the Riffs, whose coast is within a few hours of Gibraltar, are the only people on earth amongst whom piracy, slaving and wrecking are in full swing to-day. Your Riff has no Kaids, no Bashas, no laws, no roads, no Sultan, no fear, no anything—save and excepting his faith in one God, one Prophet, his own dagger,a Martini= Henry if he can get one, and failing that, his ten- foot long Riff gun; coral-studded, ivory-butted, brass-bound and deadly to handle." , "Well?"

"Well, Abdullah's a Riff. Now, a few months ago, the Fi-ench authorities here entered into a pledge with certain Ruffians, to restore to them three Riff prisoners in return for the release of a French subject then held in durance among the Seshawan hills. The Riffs adhered to the spirit and letter of the agreement, and the French, with questionable diplomacy, backed out from their part in toto. Then came a rumour that another Frenchman had been taken prisoner by the Riffs, and would be killed out of revenge. His sister appealed to the French Legation for inquiry and rescue. The French Legation had burnt its boats where the Riffs were concerned. It assured the woman that the whole rumour was a groundless canard. Evidence of its truth arrived. The Legation wavered, and sought relief in red tape, official twaddle, and procrastination. The French- woman found a Riff—Abdullah's brother, Cassim —and induced him, for a consideration, to go into the Riff country, where no European dare venture, and attempt to buy off her brother. The Legation heard of the arrangement, and decided that in the interests of French dignity, it must be frustrated. The French Vice-Consul at Mogador—the fat Algerian Moor I pointed out to you—was here at the time, and was known as a pretty unscrupulous character. His suceriors at the Legation told him that Abdullah's brother, Cassim, must be pre- vented, if possible, from goinr, to the Riff. The Vice-Consul smiled blandly, and asked for • expenses.' Doubtless these were forthcoming. His methods were Oriental, simple, and very direct. Two days later C s;iin was iniss.ng. Two days later again, his body was found on the beach, by the Mogador Vice-Consul's servants, and it was announced that the unfortunate man, being probably under the influence of drink, had valkeW into the sea, and then been drowned. Cassim, lire most Rif* was a devout Mohammedan, and had never been known to touch alcohol. His body was buried within two hours, under the Mogador Vice- Consul's orders, and the Mogador Vice-Consul's soldiers guarded the dead man jealously from the eyes of ..A.bdullah and his other friends. Rumour says the marks of the cord which had strangled Cassim were plainly visible on the dead man's neck."

"And that is countenanced by an European Legation?" I interrupted. "Amigo, you forget; this is Morocco, and not British India, or the East' of Messrs. Cook." "Well, but-", "Vas I know. .11,1 v dear fellow. the thomisaa...-..

bers ought to be in the majority, especially as the Council have to find the money. Mr. \\TALKER failed to see that it made much differ- ence, and seeing the lively interest Mr. May took in the financial matters he supported the amendment. Mr. May's arithmetic was sometimes faulty but that was perhaps due to circumstances. The Press recog- nized Mr. May as an authority on economy; in fact, the Press said he was the only economical member of the committee. (Laughter.) Mr. JOLLEY thought it was desirable that members should bear in mind the principle mentioned by Coun- cillor Wilkinson. It was not a question of personality but it seemed to him that those who paid the piper ought to call the tune. He thought it would be going back on their policy, and essentially wrong in prin- ciple, to allow a preponderence of representatives not directly elected by the people. The MAYOR said a councillor ought at least to be appointed in place of a councillor. It had been a general rule that there should be a majority of Council members on the Finance Committee, in view of their having to back up what was done when the business came up for confirmation before the Town Council.
_ The amendment WAS put and lost by a big majority. The minutes were approved,
SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE. THE FUTURE OF THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL. MR. MAY AND FANCY LECTURES.

At a meeting of this committee, it was noted that a Conference had taken place on the 24th October,between the Governors of the Warrington Grammar school and the Committee. with reference to the organization of that ischool and the position it is to occupy in the scheme for higher education in the Borough. It was also resolved—" That the following contractsrs be asked whether they are prepared to accept the renewal of their contracts bra further period of twelve months from the 31st March, 1905, viz. :—(a) Messrs. Philip. Son and Nephew, for the supply of school and kindergarten materials, and kindergarten tables; (b) Mr. John Heywood, for the supply of dual desks; and (c) Mr. Benjamin Wadsworth, for the tuning of the pianos in the various schools."
not confirmed. Every firm who could supply the goods should, in his opinion, have an opportunity of tender- ine6o. uncillor JAMES EVANS seconded. _
Councillor LORD supported an-d eXpressed the opinion that the resolution was contrary to the standing orders of the Council. _ _

who had not fulfilled the conditions of the law. He ' did not think many of the children fulfilled the condi- tion& It appeared t) him that some children were receiving special treatment and that the committee were being largely guided by the apparent need of parents. of course it did the committee great credit for their kindness of heart, but they did not see what the conse- quence of the leniency was. It was already becoming known that a child who could not produce a complete certificate could escape the other year attendance at school. He was speaking after 20 years' experience as a teacher at Town's-end, and he said without fear of Icontradiction that a child of the deserving poor always i made such an attendance at school that it could at 13 I get a certificate.A very large number'of certificates had been granted te parents who were in poverty,but he main- tained that it was no use keepinga staff of seven officers to see that the children attended school regularly if they were going to remove one of the strongest induce- ments to get parents to send their children regularly to school, and they were doing that by the too free grant- ing of those certificates. The REV. FATHER Wrr.soN gave four instances in which children had received exemptions, but who were at present at home unemployed. These circumstances had a bad effect and entailed a loss of money. The average attendance would be lowered if this was con- tinued and so much grant lost to the committee. Mr. MAY said he was somewhat opposed, although a member of the committee, in many cases to the grant- ing of the certificates. No doubt their Chairman, Mr. Ellison, and the members who had granted certificates would be able to give a complete answer to the state- ment which had been made by Mr. Wilson. There were cases where there were large families—seven younger children, and where the mother had one in arms and had to go out to wash. That was a great plea which weighed with the tenderhearted one. They, as members of the committee, had been called upon by the inspectors, the committee, and the Council to provide new schools, and yet one of their number had stated that there were 2,000 vacancies every day the schools were open. If that was correct the schoolmasters were acting wrongly in turning children away from school daily. Mr. PrxisToN said that every case was considered on its merits. With all due deference to Mr. Upson's statement, the committee were not hard-hearted or too soft-headed. (Hear, hear' and laughter). The members considered the matter to the best of their ability ; and when they found a family seven in number and the parent with an income 17s. 10d. a week—that might be taken as the average—with 4s. alweek rent to pay, and the wife earning somthing to keep the family, it was to his mind a question of bread and butter before educa- tion. (Hear, hear). As long as he was a member of the sub-committee, whether he was in agreement with the wishes of the officials, or the authority, or the majority of the committee, he was determined to bring to bear on the question a sympathetic point of view. In was in many cases a question of how people were going to exist, not to live,—(hear, hear)—and it was, therefore not fair for Mr. Upson to say that it was known in the street that exemptions could be obtained by anyone. Many cases had been refused. The com- mittee did not allow special exemptions unless the cir- cumstances of the family necessitated it. . Mr. UPSON said that if Mr. May would consult the average attendance list he would see that theattendance for the month ending October 7th, was 12,248, number on the books 14,068, and if he wauld do a little subtrac- tiou he would find the difference was 1,820, in round figures approximating to 2,000. If he took the igures for the year he would find that there were 2,000 places, as he had stated, emptied every time the schools met. He knew of cases of individual hardship, and he had endeavoured to do what he could to help, but he main- tained that it was becoming well known that a parent had only to apply for exceptional treatment to get it. In twenty-five cases recently parents applied for excep- tional treatment, and 24 out of the 25 were granted ,certificates. _ _

It was explained that all the contracts with the ex- ception of Messrs. Phillips had been running only a very short time. Messrs. Phillips had supplied materials for a year and had executed the contract so satisfac- torily that the committee thought they could not improve upon their terms. The amendment was withdrawn.

Mr; MAY criticised the decision of the committee to arrange a course of University Extension Lectures. It seemed to him extraordinary that while they were struggling to provide elementary education the School Management Committee should arrange for a course of " fancy " lectures. The social question must be debated from a certain point of view, and it seemed like intro- ducing a propaganda from a particular point of view by a particular party. That might not be so, of course, and the lectures might be given from a purely academic point of view. The first duty of the committee was to provide educatien for the very poorest. He proposed that the resolution be rescinded.

The Rev. M. STEVENSON in reply to Mr. Walker, said they were saving 4s. 6d. per evening in the salaries paid at the plumbing classes compared with the sums paid last year. With reference to holidays, the teachers in the Secondary School had to teach in the evening as well as during the day, and their duties were more onerous than those who taught only in the day. The whole question was not an easy one. It was more for the sake of the teachers than the children, at least he thought so as a teacher, that the holidays were wanted. (Laughter.) c4ith reference to the lectures, the custom of having them was of very long standing; certainly e rer since he had known Warrington. The only change was that instead of being given under the management of the committee of the old Technical Institute as it used to;be called, the work had been transferred to the School Management Committee. The lectures were practically self-supporting. The minutes w ;re then agreed to. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CONIAITTEE.

Councillor Ev&Ns said there was no case which was not thoroughly gone into and evidence produced as to tha number in a family and the wages earned. Where there was a large family and the income was small, and where it was evident there was more need of food than education, he admitted the position was a difficult one to occupy. Under those circumstances should they force the law or exercise a little commonsense? (Hear, hear.) When school managers became aware of cases such as the Rev. Father Wilson had quoted, he thought they should bring those cases before the committee and have them re-considered. Mr. JOLLEY thought the members of the School Man- agement Committee allowed themselves to be carried away by a sympathetic feeling, and thus unconsciously they did a grievous injury. This was a matter that ought toThellooked at!from a broader social standpoint,and he should like as strongly as possible to support the pro- test Mr. Upson had made against the action of the com- mittee. He confessed to some snrprise that Mr. Plins- ton, who had worked for social improvement, should de- fend a line of action which was distinctly adverse to it. (Cries of" Question.") There must inevitably be cases of hardship, awl it resolved itself into a question whether in the attempt to sympathetically deal with special cases they were not inflicting a grievous injury cn the community by encouraging child labour. They wanted to raise the age limit, not to lower it, at which children could commence to work. With regard to the cases of hardship and pnverty, it was no part of the duty of the Education Committee to act in the admini- stration of out relief. The Guardians of the poor were the persons to deal with matter. _ .

Mr. G. WALKER said he should be very sorry to associate himself with the sentiments of Mr. Jolley. (Hear, hear.) He thought food was necessary even before education When a child had arrived at that age that it could be useful to its parents, and one might even go further and say that children were being educated out of their proper spheres altogether. He (the speaker), was, perhaps, one of the soft-hearted ones, and he must admit that when a case came before him where he saw that the father was laid up with con- sumption, probably to become an inmate of the Work- house Hospital within a few days, and there were the young children inaapa,ble of working, and when the mother had to go out and earn food, in these circum- stances he should feel himself condemned if he did not liberate a child from school who might be of use. (Hear, hear.) That was one of many cases. • Mr. UpsoN: Is it typical? Mr. WALKER: Yes. Mr. UPSON: Nonsense. _ _

Mr. WALKER said that some of the members of the committee made it a point to turn up to the meetings of the committee week after week; it was not a ease of turning up every month, and they dealt with each case independently. (Hear, hear.) Possibly there were 2,000 vacancies in the schools, but Mr. Upson had not stated how many children were laid up by siekness or who had been sent home for the school fees. The statement that there were altogether 2,ooovae,ancies was not correct. Mr. UrsoN : It is correct.

Colonel BIICKTON said the question was a difficult one to deal with, and always would be, but, at the same time, it seemed to him that the committee had to do their duty. The questions of poverty, low wages, and large families were considered by the higher authorities when the limit of 14 years was fixed. The CHAIRMAN said there WRS no doubt that was one of those questions about which a great deal could be said on both sides. . _

Councillor ELLtsoN in reply, said full inquiry was made into the circumstances of each CASA, and no child was let off unless the cases were of a deserving char- acter. The committee were always informed where each child was going to work. Mr. Upson, had, he thought, been rather hard upon the committee. For the week ending October 7th, there were on the books 14,068 children, and there were in actual attendance 12,977, while the number of children who were sick was 764. The sick children had not been mentioned by Mr. Upson,and the children who were unaccounted for num- bered 327. How the 2,000 vacancies were made out he did not know. Councillor WILKINSON asked if when the committee gave a child an exemption certificate for labour it was returned signed by the manufacturer who had under- taken to employ the child. The DIRECTOR: No; that. is the weakness of the system. At present the manufacturer signs the certifi- cate to say that he will employ the child and that the employment is beneficial. The certificate is signed by me and given to the child, but we don't know whether the child goes to the place or not. Children have gone to places for a week and have been on the streets afterwards,
The minutes were then agreed to. THE BEAMONT SCHOOL.
ALDERMAN BENNETT ARGUES IN FAVOUR OF SWIMMING BEING TAUGHT.
At a meeting of the Sites and Buildings Committee held on the 11th November, the following resolutions

were passed :—ThatCouncilfor Brough be recommended for appointment as a member of this committee, in place of Mr. Dodds, resigned, and that Councillor J. Fulton Smith be recommended for re-election as a member of this committee; that an advertisement; be issued inviting architects practising within the County Borough of Warrington to furnish competitive designs for the new school to be erected in Orford-avenue; that the site for the proposed new school to be erected in Orford-avenue be purchased outright; that the school in question be called "The Beamont Council School ; that the conditions of competition which were approved by the committee at their last meeting for the "Boltot" School, be with the necessary alterations, applied to the competition to be held for the "Beamont" School it being understood that the last-named school is to comprise three departinents (boys', girls and infants') —the infants' department being a separate one-storeyed and the boys' and girls' departments a two-storeyed building; and that the Town Council be asked to make application to the Local Government Board for sanction to a loan being raised for the purchase of the sites for the "Bolton" and "Beamont" Schools. The MAYOR moved the confirmation of the diinutes. Councillor WILKINSON seconded. Alderman 13ExNErr said that when it was decided to erect a new school at Latchford he suggested that it

THE GRANTING OF EXEMPTION CERTIFICATES. "BREAD AND BUTTER BEFORE EDUCATION." Councillor ELLISON moved the confirmation of the minutes of the School Attendance Committee. Councillor JAMES EVANS seconded. Mr. UPSON asked for information with regard to the number of children who were exempted for employment

would be desirable to provide accommodation for the teaching of swimming. He was, however, told by the committee that it was to be a girls' school and for some unearthly reason it did not seem to be necessary that girls should swim. He was given to understand that if he left the matter inabeyance until the Orford school was to be built it would receive consideration. He had brought it before the committee, but he supposed it was owing to the wave of

economy that was sweeping over the town, perhaps not unnaturally, that the proposal had not a very warm re- ception. fle thought the committee ought to seriously consider the question of teaching swimming and provide the proper accommodation. The matter had been forcibly brought to his mind by what he saw when visit- ing several Liverpool schools where the experiment had been adopted with great success. It might he hoped. be possible at some future date to provide a bath in connection with Beamont school.
The CI" AIRM A.N said there were many luxuries that might beivery desirable, but as long as .they had such very heavy rates it would ba better not to indulge in them. (Hear, hear). _ _

Coundillor 'BURTON asked what price it was proposed to give for the Orford site. He did not see any reason why the new school should be called the Beamont school, although he had every respect for the late Mr. Beaniont and appreciated his many charitable acts. If the people of Warrington wished to honour his memory they might] adopt some means that would be more appropriate. If there was any honour in having one's name attached to the school it was really due to the chairman of the Education Committee who had worked so zealously in the cause of education. He would also suggest the desirability of placing in the schooli a tablet bearing the names of the members of the committee.

Mr. Max agreed with Councillor Burton, altfioughThe personally had reason to bs greatly indebted to the late Mr. Beamont. Still there were gentlemen living among them at the present time who deserved to be honoured as leaders of the committee and workers on behalf of education.

The CHAIRMAN believed Warrington men would- like to see the name of Beamont honoured in connec- tion with education. He was the first Mayor of War- rington, and a very useful man,and a handsome sum had been left by him to his wife to dispose of after her death in the way she thought best. He (the speaker) hoped the suggestion for the alteration of the name would not be pressed. (Hear, hear). Mr. UPSON thought the suggestion that the new school was going to relieve the St. George's Mission school seemed rather absurd. He was not convinced that the site was the best in the town for a school providing accommodation for 1,000 children. It would he believed, be better to erect a new infant school in the Town's end neighbourhood. The MAYOR said the site had been offered to the committee at something under 2d. per yard. It would he believed, be cheaper to purchase the land outright. The committee made inquiries with reference to baths, and the cost would be about £3,000 for each school. They d:d not think the time was opportune for the experiment. It seemed appropriate to the committee that Mr. Beamont's name should be honoured in the way suggested, as he was a very liberal subscriber to War- rington schools. The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: el. RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: el. RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
FATAL BOILER EXPLOSION AT WIDNES.

On Monday, at .the Accident Hospital, Widnes, an inquest was held concerning the death of John Catterall (71), licensed victualler, of Seaview Garden Inn, Farnwortb, who died on Thursday evening, the result of injuries received by the explosion of a boiler in his workshop at Farnworth, where he did odd jobs. The bottom of the boiler had been worn very thin.—A verdict of "Accidental death "was returned. UNPROVOKED ATTACK ON A GIRL.

At Widnes, on Monday, James Carroll, of 22, Water- street, was committed to the Assizes on a charge of wilfully wounding Grace Patience Maher,aged fourteen years, residing in Barn-street, on the 22nd ult. The prisoner, it was alleged, attacked her without any pro- vocation, and threw her violently on the roadway, causing her head to come into contact with the kerb- stone.

UNIVERSAL WEEK OF PRAYER.—The Council of the Evangelical Alliance are again arranging for the obser- vance of the Annual Week of Prayer,which always com- mences with the first Sunday in each year. Next January therefore, it will be from the Ist to the 7th. Already there are indications that the coming Week will be more extensively observei at home and abroad that in any previous year. It is a striking proof of the univer- sityof this ohservance,that the programme of suggested topics for prayer for each day of the week, prepared by the Council of the Alliance, is accepted in all lands, and is translated into a. vast number of languages ; thus even the native Christians in the various mission-fields are able to take an intelligent part with their fellow- Christians all over the world in thisseason of united supplication. The general outline of subjects is as follows: On Monday, thanksgiving and prayer for the "One Body "of which Christ is the Head Tuesday, prayer for nations and their rulers; Wednesday, prayer for our own land and possessions: Thursday, prayer for families, educational establishments, and the young; Friday, prayer for God's ancient people Israel: Satur- day, prayer for foreign missions The detailed pro- gramme and other information may be obtained on ap- plication to the Secretary of the Alliance, 7, ADAM STREET, STRAND, LONDON, W.C.

The committee further recommended—" That, in accordance with resolution No. c 743, arrangements be. made with the University Extension Committee, Man- chester, for a course of six lectures on "The social questions of the present time" to be given by Mr. S. J. Chapman, M.A., for a fee of 21 guineas, together with travellin3 expenses." The REV. MORLEY STEVENSON in moving the COM- firmation of the minutes, stated that as a result of the conference between the governors of the Grammar School and the School Management Committee, the governors requested that the committee should formu- late-their proposals in writing, and send it to them for consideration, and then four of the governors could be appointed to meet fonr members of the committee. It was thought that that arrangement would see the matter quickly and successfully settled,but he regretted to say that he had received an intimation from the Governors which practically broke off the negotia- tions, and asked them to formulate their proposals, and send them to the Board of Education, and then through the medium of that Board the proposals would coma before the governors for consideration. He was sorry that this course had been taken, because he thought it would lead to a great deal of delay, and the organiza- tion of the Grammer School and the aid they were hoping to give would probably be now postponed for a very long period by the correspondence which was always involved when a matter had to pass through a Government office. Referring to the proposal to increase the salary of Mr. George S. Pendlebury, the assistant master at the School of Art from £lO4 to £l2O per annum he said Mr. Pendlebury had been a year at the school and the success of his work had been very marked. They had in him an exceptionally good teacher. Before he came to Warrington he held a much better post, but he was a Warrington man, and thought he would like to settle down in the town and work in his old school. Even the increased salary was far below what his services entitled him to. Arrangements had been made with the University Extension Committee, Manchester, for a course of six lectures on "The social questions of the present time," by Mr. S. J. Chapman, M.A., fora fee of 21 guineas and travelling expenses. The lectures would be devoted to subjects of the hour, and would be ex- tremely interesting. He would like to call attention to the summary of the examination results. There was with one or two exceptions, in every department, a decided improvement upon last year, especially in the art section, which showed a very marked improvement indeed. Councillor ELLISON seconded.

• The first of a series of people's services was held in. the above church on Sunday evening,when the preacher, the Rev. John Yonge, took for his subject " Visions and dreams for old and young." There was a large congre- gation. The solo If with all your hearts" was well sung by Mr. A. Griffiths, and an admirable rendering was given by the choir of the anthem "Seek ye the Lord." Mr. Payton presided at the organ, and also gave an excellent organ recital, at which the following was the programme :—" Fugue in E Flat" (St. Ann's), Bach; "Intermezzo," Rheinberger; "The Question and he Answer," Wolstenholme.

The estate of Mr. Charles Morton, the father of the music-halls, has been sworn at £2,078 gross and the net personality at £1,844. Two young men named Ryan and Baxter' who were sentenced to three months' hard labour for picking pockets during the visit of the King and Queen of Portugal to London, have been released, it being believed that a mistake had been made.

At Durham Assizes a fireman was sentenced to penal servitude for life for wounding a woman. Mr. Justice Darling said it was a marvel that the woman had lived,. and the punishment must be severe—almost as severe as though she had died.

Beresford and Sir A. K. Wilson are not only' familiar figures with the public, but within the last month have had their biographies in every paper in the country, but Admiral May and Captain Jackson are less well- known to civilians. The former is always called] " Willy " in the senior service to distinguish him from Admiral Henry May, and is still a young man comparatively, though recently his retirement was rumoured. He has a fine record, both as a practical man and as an administrator. He entered the Navy just over forty years ago, and served on the Arctic Expedition of 1875-76, when he got badly frost-bitten. In 1888 he annexed Christmas Island, and in the same year became Flag-Captain on the China station. He was a naval attaché for Europe from 1891 to 1893, in which year he became Assistant Director of Torpedoes. In 1895-96 he was chief of the staff in the Mediterran- ean, and in 1897 commanded the naval contingent at the Diamond Jubilee, and three years ago he was selected as Controller of the Navy. Captain Jackson has seen thirty-six years' service and has also had a great deal to do with torpedoes. He was specially commended by the Admiralty for salvage work 801116 years ago.

The members of the above church were on Thursday engaged in a laudable effort to raise much-needed funds by means of a sale of work. The school-room in Wash- lane had been tastefully arranged for the purpose and the stalls were well laden with a pleasing variety of wares. The following discharged the duties of stall- holders. Refreshment stall: Mesdames Matthews, Fairhurst, P. Wilkinson, W. T. Wilkinson, and 'f. Albinson. Flower and Dairy stall : Mrs. F. W. Grounds, Misses E. Cliffe, E. Grounds, Ford, Wilkinson and Pearson. Fancy stall: Mesdames Samuel Albin- son, Harrison, Pearson and Isaac Wilkinson. Plain stall : Mesdames Adams, J. Albinson, Grounds, and Shakeshaft. Young Men's stall: Messrs. S. Albin- son, T. Albinson, J. Wilkinson, J. P. Conway, and E. F. Cliffe. Cake and Apron stall: Misses E. Smith, A. Caldwell, E. Wilson, and A. Ford. Mrs. Ziba Armitage opened the sale in the presence of a good attendance, including the Pastor (Rev. J. P. Matthews), Mr. F. Monks, Rev. J. S. Hughes, Mrs. Dodds, Messrs. S. Fearnley, J. Wilkinson, and W. T. Wilkinson.

The Rev. J. F. Matthews explained that it had become necessary, owing to the growth of the work they were trying to do in that little church, whose membership now numbered somewhere near 120, tkat the ordinary income of the church should be supplemented by an annual sale of work. Not that the weekly offering was small : as a matter of fact, on examination of the balance sheet of last year they were able to see that the offerings were considerably in advance of what they had been for some years past. Au additional means of raising funds was necessary, first, benuse the friends had made a very strenuous effort to increase the salary of the minister this year. Then, it was very desirable that something should be done to improve the appear- ance of the school by having it tastefully decorated. Eighteen months ago they added three class-rooms and they also needed re- painting and decorating. Mr. Matthews expressed his obligation to Mrs. Armitage for so readily con- senting to open the sale. The congregation was specially indebted to her owing to the fact that with her husband she would shortly leave the country for ft little while, and at present every afternoon was exceed- ingly precious. He extended to her a cordial welcome because he believed she was an old resident of Latch- ford, and that in the days gone by she and Mr. Armi- tage helpedlthe church to no little extent. They all knew that the citizens of Warrington and especially the members of the Congregational Churches held Mr. and Mrs. Armitage in high esteem for their good work. (Applause.) _

jars. Annitage briefly alluded to her former connec- tion with Latchford, remarking that she lived there twenty-one years. She was very glad to come to that sale and hear how the church work was progressing. It was not the first time bya good many that she had been in that schoolroom. (Hear. hear.) She hoped that every success would attend the efforts of the con,gregb.- tion.
On the motion of Mr. T. W. Wilkinson (secretary of the church), seconded by Mr. S. Fearnley,a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs. Armitage, and the busi- ness of the sale commenced.
The proceeds amount to .£33.

No moment is more terrible for a patient than when, after years of suffering, he is told at last that his disease is beyond all the skill of science to cure. Mr. Enoch Mills, a stirrup filer, of 43, Birmingham-steet, Walsall, endured the agony of piles for forty years; and when his career in various public capacities was being hampered by an apparently incurable affliction, Zam-Buk produced a cure that was almost miraculous. Mr. Mills, who is now GB years of age, isa well-known and well-respected resident of Walsall. He gave the following account of his sufferings to a " Wolverhamp • ton Express and Star "reporter It was the piles," he explained, 'Sand I had them for over forty years. During that time I scarcely knew what it was to have a good night's rest. It was the itching, and burnin,, and smarting, so that when T went to bed at night I could scarcely lie down. I used to get out of bed because of the pain, and walk about till I was quite cold. Reading an account of the success of Zam-Buk however, I sent for a free sample, and the effect of this, small as it wa; surprised me. I determined to give this wonderful balm a thorough trial. I am a different man altogether. I may add that Zam-Buk has been successful in several instances in which I have recommended it, and if anyone cares to write to me, I shall be pleased to give any information." The German Emperor at Home.—Parisians are much interested in the reminiscenCes of the Comtesse d'Eppinghoven, who has just published an account of her life and experiences at the German Court. The Comtesse was at one time lady-in-waiting to the Empress, and her revelations are anything but flattering to the Emperor. He has talents, she says, but they consist mainly of appropriating the bestworks of others which he palms off as his own. Thus when the Emperor conducts the Sunday service on his yacht, the sermon, we are told, is invariably written by a certain divine. His pictures, it is added, are the work of certain artists, and his flourishes in the minor arts, such as conducting the band, are the result of easily acquired lessons,learnt specially for the occasion. According to the Comtesse who throughout, frankly discloses names and full details, the Kaiser's speeches and his apparent versatile abilities are not original, and he is clever only in making the world believe that they are. In his personal char- acter, the Comtesse shows him to be imperious, high- handed, and fully convinced that he is a Heaven-sent ruler who can do no wrong. Roast turkey, it seems, is the Emperor's favoriteldish,and once when he received a particularly fine bird he went to the kitchen to super- intend its cooking. In his household the Emperor is described as being economical almost to meanness, and altogether the Comtesse's revelations, which bear the stamps of authority, can scarcely be pleasing to his Imperial Majesty. Lady Curzon's Recovery.—Lady Ulrica Baring, the recently.wedded wife of Lord Curzon's military Secre- tary Colonel Everard Baring, is going out to India., wherelshe will act as hostess for the Viceroy on his re- turn to the East. Happily Lady Curzon has sulicieutly recovered to enable her husband to return to India, but her convalescence is likely to be a long and tedious affair. Her recovery which was so long in doubt, is re- garded as little short of wonderful but it is hoped that in time she will be fully !restored to health. She has been removed from Weimer to Highcliffe Castle,not far from Christchurch in Hampshire, overlooking the sea, and the Isle of Wright. The district is noted for the purity of the air, and Lady Curzon proposes to stay there for about three months. After that she will go to the Riviera on a visit to Sir Edward and Lady Meet at the Chateau Malet. Heirs to Dukedoms.—The Duke and Duchess of Westminster have a little daughter Lady Ursula Grosvenor, now a pretty sturdy child of two years of age, and the birth of a son and heir no longer leaves the Duke's uncle, Lord Arthur Grosvenor, heir apparent to the dukedom. There are however, several ducal families without sons to succeed them. The Duke of Argyle's heir, for instance is his brother, Lord Archibald Campbell, and it is the same with the Dukes of Norfolk, Newcastle, Somerset, Roxburghe and Leinster, in each case a brother being heir apparent to the title, whilst the Duke of Devon- shire's heir is his nephew, Mr. Victor Cavendish, M.P. Heir to the Richest Peerage.—The King has announced his intention to stand sponsor for the son and heir of the Duke and Duchess of Westminster and the little Earl Grosvenor's christening presents are likely to be exceptionally numerous and costly. It would be difficult to say how many great aunts and uncles he possesses, to say nothing of nearer relatives, all of whom are interested in the birth Of a son and heir to the richest peerage in the kingdom. The oft-repeated story of Gros-veneur, and the descent of the family from Hugh Lupus, is a fable, but the Grosvenors are a very old Cheshire family, and trace their pedigree back for nearly 700 years. They owe their greatness and title to a marriage with the daughter of Farmer Alexander Davis, "The milkmaid of Ebury," who brought them the lands upon which a great part of fashionable London now stands. As a country baronet. the Duke of West- minster would not be very wealthy, but his London estates make him quite the richest peer, and if his son survives him he will be vastly more wealthy as the ' eases on the property fall in. 1 Old-Fashioned Parlour Games.—Nothing has sprung up as yet to take the place of ping-pong, and it is said that we are to go back to the round games of the old Victorian days for winter evening amusements. Such games took various forms, but mostly they relied upon a rather vulgar "catch" joke, to make the mirth flow freely. Some of the party sat round and thought of a word,whilst others were sent to cool their heels in the hall, and the more silly people were made to look, the better the party was said to go off. Sometimes cards were produced, and you were set to "beat your neigh- bour out of doors." or you were presented with paper and pencil and invited to write down answers to such questions as "where they met," and" what he said to her," and so on.—Then the confession Album was pro- duced, and you were required to rack your brains for suitable answers to a dozen or more silly questions. Old fashions are always being revived, and when nothing new presents itself—whether in dress "parlour tricks ' or anything.else,we are apt to go back to those ideas which did stenotyped service in our mothers and grandmothers' time. The Palmist's Re-appearance.—Palmistry as a pro- fession has at length been put down by the law, but though scotched, it has not been killed, and is re-appearing at some of the West End shops in London, where palmists have been engaged to tell the fortune, of customers. Nolcharge is, of course, made, but if you buya dozen pairs of gloves, or perhaps less, you can have your fortune told, it being expected that the increased i attraction for customers will more than pay the salary of the palmist. The clairvoyants are thu shewing their usual cleverness in enterprise, and no efforts on the part of the police seem able to prevent them from bouncing up again like the indiarubber balls The New Veilings.—Now winter has really arrive d veilings are in great demand, and the latest varieties cannot be said to enhance the beauty of wearers. The huge lace veils we had with us in the late spring and again ii, autumn proved disfiguring enough, but the new , fine black tulle veilings, showing elaborate designs carried out in chenille, are some degrees worse. The only possible way in which to don these veils—success- fully—is to drape them about the brim of the hat or toque, and let them fall at the back in the old "curtain" ' fashion. Of course it is still possible to obtain a plain • Russian net, or neatly spotted veiling, but those women who can do so should dispense with such an accessory entirely? It is better for the complexion, and— incidentally the pocket—to follow this rule. A Fashion to Avoid.—That-leading modistes are 1 doing their best to persuade their customers to return to the wasp waist,is'an indisputable fact,and many examples of this form of self torture may be seen on the stage . at the present moment. Happily the majority of women • have borne to regard health first, putting fashion in the 1 second place, and all such individuals will refuse to be t laced up until their noses become red, to say nothing of . the permanent injury such treatment must inflict upon the health. Three store years have passed since the 'wasp waist last reigned supreme and in those days a seventeen or eighteen inch waist was quite an ordinary measurement. An Old World Revival.—The long box-pleated ‘ poloaise of cloth, worn over a skirt and bodice of i velvetem, is having considerable vogue, the pleats of 1 cloth being continued above the waist, showing the ' velveteen in between. Where renovations are concerned I z this mode is likely to prove a boon, as it is ! possible to bring a middle aged or elderly velvet gown ; quite up to date by means of the polonaise and at the ' same time hide the parts rubbed or worn. Concerning Ribbons.—Ribbon manufacturers should be doing well,for the toilette showing no such ornament- ationin some shape or form, is rare indeed. Many elaborate evening gowns boast the most exquisite Iribbon embroideries,a form of trimming greatly favored by the Princess of Wales. Goffered ribbons too produce an excellent effect, on airy fairy dinner or ball gowns, also dainty evening blouses. Then we haJe ribbons shaded, ribbons shewing pompadour effects, plaid ribbons, spotted ribbons, stripped ribbons, &a. &c. in widths varying from the Lilliputian to the broad sash varieties. The woman who cannot find ribbons to suit her particular requirements most indeed be difficult to please.
MADGE.

div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.
ECCLES v. STOCKTON HEATH IST.

Played at Eccles last Saturday. The game opened with Stockton attacking strongly, and Longdin scored a good goal. Before half-time play was fairly even but Stockton obtained a second goal. In the second half Stockton had things their own way, and scored four more goals before the whistle finally sounded. Final score :—Stockton, six; Eccles, nil.
WARRINGTON_ ROYAL v,. ALTRINCHAM ST.
MARGARET'S A.

Played on Saturday on the ground of the former The game was very fast and interesting,and both teams worked hard to win. At half time St. Margaret's were leading by 1--0. In the second half the bomesters pressed. Result: Altrincham St. Margaret's A, 4; Warrington Royal, 2.

Undaunted by five degrees of frost, 19 members of the Serpentine Club undressed in the open air at the Serpentine on Wednesday morning to contest a 55 yards race.. The water was at its lowest temperature this season, and had a perceptible effect upon the swimmers. Otto Mayer, a merchant who it was stated was also a German Count was in London,to-day remanded charged With stealing a Pair of valuable field glasses from Mr. Max Mrdtich, a manufactnring draper, who had be- friended him by lending him money. •

div.head: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

Just now most of us have several, if nof many, little social functions of one kind ol another in view, for there is always quite azi gay season just before Christmas, followed. of course, .by the annual family dinners, etc.. which extend into the New Year, for which. as yet, it is too early to discuss the question of dress. Those of us who live in or near town require a serviceable frock for restaurant wear, for nowadays the cheap but well. cooked and served dinner has become quite an institution, and there are many people wile find it more convenient to entertain their friends in this manner than to risk the un- certainty of a meal served at home. For these occasions there is nothing so useful of course as a black gown, and since the restaurant evening meals entered so much

into !the !everyday life' of the suburban matron and maid she has wisely relinquished the decollete gown and wears one which is high to the• throat, although in many instances the yoke and collar are of transparent net or filmy lace. There are some evening frocks which can be worn with or without a yoke, and these are the most useful in such circum- stances for the yokes can be quickly tacked into place or in some instances buttons and loops are employed. In this way a dress of black net embroidered with glittering sequins will, with a large black pictt7e hat and a fur or cloth coat, do duty for restaurant wear, while with these accessories and the yoke discarded it may be worn at a dance or a private_ dinner,

- My first sketch shows an evening gown of charming design which can be worn in either of the circumstances described. It is made of soft silk with the trained skirt finished by double flounces caught by rosettes of black velvet ribbon. The waist is finished by a band of wide chine ribbon of a blurred floral design which is tied in a double looped bow at the back with two long sash ends falling down almost to the flounces trimmed at the ends by some silk fringe which matches in hue the leading colours employed in the floral pattern. The bodice is draped with a soft fichu of lace. which also forms the long frills covering the arms. The style is simple yet charming and offers one or two hints to those girls who want to make a last season's dress do secondary gprvice for another winter. The sash and

div.head: CHIC BLOUSE.
div.p: A CHIC BLOUSE.

the fichu, sleeves, etc., are all within the powers of a home worker to make, thereby Leaving more to be spent on the fresh evening toilette on which she has set her heart. Chiffon is much used for ball gowns, but it is not a fabric which can be depended on to wear for any length of time, for its beauty Lies in its 'fragility. Japanese fine silk to which a crepe de chine finish has been im- parted is also a favourite material and looks especially well in some of the fashionable tones of brown. My second illustration shows a chic blouse in which the popular tones of colour are employed. The blouse itself is of a beautifu? ;olden brown crepe de chine over yellow silk finished with a series of smart little bows of dark orange red velvet fastened with pale gold buckles. It is made with a long yoke edged with a little passementerie, which also finishes the cuffs. The style is very simple and could easily be made at tiome from a good pattern but it is one which will meet, I feel sure, with general admiration ind is also so free from any sort of exaggera- tion that it can be worn with or without a :oat, which at this seakn of the year is a quality not to be despise 4, for wraps of some sort or other are a necessity. It would look very well for wear with a brown skirt ex- pressed in cream voile over pale yellow silk. with orange velvet bows and black buckles.
A SMART COSTUME.

The blouse in all its simplicity and likewise its elaborateness, becomes daily more closely endeared to feminine affections and its iemise will certainly not occur this season. My last sketch depicts a very smart cloth costume enhanced by narrow fanciful beard. ing. It is 'made with a basque which extends for a short distance below the soft kid bell which confines the waist. The revers and rolling collar are cut in one and are open tc show a dainty blouse with its completion of a dainty collar and neatly knotted silk tie. It is worn with a hat with a soft beaver brim and a crown of drawn mirroir velvet. The muff is of the fashionable large flat Granny shape and is of velvet bordered with flat bands of fur while a bunch of Neapolitan violets are fastened in. the centre of the velvet. In brown mauve, or even dark red, this would make an ideal costume for im- mediate wear, only requiring the addition of a fur necklet on cold days. The skirt should be cut so as to clear the ground all round for fashion does not smile upon the trailing skirt for wear out of doors for those who seek their pleasure or their business on foot. The long fussy skirt is reserved for house wear, in which Zircumstance it is certainlyAseen at its best.

div.head: ROTE
div.p: THE ROTE
'LAND.

The visit of the King and Queen ot Portugal has been a most brilliant success, and the most satisfactory part of it all is the announcement that another of King Edward's famous arbitration treaties was duly signed at Windsor prior to the State Banquet. With the exception of the visit to London Ind the luncheon at the Guildhall, which was only clouded by fog, the: whole of last week was spent at Windsor in a round of sport and amusement and, as is always the case, King Edward proved himself a host of truly regal magnificence. Unfortunately His Majesty owing to a slight strain was per- sonally debarred from taking part in the shooting in Windsor Park, but King Carlos a.nd the Prince of Wales, who are the two best royal shots in Europe, annexed an enormous bag and had splendid sport. Each day, with the exception of Thursday, there was a big shoot, and in the evenings there were splendid entertainments in the Castle, Nit-. Tree's Company appearing on Thursday evening and Mr. Lewis Waller on Saturday evening, while on Friday after dinner there was a grand concert. -Madame Clara Butt sang with her husband, Mr. Kennerly Rum- ford, and Madame Giachetti and Signor Anselmi, of the San Carlos Opera House Company, now giving a season at Covent Garden, completed a striking programme. Sunday was, of course, spent quietly, the King and Queen of Portugal attending Mass in Windsor, and on Monday the visit to Windsor concluded. Their Majesties, after bidding farewell to King Edward and Queen Alexandra, proceeded by special train to Chatsworth, where they are the guests of the Duke and Duchess of Devonshire, who have so often entertained our King and Queen. The shooting at Chatsworth is some of the finest in the country. and King Carlos till 3 again shown himself in fine form with his gun. This visit concludes on Friday, when the King and Queen come up to London to spend the week-end at Bucking- ham Palace, whioh has been placed at their disposal by King Edward. Next week they go to Welbeck, another of the great show houses of the country, where they will be the guests of the Duke and Duchess of Portland.

div.p: THE FRENCH MINISTER OF WAR.

followed the Government majority sank to two. So high did feeling run on the subject lhat General Andre was actually assaulted in the Chamber by M. Syveton with serious ulti and the debate ended in a riot and zevcral duels. The most important outcome ha; been the resignation of General Andre, who handed in his portfolio -:-at a Cabinet Council last week, and, though his colleagues pro.ested their grief, there ,is little doubt that it is a relief .and an addition of strength to M. Coombes. He has appointed M. Berteaux to succeed General Andre, and the election has met with approval on all sides. The new Minister is a millionaire, a Socialist, an old Parliamentary hand, a military expert, and a glutton for work, so it will be strange indeed if he does not make a success in his new role. He is young, too, being only just about fifty, and a business man, being a member of the Bourse by profession. For twenty-two years he has represented Versailles without a break, an he was chosen chairman of the important War Budget Committee. He has a charming house in the Champs Elysees, which his big fortune allows him to make a great centre of hospitality, but, apart from it, for himself and his personality alone he is a highly popular man and a delightful companion. Best of all, he has warm feelings of friendship towards this country, and, though War Minister, he is an 'advocate a International Arbitration. Alto- gether the appointment is a very satisfactory me.

the sphere of farcical comedy, and the final selection fen upon Mr. James Welch, the well-known comedian, who has run his own company tor some years. " Jim " Welch, as he is familiarly known, was originally, in a char:. tered accountant's office in Liverpool, but always had a desire to go on the stage, so with his present brother-in-law, Mr. Richard Le Gallienne, he came up to town and obtained an engagement in Mr. Wilson Barrett's company. Feeling, however, that his bent was comedy, Mr. Welch, after having gained his experience, gave notice and struck out in a ,new line. But in ad- dition to comedy he appeared in the Ibsen productions, of which he was a keen sup- porter, and the early George Bernard Shaw plays. After numerous successes he started his own company and produced "My Artful Valet" at Terry's, and, later on, "The New Clown," which caught on at once. In it Mr. Welch appeared with a humorous donkey called "Ping-Pong," who accom- panies him to Drury Lane. His conception of a Drury Lane part will be watched with great interest, and it is certain to be witty and polished.
EARL GROSVENOR.

One of the babies in the world is the little Earl Gro:Nencr who was born last week at Eaton Hall and will in due course succeed to 1.11:t dukedom of Westminster and the vast rent roll it carries. with it.. How- ever, that day tthould be in the Very distant future aishi father, the present duke, is

This great estate came to the Grosvenor family through marriage with a Miss Davis, daughter of a dairyman who owned the farm which has long since been 'turned into squares and streets. The present duke was the grandson of the first duke and succeeded to the title in 1900, while serving on Lord Miler's staff in South Africa. His father, the late Earl Grosvenor, died many years ago in the infancy of his son, who was known as Viscount Belgrave. His Marriage was full of romance. As boy and girl, he and Miss Shelagh Cornwallis- West were sweethearts, but the late duke would not allow the engagement and sent his grandson to South Africa. Immediately upon succeeding to the title he returned home on lea‘. a, and the , engagement was officially annowneed. The wedding took place three years, ago last February, and in the following year a daughter, Lady Ursula Grosvenor, was born. Now two years later comes the desired son and heir. _ .

div.head: T H 1114 FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: T H 1114 FREE CHURCHES.
WELSH EDUCATION CRISIS.

Among Free Churchmen in Wales the Edu- cation controversy continues to overshadow all other public interests. The slight reverse the Welsh Nationalist Party suffered at Cardiff during the recent elections does not count for much. Cardiff, like all other seaports, has a mixed population, and is probably the town least representative of national opinion in Wales. Its verdict merely serves to throw into stronger relief the unexampled unanimity which prevails everywhere else. Meanwhile the Church Party are still in grave difficulty. It is clear at once, says a writer in the Iree Church Chronicle, that even if the Voluntary Schools were given a share of the rates they would still have to face heavy financial responsibilities which none of them foresaw when they welcomed the Act as bringing them salvation. In all the Welsh counties, the authorities are quite rightly in- sisting upon the Voluntary School buildings being put into a proper state of repair before their financial transference to the public authority. This involves in some cases the erection of new buildings and in others expen- sive repairs and reconstructing which in each diocese will run to some thousands of pounds. The Welsh Bishops are appealing for help to their friends in England, but so far there has been no very marked response.

div.head: PROBLEM OF THE UNEMPLOYED.
div.p: THE PROBLEM OF THE UNEMPLOYED.

Everywhere the attention of authorities is being directed to the problem of the unemployed. There is a growing tendency on the part of municipal authorities to tackle this great question. Free Church Councils in some parts have also given their attention to the subject. The Leeds Free Church Council has appointed a Committee to make inquiries in connection with a municipal register open in that city. This Committee has asked 100 churches to make reports as to how far those associated in any way were suffering. It is intended to link up the stronger churches with the weaker to further help the unemployed. Some of the churches in the suburbs have no claims upon them, whilst others will soon be unable to meet the many they will have. In other towns besides Leeds this idea might be taken up. The problem of the unemployed is becoming more and more acute in Manchester. The great Wesleyan Mission there is doing a vast work in coping with the crowds of homeless people who stroll the streets at night. Probably there are few Free Church agencies doing so much in this direction as Mr. Collier's large organisation.

div.head: PRESIDENCY FOR DR. lIORTON.
div.p: A PRESIDENCY FOR DR. lIORTON.

Dr. Horton, who is even now still feeling the effects of his eye trouble, becomes President of the National Free Church Council in March next year. It is not anticipated that his health will permit of his engaging in such a large itinerary as the Rev. F. B. Meyer was able to undertake, but it is anticipated that large meetings will be held in seven or eight centres in the Provinces which representatives from all the local Councils will have facilities for attend- ing. These Conferences are to be of a somewhat special character, details of which are to be announced later. That Dr. Horton arouses the respectful attention of the Free Church world, and, indeed, of the entire religious public, is shown by the fact that his new book "The Open Secret: A Manual of Devotion," which he wrote during hie illness, and which is published by the National Free Church Council, has already demanded a second edition. In this further issue Dr. Horton makes some remarks on criticisms of the book.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.

At the recent municipal elections, although the Education question was not at all pro- minent, Free Church organisations were able to exert a sensible influence upon the conditions. In some instances, Free Church candidates were run, but in most cases the Councils suc- ceeded in calling attention to the importance of electing men who pay regard to gublic morality. The questions of drink and educa- tion were also urged. All along the line the elections have turned more favourably to Free Church inteliests, though, of course, there have been one or two set-backs.
DR. MCLAREN AT MENTONE.

Dr. McLaren, the venerable Baptist preacher, has gone to Mentone to escape the English winter. Now that he has dropped regular pulpit work he is beginning to enjoy his leisure, and the opportunities he has of travelling, which he never had before, are • keenly appreciated. Dr. McLaren is to preside at the all-world Baptist Council next year. This is expected to be a most important event.

div.head: GIPSY SMITH.
div.p: GIPSY SMITH.

Gipsy Smith has now thoroughly entered into his Autumn Mission campaign. He com- menced with a splendid mission at Woolwich. and has conducted another successful mission at Harrogate. He has found time to revise the interesting diary of his tour in South Africa, and this will shortly be published by the National Free Church Council, under the title of "A Mission of Peace: Evangelistic Triumphs in South Africa.' The volume will be illus- trated by many new photographs of incidents connected with the tour.
NEW YOUNG MEN'S WORK.

There is every indication that the new work for young men which the National Free Church Council is initiating will meet with success. During the mission of Gipsy Smith at Woolwich a special meeting for young men was held. Gipsy Smith presided, and was supported by a number of local ministers. Mr. G. S. Hirst, the Acting Secretary of the National Auxiliary, attended and gave an address describing the aims and objects of the Auxiliary. Ninety-four of those present gave in their names to form an Auxiliary for Woolwich. At Islington the work has been taken up. At the annual meeting at which Rev. F. B. Meyer was present, and which was addressed by Mr. G. S. Hirst, an Auxiliary was formed. Auxiliaries have been formed at Cheshunt, Halesowen, and other places.
WORK AMONGST GIRLS.

Whilst the National Free Church Council is giving attention to Young Men's work the in- terest in the Girl's Guild :Movement is being well sustained. In the Free Church Chronicle for December there is a splendidly illustrated article on the Guild Home at Bristol. This home is practically the best ever erected in connection with the Girl's Guild Movement. The freehold of the house has been secured, and although a mortgage was taken. the home was opened without debt. Mr. T. J. Lennard, the Liberal candidate for Bristol, generously contributed the whole of the furniture.

div.head: FREE CHURCHES ABROAD.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES ABROAD.

It is plain that the Free Church movement will soon belt the globe. A Free Church cause has been established at Cairo, Egypt—Baptists, Congregationalists, Primitive Methodists, and Wesleyans uniting. An appeal has been made by the Rev. T. Cooper, the pastor, to all English and American tourists passing through Cairo to attend the services which are at present held in the German School.

FREE CHURCH TEMPERANCE POLICY'. It is the fixed determination of Free Church- men not to allow the Licensing Act to con- tinue as it stands for a longer period than can be helped. The Temperance and Organising Committees of the National Free Church Council,have had the matter of a Free Church temperance policy before them, and a sub- committee is WOW at work considering various points. A resolution is to be submitted to the next meeting of th.e.General Committee meet- ing at Bristol early in December.

Dr. George Vivian Poore died at Andover on Thurs- day evening. The deceased. who WAS born at Andover in 1843, was the author of " Essays on Jurisprudence" and other works. He was medical attendant to King Edward in 1872. The deceased was unmarried. Professor Sir William J. Sinclair, M.A., M.B. (Aberdeen), of Manchester, has been elected chairman of the Universities of Glasgow and Aberdeen Conserva- tive and Liberal Unionist Association and of the Com- mittee of Graduates for promoting the candidature of Professor William R. Smith, M.D., for the Parliamentary representation of the Universities.
