div.head: DRAUGHTS. I
div.p: DRAUGHTS. I

An important tournament for the draughts champion- ship of the Manchester and District League, and a hand- some silver cup presented by the proprietors of the "Manchester Weekly Times," will commence to-day at the County Forum Hotel, Market-street, Manchester. International players are debarred from entering, but otherwise the tourney is open to all players within a radius of 20 miles round Manchester. The list of entries numbers over 50, and includes two well-known Warrington players, Messrs. W. Tomkinson and J. Roberts.

div.head: = SIMULTANEOUS DRAUGHTS PLAYING.
div.p: = SIMULTANEOUS DRAUGHTS PLAYING.

An exhibition of simultaneous draughts playinc, was given by Mr. Frank Dunne, last Saturday evening at the rooms of the Golborne-street, (Baptist) Young Mons' Club, and brought together a goodly number of the Warrington League players. Mr. Dunne contested games on 20 boards at once, against as many opponents, moving quickly from board to board. Play never flagged, and the interest of the players and spectators was maintained for upwards of two hours, when the score was declared as follows :—Mr. Dunne wins 36; draws,: ; losses 2. The draws were scored by Messrs.W. Ogden and T. Albinson ; and the wins by Messrs. H. Richardson and W. Massey, members of Cairo Street team (the cupholders). These players both contested two games, losing the first and winning the second. A small charge was made for admittance, for the benefit of the League funds.

Some Aspects of Social Evolution. The above subject was dealt with by Mr. A. J. Jolley in a lecture which he gave last night at a meet- ing•of the Warrington Society held at the Old Academy. Mr. Jolley gave an historical sketch of the development of man, and spoke of the progress which had been made in the past, and of the progress which must be made in the future—progress on the lines of a combination of new scientific truths with old Chris tian doctrines.

LORD LONDONDERRY PROTECTIONIST has been telling us that LOGIC. the General Election must come some time or other, and that it cannot :very well be post- poned beyond the year after next. The Chancellor of the Exchequer has expressed his surprise that an Opposition should be so " childish" as to demand a dissolution from al Ministry which still commands a majority in the House of Commons. According to the " Times," it would be just as un- reasonable for the constituents of a Member of Parliament to call on him to resign his seat because he had ceased to represent their views. Well, that is precisely what constituents do when they think the circumstances justify it. If a member suddenly professes opinions which are certainly net those of the majority that elected him, it is the unquestionable right of that majority to demand his resignation. There is an unwritten law of good faith, moreover, which should prompt him to take the sense of the constituency on his new attitude. A Member of the House of Com- mons is not a delegate; but he cannot be said to represent the constituency fairly when, in spite of an acknowledged change of views, he declines to ask for a fresh mandate. The application of this principle to the position of a Ministry is so well understood that Mr. BALFOUR. and his friends are constantly laying stress on his resolve not to press his new Fiscal Ipolicy on the present Parliament. They seem to [think this de- vice relieves him from any obligation to take the sense of tho electorate without further delay. But all the time they are advocating the new policy with all their might. They set uplcandidates to champion it at by-elections, andlwhen these candi- dates are in nearly every case decisively beaten, they profess, as the "Times " does, complete indifference to these repeated proofs that the Government does not possess the confidence of the country. The absurdity of this profession is patent, because [everybody knows that if the Government candidates had been successful in a few trials of strength Mr. BALFOUR. would hay dissolved months ago in the belief that th. country was with him. The real reason why he postpones the dissolution is that he entertains the opposite belief. Lack of:candour is the note of all the Ministerial polemics. We are blandly assured that Mr. BALFouR remains a Free Trader; and the assur- ance, strange to say, seems good enough for such a resolute Free Trader as Lord GEORGE HAMILTON. He has announced his conviction that Mr. BALFOUR is unalterably opposed to the policy of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. We are driven to assume that he is taken in by the sort of evasion of which we had an edifying specimen in the " Times " "The country is not asked to abandon Free Trade, which, as Mr. AUSTEN CHAMBERLAIN observes, it has never had. Still less is it asked to adopt Protection, which the Govern- ment, at any rate, has been careful to declare undesirable if it were possible, and impossible if it were desirable." But " the Government, at any rate," accepts the support of Mr. CHAPLIN and his friends, who are strongly of opinion that Protec- tion is both possible and desirable. It accepts the support of the Tariff Reformers, who are engaged upon the construction of a "scientific' tariff which is to show us that Protection is both `desir- able and practicable. To say we have never had Free Trade is simply a juggle, :by which Lord GEORGE HAMILTON should be the last person to be deceived. "What the nation is really asked to do," says the "Times," "is to adhere to the principle of free exchange, but to recognise that, as there are two parties to every transaction, there can be no free exchange so long as one of them imposes artificial restrictions so severe as to be in many cases prohibitive, and in all slightly embarrassing." It is droll to find this parade of novelty for an argument which was ' employed by all Protectionists sixty years ,ago. The

answer then is the answer now, backed by the experience of those sixty years; namely, that the restrictions of protective duties at this era would embarrass our trade far more than the protective duties imposed by the foreigner. We cannot lower those duties, says the "Times," ex cept by making our rivals feel that Protection "does not pay." In other words, we are to entar on a war of tariffs with a light heart; and we are to do it not as Protectionists, but as Free Traders. If Lord GOORGE HAMILTON likes this application of the blessed formula, "Let us retaliate," we can only wish him joy, and wonder at his logic.

Free Trade has been given a fine fillip in Warrington this week. On Saturday the iron- workers pronounced themselves unswerving adherents to the grand old cause while the Liberals of Grappenhall also re-affirmed their staunchness in support of Mr. King, the candidate for their division. On Monday the women liberals were strongly: en: evidence, while last night, the progressive and essentially Free Trade forces of Warrington assembled in large numbers at Parr Hall to welcome once again that fine old stalwart,Henry Broadhurst M.P. The ironworkers were privileged to listen to a couple of sound fighting speeches, from Mr. Cox, their general secretary and Mr. A. H. Crosfield. No one could be more determined in his opposition to Mr. Chamberlain's Protectionist fallacies than Mr. Cox and the weight of his intellect and voice must tell powerfully in the struggle which is fast coming to a head. Among the ironworkers—an intelligent and hard headed body of toilers—the word of the general secretary is law, or very near it, and Mr. Cox holds this unique and flattering position not by force, but by reason of the respect in which he is held. When he says that "it was because they were not going to be placed in the power of monopolies and trust magnates. . . . that they were going to fight the question of Protec- tion until its promoters were forced to drop it," those promoters may take it for granted that notwithstanding honeyed words in the ear of the worker about more work and increased wages, the solid vote of the ironworkers will be cast for Free Trade.

It was a great compliment to Mr. L. H. Cros- field—and one that indicates the determination of these men on the fiscal policy—to ask him again to join Mr. Cox on the platform and give an address To the ironworkers as a body in Warrington Mr. Crosfield is first and foremost the Free Trade candidate, and their support is assured. The opportunity was one that Mr. Crosfield made the most of in a fair and reasonable way. He was not on this occasion, the advocate of Liberalism per but the Free Trader and Progressive with deep-rooted idoas as to the seriousness of the situation for his hearers. Wide personal experi- ence in the export trade gives Mr. Crosfield an authoritative position as regards the fiscal policy, and the fact that he was completely in accord with Mr. Cox was a significant point not lost sight of by men, who, a large number of them probably con- sidered the two speakers as representative of Capital and Labour.

By their services on behalf of the progressive cause the members of the Women's Liberal Asso- ciation have earned the right to be counted a valuable asset of the party in Warrington. A particularly eventful year which has witnessed useful and earnest work was under review at the annual meeting on Monuay& It is distinctly grati- fying to see such activity displayed as the time for the election draws nearer, and Mr. Arthur Crosfield can rely upon a cordial backing from the organization, especially having regard to his sound vie ss upon the justice of women's suffrage. The great undertaking of the year has been the successful bazaar in the Parr Hall and the enthusiasm with which the ladies entered into a project entailing much sacrifice of time will be long and gratefully remembered. We are pleased to know that the persuasive powers of members of the Association have been effectively exercised at the recent municipal elections,and the progressive candidates who secured notable victories owed much to the willing help of the lady workers. A new departure in the shape of frequent meetings for educational purposes is shortly to be embarked upon, and we make bold to prophesy a career of increased usefulness for the Association under the continued able presid- ency of Mrs. Armitage.

The School Attendance Committee, think some of our local educationists, have been too liberal in the granting of special exemptions from attend- ance at the elementary schools. A warm discussion was engendered at the meeting of the Education authority on Monday, but we feel that the result has been to justify in a great. measure the School Attendance Committee's policy. On the grounds of humanity, the members have considered it their duty to release certain children from school and allow them to render some little help to struggling families by following "beneficial employment," even though the legal conditions as to age and attendances have not been fulfilled. We have every sympathy with. the effort to raise the educational standard, but it is easily conceivable that useless hardship may . be inflicted by an insistence upon a strict compliance with the letter of the law in every case. Food before education i is, we fear, the pressing 'red n many:homes. We would, however, emphasise the necessity for a thorough investigation of the circumstances of every applicant so as to prbvent any suspicion of laxity or an abuse of the committee's sympathy.

On the discussion regarding the new school to ,be erected in Orford Avenue, Alderman Bennett introduced the question of:swimming accommoda- tion for the scholars, but obtained practically no support. Even the Education Committee is be- ginning to realize the necessity for economy, and swimming baths for the schools proposed to be built in the near future are apparently out of the ' question. It is unfortunate if the financial position 'of the town ih such that so excellent an innovation cannot even be seriously considered, but we will not go so far as to advocate the carry- ing out of Alderman Bennett's proposal much as we are in sympathy with it. Still we should like to know what the additional cost would be for a swimming bath in connection with such a school as the one to be erected. It is interesting to learn that the Stockport Education Committee have already decided to provide swimming baths in con- nection with their new schools, for the erection of which £7,000 are to be spent. Plans for the first of the schools—one to accommodate 900 scholars —at £9,998 with a swimming bath 45ft by 22ft, seem to us to be economically designed. S tock- port is certainly leading the way boldly, and we hope Warrington will find it possible to proceed on similar lines.

I CO NM MIX - Users of the leafy high-roads of Cheshire will have to resign themselves to the idea of sharing the pleasant thoroughfares with the cars of the light-railway. We understand that the construc- tion of the Warrington to Northwich light railway will be commenced next year, and the preliminaries to an application for power to qonstruct a similar line between Warrington and Knutsford have already been completed. In the minds of cyclists and motorists there has always been something almost sacred about the Knuts- ford-road, and a light railway will not, at first thought, be welcomed. But we are glad to assure our readers that the proposed Warrington- Knutsford line will not cut up the beloved surface of the roadway. There is sufficient space along- side to accommodate the railway,and the metalled portion of the road will probably not be touched. A private company for the construction of this line has been formed locally, and judging by the men who are interested financially and otherwise the business of the concern should not lack energy and enterprise.

Why should not Warrington have a Nurses' Sunday? The congregations at our places of worship willingly subscribe to the Infirmary funds on Hospital Sunday and we believe an annual appeal on behalf of the District Nursing Associa- tion would call forth a generous response. Is it

too much to ask those who are responsible for the finances of our churches, embarashed as they may be with many pressing calls, to set apart at least one collection for the benefit of so deserving an institution? The funds were never more urgently needed than they ars at present and we feel sure that no one reading the review of seven years' work published in another column will deny that the Association has a just claim upon public support. At several chnrchee donations are already raised, but the total is very inadequate for a town of Warrington's size. A united effort is asked for and will, we sincerely hope, be soon organized.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

The Perjury Case. This week Mr. R. Pierpoint, M.P. has presented to the Home Secretary the petition from Warrington in favour of a reduction of the sentence of the man Wood, convicted of perjury, at the Chester Assizes. The petition contained about 8,000 signatures, and a reply has been received to the effect that the petition is being fully considered.

St. Mary's Dramatic Society. We draw attention to the announcement of the series of performances of the fine old drama "Belphegor " which will be given in the Parr Hall December 6th to December 10th. The St. Mary's Society has had such a run of success during the past four years in catermg for lovers of the drama that we anticipate that further honours will be reaped. The object of the performances is one that commends itself forcibly to Warringtonians and we know of no more deserving cause than the District Nursing Association. It has many claims on our charity and we wish the present effort to wipe out an adverse balance every success.

Tne Iron and Steel Institute.--4„wzr.„ Sixty memeber of the Iron and Steel Institute who have been visiting America to study the methods of " manufacture arrived at Liverpool by the Oceanic on Thursday after an exceedingly rough passage. The Idelegates'included Mr. C. E. Bunch aud Mr. T. Ather- ton (of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, Warrington), who have had a most interesting tour. Mr. 11. Owen (of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co.), a third War- rington representative, has not yet returned. Last evening an" Examiner " reporter waited upon Mr. Bunch who, however, was not prepared to give his impressions of American methods and enter- 'prise in this important industry at the present stage. He said that Mr. Atherton and he had visited all the liron and steel works in the States, and had travelled about 10,000 miles. They had the pleasure of seeing President Rooseveldt at the Whitehouse, as well as Mr. Carnegie. FOR SMART DESIGNS in Ladies', Gents' and Children's Boots in Chrome and Box Calf for Winter Wear see Booth & Son, Sole Agents for the Ladies' White Heather Brands.-29, BUTTERMARKET ST.-- Advt. Hospital Sunday. The annual meeting of the Warrington Hospital Sunday Committee was held at the Infirmary yester- day afternoon. The Rev. Canon Willis presided and there were also present the Revs. John Yonge, Father Wilson, W. Bracecamp, E. C. E. Carleton, G. G. Briggs, H. V. Pigot and H. Cook, and Messrs. H. Monks, and A. J. Jolley (hon. sec.) Mr. Jolley gave his annual report which showed that the collections for the year just ended amounted to "£298 is. 7d., as against £304 ss. 6d. the previous year. Of that sum £195 135., was collected in Warrington and £lO5 14s. id. in the outside districts.—lt was unanimously decided to hold Hospital Sunday next year on March 26th.—Mr. A. J. Jolley was re-elected hon. secretary of the committee. A suggestion was made by Mr. F. Monks that the collections upon some Sunday in autumn should be set aside for the District Nursing Association but several difficulties in the way of the proposal being mentioned nothing was done in the matter.

Warrington Band of Hope Union. On Thursday evening in the Winmarlegh Cafe the above union held a social which was attended by about 140 Band of Hope workers and friends, who were received by Mrs. Simpson, Mrs. J. S. Hughes and Mrs. Dunnico. The Rev. J. S. Hughes presided. The musical part of the programme was contributed by Mrs. Monks, Miss Gibson, Miss Plinston, Mr. A. Grounds, Mr. H. 0. Hughes and Ur. F. Sherburn. Mr. G. Whitfield gave a recitation. Mr. A. F. Edwards, Lecture-Demonstrator, Owens College, Manchester, and evening school lecturer of the Lanca- shire and Cheshire Band of Hope Union, delivered an address, with chemical experiments, on "Some Alcohol Fallacies." Refreshments having been partaken of, a. vote of thanks moved by Mr. T. Dale and seconded by Mr. F. Gandy was accorded. A pleasant and success- ful social terminated with games. The musical part of the programme was arranged by the newly-formed Ladies' Auxiliary,of which the secretary is Miss Gibbs SEE OUR NEW DESIGNS in the Gents' Healtherie, Waukeezie, Globe and "G" brands of Boots for Winter wear.—Boom 64 SON, 29, Buttermarket St. —Advt.

South Lancashire Memorial Fund. ' With a view to making some substantial financial addition to the fund which is being raised for the erection of a memorial to the members of the South Lancashire Regiment who fell in South Africa, a foot- ball match between Crosfield's team and a tear of Veterans, was played on Saturday on the Wash-lane ground. Mr. A. H. Crosfield kicked off before an attendance of nearly 400 spectators, and the League side playing against a stiff breeze was soon repulsed by the Veterans. A corner was forced but nothing accrued and the subsequent clearance was followed by Dunbobbin racing into the Veterans' quarters- Five minutes later the Vets were seen hovering round the opposing goal, and from a centre by G. R. Cros- field, Evans scored. The locals were still kept on the defensive and after some 7wild shooting by the forwards the ball was netted. Interval : Veterans two goals to nothing. On resuming,the League team took up the attack, and after some neat passing the wing man netted the ball, following with a second a few minutes later. This roused the Veterans and on the re-start G-. R. Crosfield made a fine run along the touch and centred, but he received no support. The locals were soon again attacking and E. Ball getting possession notched a third point. Soon after 0. Dickenson scored a fourth. Final: Crosfields, four goals ; Veterans, two goals.

Tramped through Warrington. A tramp who entered Northwich Workhouse last week was on Monday certified to be suffering from small-pox, and was at once removed to hospital. The man had tramped through from Warrington. GREAT SALE OF BOOTS AND SHOES 110 W on UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt. Sudden Death. Shortly after nine o'clock on Saturday evening, Mrs. Elizabeth Rogers aged 74 years, a well-known stall holder in the Warrington Market, who resided in King-street, feeling unwell, left the market, and on reaching home sat on a chair. Shortly after, she fell -to the floor and expired immediately. 'Visit of" The Merrions." An entertainment was given in the Parr Hall on Tuesday evening by the well-known entertainers "The Merrions,' in aid of the funds of the Legh street brass band. Humorous songs, trios, and sketches were contributed, and a first class entertain- ment was provided, the audience expressing by their applause their appreciation of the efforts of their entertainers.

GREAT SALE OF BOOTS AND SHOES now on UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt. Sankey Harriers Sankey Harriers visited St. Helens 'on Saturday, and hod an inter-club run with the St. Helens Sacred Heart Harriers. Sankey chose a run through, and won easily by 22 points. Details: —Sankey: Joseph Riley, 1; R. Gibson, 3; S. Winstanley, 4; John Riley, ;G. Gibson, 7 ; L. Edwardson, 9; total, 30. Sacred Heart : P. Connaughton, 2 ; J. McGowan, 5; J. Flynn, ,8; J. Caldwell, 11; F. Briordy, 12; E. Glennon, 14; total, 52.

Personal. The Rev. A. S. Cameron, senior curate at the Warrington Parish Church, has accepted the living of Weston, Lincolnshire, offered him by the Lord Chancellor. During his connection with the Parish Church Mr. Cameron has made a large circle of 'friends, and the news of his forthcoming departure will be generally regretted. He has done a great deal of active and useful-work not only in connection with the parish itself, but also in connection with St. Clement's Mission, and there is no doubt that his loss will be greatly felt.

div.head: H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF Toncs.-63, SANKEY STREET, Warrington.—Advt. Proposed Light Railway From Warrington to Knutsford.
div.p: H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF Toncs.-63, SANKEY STREET, Warrington.—Advt. Proposed Light Railway From Warrington to Knutsford.

As we briefly announced last week an application to the Light Railway Commissioners is to be. made for power to construct a light railway from Warring- ton to Knutsford. The Rae will commence at Latch- ford, near the termination of the Warrington tram lines, and will run to Canute-square, Knutsford, through Thelw-all, Lymm, and High Legh. Tw continuations will carry the line to the Knutsford Station and the goods yard connected with the station. The railway will be worked by electricity, or such other motive power as the Board of Trade may direc.t
GREAT SALE OF BOOTS AND SHOES now on UNDER THE CLOCK.—AdVt.

Ambulance Certificates Presented. The successful candidates at Messrs. Crosfield and &Ins' works in the recent examination in connection with the St. John Ambulance Brigade, were on Tues- day presented with proficiency certificates for last year's ambulance class. The presentation, which was made by Mr. H. Roberts, took place in the assembly rooms. Mr. Roberts strongly advised that as many as possible should be engaged in ambulance work. Only a -.few days ago one of their workmen met with a fatal accident, and he as well as the directors, deeply regretted it. Accidents did happen at times, but if men had even a rudiment of knowledge of ambulance work they could by rendering first aid, prevent con- siderable pain, and possibly save life. An ambulance lecture was given by Surgeon-Major Harrison, of Chester, being illustrated by lantern slides.
ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERAL WATERS.—Advt.

The Origin of the Bible. This formed the subject of a lecture delivered by the Rev. C. Harris at a well-attended meeting of the Warrington Church Society which was held in the John-street schools on Monday. During his address Mr. Harris remarked that the errors which were made in the Bible were very few and in the majority of cases were most trifling. After comparing the manu- scripts with the ancient ones they had beensable to correct the errors. Illustrations of copies of the Greek and Hebrew manuscripts were given by means of lantern .slides, the lecture throughout being fully illustrated by this means. The Rector had great pleasure in proposing a vote of; thanks to the lecturer, also to the Rev. B. Percival for the use of the room, and to Mr. Houghton for manipulating the lantern. The Rev. H. V. Pigot seconded and the motion was heartily agreed to.

Sale of Work. On Saturday afternoon, a small Sale of Work and Jumble Sale, in aid of the funds of St. John's Presby- terian Church,was held in the schoolroom # John-street. Mrs. W. R. Neil, of "Waverley,"Latchford,in formally declaring the sale open said she was pleased to be there and wished the effort every success. She re- minded the workers that though, as a congregation, they were small in numbers, yet if each and everyone put their shoulders to the wheel they might do a great deal. On the motion of the Rev. J. L. Milne, B. D. seconded by Mr. R. Young, Mrs. Neil was accorded a hearty vote of thanks for her services. The sale, which was in charge of the ladies of the congregation was continued during the afternoon and evening, almost the whole of tho goods being sold and a very satisfactory sum realised. BASSINETTES AND MATE. CARTS in latest art 4hades.—J. S. a RLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt.

Fatal Fire at High Legh. fatal fire occurred early on Monday in the barn and stables of Mr. Edward Stelfox, of Lime Tree Farm, High Legh, about six miles from Altrincham —lnformation was sent to the private fire brigade at High Legh Hall, but owing to the early hour no horses could be procured, and the engine had to be dragged some half-mile to the scene of the fire. Two jets were got to work.—The fears expressed for the life of a man named Monaghan, who slept over the stables, were realised, for when the fire had been subdued the body of Monaghan, burned to a cinder, was found lying close to the body of a valuable mare, which it had been found impossible to rescue. The buildings were gutted.—The fire is supposed to bave been caused either through Monaghan walking about with a lighted candle or by the ashes of his pipe. Methodist Free Church, Buckley-street. On Monday evening, a very successful concert was given in the above schoolroom under the management of the P.S.A. Society officials. The proceeds were to defray the cost of the new heating apparatus, in tlße church and school. Mr. Thomas S. Steel occupied the chair, being supported by Mr. A. Jennings. The .room had been decorated for the occasion with flowers and plants. The programme opened with a march, entitled "New York Patrol" by Master Tom Barton's Juvenile Orchestral Band, which rendered other selections during the evening in a very credit- able manner. Madame F. Christian gave "The promise of life" and "Only once more," the latter receiving a well deserved encore. Mr, W. Critchley's sweet tenor voice was heard to great advantage in his songs "Rivers of yore" and "Bid me to love." Miss L. Plinston sang with excellent taste "Sing me to sleep" and "Japanese love song," each receiving an encore. " Curfew " and " Anchored " were the solos given by Mr. P. George, who was loudly applauded. The Lyric Prize Quartette (Misses A. Woodland, L. Fairhurst and Messrs. R. Cook and Percy George), came in for a good round of applause for their inter- pretations of " Killarney " and "Moonlight and music," the latter] beingiso well rendered as to gain a recall. Master T. Barton skilfully gave a violin solo, accompanied by Miss Blair (of Glazebrook). Mr. F. Aukland supplied the humorous part of the programme, and kept the audience in roars of laughter with his songs and jokes. Miss M. Plinston, A.L.C.M., and Mr. A. E. Trow accompanied the vocalists. At the close of an enjoyable evening, Mr. A. Scott pro- Posed and Mr. E. Plinston seconded a hearty vote of '-ianks to the artistes and chairman which was artily accorded.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, November 26, 1904.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, November 26, 1904.

Parish Church Tea. The annual tea and dance in connection with the I GREAT LIBERAL MEETING. Warrington Parish Church were held in the Parr Hall on Thursday evening. About one thousand persons sat down to tea, after which the hall was cleared for dancing, which was kept up to music supplied by Mr. P. Randall's band, until shortly after midnight. For those to whom dancing did not appeal enaerpainments were provided:in the crush room. All theses items were given by girls from the Fairfield Higher'Grade; school, the Parish Church choir boys the Revs. T. A. G. Ridpath, and G. W. Dickinson, and Mr. P. Brimelow. A tambourine dance was also given by a number of the students from the Priory School. The proceedings throughout were very successful and enjoyable. FOR CLASS AND CHINA of every description try J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street Warrington.—Advt. Winwick Hall Scheme. The foundation stone-laying in connection with the above Hall, now in course of erection at Winwick, is th. realization of a project started nearly three years ago by the Warrington Free Church Council. The i object sto provide a place of worship for Noncon- formists, who are employed in the Cotknty asylum, and others resident in the village. The building which will seat about 250 persons is of chaste ',design and will be simply but tastefully decorated. It will be provided with all the necessary and up-to-date arrangements of a well-appointed village church. The Hall will be ready for use in the early part of the year. There is every prospect that it will quickly become a centre of social educational and religious activity in Winwick. FIRE GRATES of every description.—J. S. GAR- LAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, I Bridge-street,Warringion.—Advt. ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERAL WATERS.—AdVt. The Late Mrs. T. Wallington. ' Preaching at Wycliffe Church on Sunday morning the Rev. John Yonge referred in fitting terms to the late Mrs. T. Wallington, whose death occurred on the , 15th instant, and -who for a large number of years ' was a prominent member of the congregation of Wycliffe Church. His remarks were based on the words "He giveth power to the faint : and to them that have no might he increaseth strength." Isiah 40, v. 29. There was not, he thought, courage so true or so great, as that which enabled a suffering woman to steel herself against perpetual pain, and pursue day after day the duties of her home, and maintain throughout a calm, cheerful, self-forgetful demeanour. Such was the manner and life of their departed friend who despite constant pain was always found at the post of duty, strengthened by her confidence in God. She knew that to the faint God gave strength, and in her they had another witness to His faithfulness and sufficiency, and to the inculculable value of simple trust. GREAT SALE OF .BOOTS AND SHOES now on UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt. Warrington Ragged School Band of Hope. A concert in connection with the above took place on Monday, before an audience of 550 persons. Mr. F. Merlin presided, and his well chosen remarks were greatly appreciated. The following items were ren- dered by the members. Song "I would not be a drunkard "by May Johnson; dialogue "The Tem- perance Pledge" by Misses S. J. 0 Neil,Clara Cowell, Ada Buckley, Amy Rogerson, Masters John Green, George Potts and Paul Cowell: recitations, " Sermon by a bee " Jane Potts. "The Blue Ribbon Badge by Ada Woods," The Inventor's Wife" by Mrs. Barlow ; duett "There is beauty all around " \figs Richards and Mr. Wright; flute trio " Blue Bells " Messrs. Johnson, Brandwood and Wright; recitation " Goodthristian Jim" by Edith Brandwood ; songs "I have a most confiding wife" by W. ; "The Social Glass" by Polly Green and Co. Dialogues" Mr. Caudle gets hoaxed" by Misses S. and M. Richards,M. A. Titchard, H.?. and J. Wright; "A domineering Wife" by Misses C. J. Wright, S Potts,Jane Buckley,Messrs. E. Fear, Hand,and W. E. Wright. Mr. Frank Owen ably discharged the duties of accompanist. A. vote of thanks to the Chairman, brought to a close a most successful concert. '

H. M. ASHTON'S LIFFI TONIC is the RING of' TONICS. I 63. SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. Garden Cities. Mr. Northcote, secretary of 'the Garden Cities Asso- hiation delivered an interesting lecture at a well- attended meeting of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society which was held in the Masonic Hall:on Wednesday evening. What the Garden Cities Association advocated, he said, was the de-centraliza- tion of industries and the controlling by municipali- ties of the development of cities and towns so that they should grow in a: systematic manner and in a way which would prevent overcrowding in certain districts. They did not believe in making comfort- able suburbs but believed in the placing of works in the suburbs where they could be surrounded by proper dwellings for the vrorkpeople.Mr.lforthcute pointe I out that it was extremely probable that the Admiralty would construct the new naval depot on the Firth Of Forth upon garden city lines, and also pointed out that in places where new works were being put down the surrounding land was being laid out on similar lines. With regard to existing little towns, could be done without facing a tremendous expenditure, bat ' what could be done was that the municipalities sholild control the future development of the towns under 1 'their charge. The lecture was fully illustrated by means of lantern slides, the instrument being manipu- lated by Mr. Sutton. Successful Gymnastic Display. An additional attractiveness was lent to the twelvthl annual gymnastic display held at the Warrington Gymnasium on Monday evening by the inclusion in a capital programme of wrestling and weight-lifting competitions. It was evident that the large audience thoroughly appreciated the efforts to demonstrate the usefulness of physical exercises, and the performers were rewarded with hearty applause. A contingent of members of the gymnastic class, under the direc- tion of Mr. J. Kinsley, the able instructor gave highly creditable exhibitions with the dumb bells and Indian clubs, and went through evolutions on the flying rings,horizontal:bars, parallel bars, and vaulting horse. The items were all well received and Mr. ICinsley is to be congratulated upon the gratifying results of his training: For the weight- lifting competition there were six entrants: R. Unsworth, H. Berney, R. Hawthorne, T. Blower, T. Cooper and W. Unsworth. .The competitors were put through a severe test, having to muscle up weights first with the right and left hands in turn and after- wards with both hands. The prizes were awarded on the aggregate weights lifted, and the winnesi3 were :—W. Ungworth, 3581b5. ; T. Blower, 3141b5.; R. Unsworth, 3101bs. In the single hand test W, linsworth was the most successful., ' raising 1201bs. T. Blower achieved the best feat in the ',lift with both hands, muscling up 1301bs. and then 1481bs. Unsworth lifted 1201b5., 1301b5., and 1401bs. in succession. A fine wrestling exhibition was given by Mr. H. O'Brien, the 9 stone amateur champion of Liverpool, and Mr. S. Price, of Warrington. Price was victorious in the Grreco- Roman style, while O'Brien gained the fall under the catch-as-can rules.—The entertain- ment was presided over by Sir Gilbert Greenall Bart., who was accompanied by Lady Greenall. In. the course of a short speech Sir Gilbert said he con- sidered the education of the body was of as vital importance to the nation as any education of the mind. (Hear, hear.) He thought that when English- men lost their love of sports and pastimes we would cease to be the premier nation of the world. (Applause.) A vote of thanks was accorded to Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall for their attendance on the proposition of the Mayor seconded by Councillor Tinnion. An unfortunate accident which occurred at the Gymnasium a few days ago—a little girl falling off a ladder and breaking her arm—was alluded to by Councillor Tinnion who pointed out that there was no cause for alarm Every possible care was taken of the children, as was shown by the fact that there had only been one serious accident since the Gymnasium was opened in 1890, while the attendance had averaged 125,000 a year.

SHORTBREAD.

performance of the" Sheffield Shuffie"—(Leughter)— and in his dextrous attempts to make John Bull swallow not only himself as Premier but any policy that may be sprung upon him and forced down his throat however much he dislikes it. But there is abundant evidence that the great majority of people think there has been quite enough of this political legerdemain. (Hear, hear.) I listened to the advice which

powerful workman. (Hear, hear.) If they limited his food they would limit his physical and mental resources, and therefore he must of necessity be a less profitable person than the one who was well filled. To the workmen and their families it would only mean suffering, deprivation, misery and hunger. There was no corresponding recompense, no compensa- tion, and he could not think that any serious work- man could entertain the proposal for a moment. (Hear, hear). Mr. Chamberlain had made vast numbers of sug- gestions, a great number of spee3hes,—each one differ- ing from the other—(Laughter—tried all sorts of sugges- tions, made all kinds of propositions, and none of them seemed to have taken hold of the people up to the present. What he would still try heaven only knew for the necessity of his situations (Applause), He (the speaker) was for free food, and free commerce (Applause). They had beaten all the nations of the world in trade and commerce under free trade. Dont't let them

div.head: DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE
div.p: THE DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE

and Lord James Hereford gave the other day at Rawten- stall to our Unionist friends. And I think it is likely to weigh with them and all thoughtful people a good deal more than what is urged by those leading lights of the .Protectionist party, Mr. Chaplin, and Colonel Howard Vincent, till lately, as we all remember, the laughing-stock of the countiy—that is until they joined the spoilers—(laughter)—l beg pardon, the Tariff Reform League. But, ladies and gentlemen, don't let us grudge the hard worked politician his little bit •of humour—his delicious F.C.G. cartoons. Without some relief of that kind I do not know Mr. Broadhurst how you would stand your late hours and all night sittings. Last summer when in Switzerland I was talking to Mr. Labouchere and a lady who was there complained that in the high altitude of the .n,,cradine she found it diffi- cult to get enough sleep. "I will find you a cure " said `Labby' "Go to the House of Commons. The speeches I listen to there are," he said, "as the grinding and dron- ing of a mill, and rarely fail to soothe me into slumber." (Laughter.) Of course in all large assemblies you will find a percentage of very long winded men.

Who are the most tremendous bores .of all the bores we know, They should be sent to that weird place where other sinners go. (Laughter.) But the sample of oratory we shall have to-night will be very different. (Applause.) Political friends of mine who are very good judges have told me that there are scarcely half a dozen men in the country who can hold their own with our guest this evening. (Applause.) Well, ladies and gentlemen, the issues we shall have to face and decide are serious enough in all conscience.l heard Mr. Winston Churchill—(applause)— whom we hope and expect to see on this platform at no distant date—(applause)—l heard him describe these issues in tolerably drastic language the other day in Manchester. Speaking of what would happen if Mr. Chamberlain won he said :

"We know perfectly well what to expect—a party of great vested interests banded together in a for- midable federation—(hear, hear)—corruption at home, aggression'ito cover it up abroad—(cheers) —the trickery of tariff juggles, the tyranny of a party machine; sentiment by the bucketful— (laughter) '--patriotism by the imperial pint— (laughter) ;—dear food forthel million, cheap labour for the millionaire. (Laughter and applause. lam afraid that is a literal truth, and having regard to the strong appeal which is going to be made, which is being made, to interested people in this town and elsewhere, and bearing in mind that the great brewers are certain to play into the hands of the apostles of re-action—though to their honour be it said there are a great many publicans who will refuse to do so—beariug all this in mind I think Mr. Churchill is quite right in warning the Liberal Party that the final victory for Free Trade will not be won easily, and that we must be con- tent'with a negative policy in support of it. We certainly won't in Warrington—(hear, hear)—and I would ven- ture to remind you of

THE VERY PosrrivE AND PRACTICAL PROGRAMME which the Progressive Labour League in Warrington is advocating. 'And when it urges a national system of education which shall give everyone a fair chance both to teach and to learn, or the reform of the House of Lords which, as a committee of the Charlton Club is such an anomaly and an anachronism in our Constitu- tion, or the Taxation of Land values through which alone we shall ever be able to clear out our slums and deal effectively with the Housing problem, these and other questions which it urges are not dry abstractions, they have a vital and far reaching effect on the well being of the great mass of our people. (Applause.) And it is this simple fact, the pursuit of—to use a long familiar but time honoured phrase—the greatest , good of the greatest number, which makes true statesmanship one of the noblest occupations to which human energy and effort can be devoted. If my friend Mr. Garnett will forgive me for detaining him for a couple of minutes more before I ask him to move the resolution, I would like to close my remarks by reading you a quotation from a very important address at the Church Congress in Liverpool. It was delivered by a man whom Lord Derby has described as the greatest ornament to Liver- pool, one of the ablest men of science in the country, who is now the principal of the Birmingham University, Sir Oliver Lodge. (Applause.)Speaking of the progress of humanity he said "Our progress already has been considerable. It is but a moderate time since our greatest men were chipping flints and carving bone into the like- ness of reindeer. More recently they became able to build cathedrals and compose poems. Now we are momentarily diverted from immortal pursuits by vivid interest in that kind of competi- tion which has replaced the competition of the sword, and by those extraordinary inequalities of possession and privilege which have been rendered possible by the invention of an indestructible and transmissible form of riches, a form over which neither moth nor rust has.any power. We raise an incense of smoke and offer sacrifices of squalor and ugliness in worship of this new idol. But it will pass; human life is not, meant to continue as it is now in city slums; nor is the strenuous futility of mere accumulation likely to satisfy people when once they have been educated; the world is beauti- ful, and may be far more widely happy than it has been yet." (Applause.) And another man who in the world of letters and affairs holds as high a position as Sir Oliver Lodge, has expressed the same idea in still more eloquent terms. Speaking of the inevitable eff act of science in modify- ing the most ancient forms of religious belief,he says : "rhat'swelling consciousness of height and freedom which we findlin the older religions may still remain; for how shall the universe ever cease to be a sovere- ign wonder of overwhelming power and superhuman fixedness of law. And a man is already in no mean paradise if at the hour of sunset a good hope can fall upon him like harmonies of music;that the earth shall still be fair; and the happiness of every feeling creature still receive a constant augmentation; and each good cause find worthy defenders when the memory of his own poor name and personality has long been blotted out'from the brief recollection of men for ever." (Loud applause). MR. BROADHURST'S SPEECH.

Mr. BROA.DHURST, who was received with prolonged applause said he was very glad to be present because they were approaching a time when they would come to close quarters with their political, opponents. (Applause.) As he understood it they in Warrington had chosen the colours under which they would do battle and they'would have a clear issue and

div.head: STRAIGHT-FORWARD CONTEST
div.p: A STRAIGHT-FORWARD CONTEST

and there would be no confusion. There would be their chairman against a Tory—(applause)---and they would only have two cards from which to choose and he sincerely hoped as he truly believed, they would send their friend triumphant to Parliament to represent that great industrial community. (Applause). Mr. Crosfleld was not a dark horse. His course was perfectly true, and if returned to the House of Commons was not likely to play tricks with their interests. He would go *might to the post on every occasion. (Applause). Hof hoped there would be no further division and that they would prepare themselves f)r the coming contest and would give a good account of the Liberalism of Warrington. They had a great duty to discharge. Twenty years ago the Liberal party gave the franchise to the people. They gave the great scheme of re-distribu- tion, extended hours for the ballot, which gave the people facilityi for advancing the interests of the nation against that of the classes. Unfortunately during the last sixteen years we had lost a great deal of ground and it would take many years before we could recover that lost ground. There was no subject which should be more dear to the parents of the working classes of this country than that of education for their children. They should insist upon a pure,undefiled system of elementary education for their children. Knowledge was the greatest power in the world, and they should hold dear the most precious prize of the acquirement of sound, solid, useful education for their children. Th it could not be under the present system. They had

div.head: HANDED OVER TO THE PRIESTHOOD
div.p: HANDED OVER TO THE PRIESTHOOD

their ednation and the people had lost control. Kno- wledge was subordinated to dogmas and until that policy was reversed they could not look forward to any great progress among their industries because those nations which were most highly and technically educated would rise in commercial supremacy. The application of science and inventions in production had superseded physical strength and therefore knowledge was an absolute necessity. We must have knowledge if we were to hold our own in the future of the countries of the world. (Applause.) We must have a sound elementary education, aud that must be controlled by the people, and above all those religious nostrums and religious animosity must be eliminated fom our own national school system. (Applause). He believed in religious education in our elementary schools, but the religious education he advocated was the religion of the New Testament—teachings of truth, honesty, sober industry, and dutifulness' and if people wanted other flavours added they should pay for them out of their own pockets. (Applause). He thought they might leave the education question at that point. There were many church people who were as strongly opposed to"the undue influence of priest- craft as the Dissenters were themselves. When he used the phrase priestcraft he did not apply it to any denomination. He wanted for all denominations full , and absolute freedom of worship as he claimed himself, —(hear, hear)—but for those particular purposes he I thought that each denomination should find its own Ifunds as the Free Churches did at the present time. . (Applause.) The Chairman had referred to the great question that was now occupying a vast amount of public attention, namely, what was described as
THE FISCAL_ REFORM MOVEMENT.

On that subject he could not think there should be two opinions in Warrington. To tax food was a movement which he could not imagine that any serious people, either employers or workmen, could entertain for a moment. A workman to be a profitable Pperson to the employer must be a well-fed—(hear, hear)—strong, and

div.head: SURRENDER THEIR ADVANTAGE
div.p: SURRENDER THEIR ADVANTAGE

on the suggestions of a.man who had promised them so many good things, none of which had been realised. (Hear. hear). He had no confidence that Mr. Chaplin and Mr. Chamberlain with their combined genius could improve the affairs and condition of trade created by Mr. Bright and Mr. Cobden. (Loud Applause). Mr. Ritchie, who was Chancellor of the Exchequer before Mr. Austen Chamberlain—(laughter)—mader a speech on Thursday night in his constituency. Mr. Ritchie was a Scotchman and his goodsense and sound knowledge seemed to be bursting the bonds of Toryism and had compelled him to resign his Chancellorship of the Excequer, to practically wash his hands of Toryism and to come out in defence of sense, of freedom of trade,and prosperity of the people. (Applause.)ln that speech Mr. Ritchie proved that statements made at Birkenhead by Mr. Bonar Law, secretary of the Board of Trade, were founded upon fallacies, fancies and other misleading conclusions and not upon fact. Mr. Bonar Law sought to prove that while the population had increased 15 per cent. our trade had only increased 4 per cent. Mr. Ritchie who was president of the Board of Trade before he (Mr. Broadhurst) ever heard the name of Bonar Law—(laughter)—showed that the increase of population was 13 per cent. while trade had increased 20 per cent. (Applause.) As a matter of fact, all the reliable evidence of the statistical depart- ment of the Board of Trade wal a constant living pro- test against

THE QUACKERY OF MR 01A.MBERLAIN and his co-workers in connection (nth tariffs. (Applause.) They took certain years and placed them ?against cer- tain other years. (Laughter.) Then they left out certain parts of our trade and addei others and left out certain parts—and so they went on ringing the changes to such an extent that it amounted to absolute; wilful misleading of the public on matters of fact and truth. !Applause.)He regretted that public-discussion of affairs affecting the common-wealth should have descended to these tricks of the trade—(hear, hear)—and not retained I the old-fashioned, honest, truthful, straightfor- ward statements, whether they were for or against the arguments used. Their object was to prove that we were going backward instead of forward. The whole of the Board of Trade returns showed that we were going forward and not backward we were continually exceeding the over-sea trade of all the nations of the world—(hear, hear)— and to say to the contrary was to oppose the figures of our Customs and trade reports presented by a Govern- ment department. The fact was that Mr. Chamberlain and his friends seemed to have put on their garments wrong ,ray about. (Laughter.) They were dressed the hind before. (Loud laughter.) They were buttoned down the back instead of down the front, and they stemed to be following their buttons. (More laughter.) They were marching backward and they thought every- one who was going forward was misled and was going in the wrong direction. (Laughter.) These men would argue against the sun, the moon and the stars and make us believe that the whole of the laws of nature were utterly mistaken, and only this new prophet and his satelites were the truth of the world. (Laughter and applause.) They were trying to set us back to sixty years ago. He did not know whether many of those present remem- bered sixty years back. He remembered it only too well. If the workingmen of Warrington remembered the low wage, the long hours of labour, the constant want of employment, the dearness of food and clothing, when bread of the nature that no labourer would eat to-day cost Bd. and 10d. a loaf, when tea was a luxury in the homes of the poor, and sugar often an unknown article, when coltsfoot was gathered and dried and used as tobacco, because tobacco could not be purchased from the wages of those days—if the whole of the electors of , this country could remember those times as vividly as he could, there would be 93 per cent, at least against thi

THIS WILD CAT SCHEME of returning to the days of sorrow. (Applause.) The garish lamp of Mr. Chamberlain and his party was only lighted up in order to distract our attention from the crimes and the failures of the past. His great African failure and crime had to be obliterated if possible and he had started a new craze in the interest of the same class of people and against the workers as the South African policy was. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Ritchie in his speech referred to the want of employment and he coupled with it the waste of public money. (Applause) He referred to the vast millions that were sunk in that African venture and he stated that however necessary it might have been it was unprofitable and every pound sunk in it was a pound lost for ever. (Applause.) It was unneeessary for anyone except for the millionaires who had brought
DISHONOUR AND DEGRADATION UPON THE NAME OF GREAT BRITAIN

by the institution of slavery after the destruction of freedom. (Applause.) Mr. Ritchie knew trade and commerce, ancihe had givenup a.great political future rather than be a party to taxing the stomachs of the working people—(applause)—and that was what Pro - tection meant. (Hear, hear.) What had been the result of this war? The country which was to find employ- ment for the over-flowing population of Great Britain was now a country from which the whiteman was barred and where only the yellow men were welcome (Shame). Our out of work populations were not wanted in South Africa. They would want reasonable, decent, human freedom—(hear,hear)—and the great millionaires did not want people of that kind. They only wanted slaves in order that they might coerce, crush and manage them to their own increased profits. There was no curse in the world greater than that of gold when it was used against the progress of nations and the prosperity of the people. Look what we are coming to in our own country! Only a week or two back we had a great Conservative organ called the" Standard," one of the best written, most independent, truthful and fearless organs ever issued in the name of the Tory party. It had been captured by the millionaires because it defended truth, justice and right, and they were going, no doubt, to use its columns to disseminate the law of monopoly in trade questions as they had disseminated monopoly in South African gold mining in other organs of public opinion. (Hear, hear.) They were new actually trying to capture the universi- ties. They were going to the very seat of knowledge an 4 endowing chairs to promote what they called knowledge and professorships of Imperialism. That was all against liberty, progress, and the highest peace and lastin,, interests of the greatest number of our popula- tion. b(Applause). Unless the people of the country rose in great numbers at the coming general election and stamped out those pests, the country would become a mere addendum to the foreign capitalist, and would be no longer the home for the Briton, as we understood him to be in the days of old. (Applause).

div.head: WE COULD NOT ACCEPT RETALIATION
div.p: WE COULD NOT ACCEPT RETALIATION

or preferential treatment without lultimately landing ourselves in the meshes of protection,—without getting on the inclined plank of protection upon which we could not stop ourselves from reaching the bottom, probably more quickly than we anticipated. Retaliation, pre- ferential treatment and protection were all of one family and were 'against the interests of the people. All three had one object in view and went to one end and he was opposed to the whole of them and would not have anything to do with them. (Applause.) He would not discuss them, but would say to those who advocated them "Let well alone and take your meddling hands off our pros- perity. (Applause.) We have no faith in your recom- mendations or your treatment." The workingmen would have to give a little more time to the watching of their own interests. 'They must look at the enormous expenditure and extravagant public outgoing to-day. Our public expenditure had nearly doubled itself since he first entered the House of Commons. To-day half of the purchase price of a pound of tea was made up by taxes. The same thing applied in other cases and by that means the industrial classes of the country were being ROBBED AND PLUNDERED BY THE GOVERNMENT._

If those taxes were paid directly working men would have 3s. or 4s. per week deducted from their wages,and they would then know what they were paying,and there would be a revolution and the spend thrifts would quickly be turned out of office. What the Liberals advocated was that the taxation should be matle equal according to the income—that every man should make a iproportionate sacrifice for the maintenance of the State. (Applause) The Liberals heldthat every man earning £1 a week should pay proportionately no more than the man who reckoned his income by £lO,OOO a year, though at the present time the poor man contri- buted proportionately a much greater sum than was paid by the weathly man. Mr. Broadhurst illustrated his point by taking the day on tea which he showed was exactly the same per lb. in the case of tea costing Bd. on the plantation as it was in the case of tea cost- ing 3s. Continuing he said we wanted to

div.head: RESIST THAT DOWNWARD POLICY.
div.p: RESIST THAT DOWNWARD POLICY.

If the nation did not stop its financial extravagance it would suffer, and history had repeatedly shown that the first to suffer and the persons who suffered longest were the industrial classes. We wanted our ' rural population to stop in their native villages earning' decent wages and being good customers cd he factories and stores in the adjoining towns. To tax the food of the people in order to increase the revenue was like starving the horse upon whose labour a man depended for his livelihood. No sane person would attempt anything of the kind. He sincerely trusted they were arriving at a time when those pro- posals would oe ignored, repudiated and denounced. He alluded to the great war in progress between Japan and Russia, and also the large amount of money which was being spent. Could there be gieater human folly than a war of such a nature as that? Thank God they were living in days when there were indications towards

universal arbitration. They had not done very much up to thepresent, butsomething had been doneto estab- lish the appeal of reason as against the folly of force, and that policy_ had been advocated and encouraged in high places. He remembered the time when

TO MENTION ARBITRATION in place of war was to bring down upon one's head torrents of ridicule and contempt. He thanked God something betterprevailed to-day. (Hear, hear.) They were now discussing, a treaty with the great Republic of America which might settle all differences which might arise in the best possible and peaceablemamier. Healso alluded to treaties which had been made between smaller countries and England, which he contended showed marks of time and progress. It was glorious to live in the days when the occupant of the throne of old England had gained the universal voice of the people by his work in the cause of peace, progress and pros- perity. (Loud applause.) There was no greater curse to the poor than war. (Hear, hear.) They had to find the bodies, they had to suffer the privations, and they had to pay the overwhelming proportion of taxation in proportion to their resources or means. Let them hope to see the day when peace should prevail, and reason prove stronger and more powerful than the sword. (Hear, hear). He wanted them to remember their great and grave responsibilities. They were a great grand jury of the nation, and if they sowed the wind of indifference they must reap the whirlwind of disaster and extravagance. (Applause). He urged them to be up and doing in the great conflict which would come, and be ready to defend their country from the backward policy to which they had been subjected, and not to be led by that false and tinsel imperialism. In conclusion he asked them not to spare of their labour, and make their land happy, true, glorious, and all that was honest and whole amongst the peoples of the world. (Loud applause.) THANKING MR. BROADHURST.

Councillor JAMES EVANS proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Broadhurst for his address. He pointed out that ttie next election would be fought with special im- portance as its results would no doubt largely influence the conditions undor,which;the future generation would live. (Hear, hear.) Mr. E. OSBORNE seconded. Young men he said ought to take a keener interest in politics because they were told that politicans as a rule were rarely sincere. He was quite satisfied that they had that night, at any rate, been listening to a man who was thoroughly sincere. (Applause.) The resolution was carried with great cordiality THE "FUTURE MEMBER."

Councillor TrNmoN proposed a vote Of thanks to Mr. Crosfield for presiding and expressed the hope that at a public meeting in the near future they would be able to thank him as the member for Warrington.—(Applause). —for his able and excellent services as their represen- tative in the House of Commons.

The Rev. H. DUNNICO seconded. He was delighted to know that at the corning election they would have the opportunity of giving a straight vote for the pro- gressive candidate. He was glad the workingmen had seen the wisdom of uniting at this criticat time and he urged them to sink all petty differences and work as one man for Mr. Crosfield.

The resolution was carried with acclamation, In responding, the CfrAIRAIAti said that as regarded the allusion to his candidature it might be news to some of them that he had already sat in the House. (Laughter). He meant as a visitor—(laughter)—but if Mr. Pierpoint continued to play the " whole-hogger " and they should want someone to represent them in a less dangerous capacity—(laughter)—perhaps, by their favour, he might pay a rather longer visit to the House one of these days. (Applause). For a great many years now Mr. Pierpeint had served up Cyprus to them. (Laughter)—he supposed as a sort of political hors d'ceuvre. They had been waiting for the banquet a very long time, and now that at last they were invited to eit down to it they found that rations were to be dear and scanty. (Hear, hear.) He was afraid they must decline that invitation. (Laughter.) The meeting then concluded,
