div.head: SPEECHES BY MR. HENRY BROADHURST M P., Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD
div.p: SPEECHES BY MR. HENRY BROAD- HURST M P., Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD
AND OTHERS.
Free Trade and Liberal Principles Upheld.

Mr. Henry Broadhurst, M.P., is always assured of a hearty reception on visiting Warrington for prob- ably in no town are his stirring and well reasoned speeches more eagerly anticipated and fully appreciated. It was therefore not surprising that a large and enthusiastic audience assembled in Parr Hal last evening for the great Liberal meeting at which Mr. Broadhurst was the principal speaker. The meeting had been arranged by the Warrington Liberal Association, a large and attentive gathering testifiying to the great interest which is being taken locally in the fiscal controversy and other political questions of the day. Alderman Pierpoint had been announced to preside but unfortunately he was prevented by indisposition from attending. The chair was occupied by Mr. Arthur H. Crosfield who was supported on the platform by Mr Henry Broadhurst, M.P., the Revs. H. DunnicO J. L. Milne, and J. S. Hughes, Coun- cillors Tinnion, Wilkinson, Ellison, Evans, Clegg, P. Peacock and Barton, M • ssrs. P. Rathlyme' James Critchley. C. Jackson Holmes T. Dale, E. Osborne,W. Vose, J, Higham, J. Bailey, q. Dunbobhin, E. Hackle, A. Downes, P. C. Garnett, J. Morton, J. Vose, W. Jeffreys and others. There was a good attendance of ladies, including Miss Crosfield, Miss Mackie, Mrs. Jacksin-Holines, Mrs. Walker, Mrs. Pierpoint, Mrs. Osborne, Airs. Clay, Mrs. O'Brien, and Mrs. Clegg.

div.head: LETTERS OF APOLOGY.
div.p: LETTERS OF APOLOGY.
"THE MONOPOLIST THE ONLY BENE7ICIARY UNDER PROTECTION."

The Chairman read the following letter from Mr. C. E. Parker: "I am very sorry that an engagement, made before the Liberal meeting was arranged, will prevent me from supporting you in person on Friday. The country's faith in Free Trade so recklessly attacked, I trust will be strengthened by the meeting. The-crude- ness of the proposals of Mr. Chamberlain is what has surprised me. There has been no attempt to test these by the economic laws which control the con- ditions of exchange, no loyalty to definite principle§.., no attempt to construct upon a logical basis a workable scheme either of Protection or Retaliation. Instead of this there have been appeals to different sectional interests and pre- judices, the awakening of an unhealthy appetite for privilege and monopoly, and it is well to remember that the monopolist is the only beneficiary under Protection. Economically l the Protection advocated by Mr. Chamberlain appears to me altogether unsound. Its effect would be to encourage production which is unprofitable on its merits, and could only be made profitable by the consumer having to pax more to make it so. Production diverts industries into less economical channels of activity. On the other hand the natural and inevitable effect of Free Trade is to cause industries to gravitate towards their most economical conditions. Unprofitable production diminishes the wealth of a nation, and diminishes that wealth amongst the classes who most require it, and most deserve it. It would surely be folly to endow one class of trades with the privilege of becoming wealthy at the expense of the general community, since protec- ted trades, hothoused by legislation into unnatural pros- perity, would secure a kind of vested interest through which they would prey upon the unprotected con- sumer. Our export trade would be handicapped by the increased cost of production, and our home trade would be crippled by the general reduction in the real wage as distinct from the nominal, in other words by a lessening of the purchasing power of money. Let the condemna- tion of these crude proposals be strong, emphatic, and final.—Yours very truly, CHARLES E. PARKER. Alderman Pierpoint wrote :—" I regret very much that I am not well enough to take the chair at the meeting to-night. I axi much disappointed as I had been looking forward with pleasure to hearing the address by Mr. Broadhurst, M.P.—always a combination of good humour and. sound common sense—also to have advocated the claims of Mr. Crosfield to the sup- port of every true Liberal in Warrington. The object of every elector who places the welfare of his country before the claims of his party should be to get rid of the present Government which by its home and foreign policy and extravagant exponiiture is mainly responsible for the disturbed conditions of our trade. In 1900 the Government were given a mandate to clear up the muddle caused by their war in South Africa.. Instead they have used their large majority to inVOSe upon the country a truly selfish policy. They have not only doubled the national expenditure, increased taxation, and endowed the brewers and the voluntary schools, but they have also dumped yellow labour in the Transvaal in order to increase the wealth of a few millionaires there. In conclusion I hope workingmen of Warrington will think carefully at the next Parliament election what is best both for their country and for themselves, and then I would not fear the result."
_ Letters of apology were also received from Mr. T. Birchall and Miss Bessie Dutton.
THE CHAIRNIAN'S SPEECH. THE EVILS OF PROTECTION AND ADVANTAGES OF FREE TRADE.

The CHAIRMAN, who was very warmly received, said: Ladies and Gentlemen,—l am very sorry indeed that the President of our Association cannot be with us to-night, but lam sure you will give due consideration to the cogent and forcible letter which he has sent us.-%(Hear, hear.) lam also very sorry that illness prevents Mr. Pierpoint joining us to-night. As a tried, trusted, and very influantial leader of the Liberal Party we should all have liked to see him in thechair. (Applause), We are very glad indeed to have Mrs. Parker and Mrs. Pier- point with us, and for Mrs. Pierpoint's sake I hope her husband will soon behimself again. (Hear, hear.) But if his absence is a disappointment, on the other hand there is a great treat in store for us. An eminent observer has said that two excellent things are good water and good wine, but that nothing is worse than a mixture of the two. (Laughter.) Now you are presently going to have some wine of the rarest vintage, some of the oldest and best in the cellar : I am afraid you .von'tthank me for treating you to a glass of water before it. (Laughter). Still I should hardly be doing my duty if I did not say a word or two on the peat Fiscal controversy which is to be the all-important issue at the next election. In a speech to the iron- workers last Saturday I alluded to the overwhelming advantage we have in neutral markets, and I quoted roughly what a Lancashire cotton spinner told me, namely, that while our exports of cotton to India are roughly—very roughly—something like twenty millions sterling a year, Germany and the United States send less than a paltry couple of hundred thousand pounds worth each. But on the spur of the moment I forgot ta quote what followed in our conversation; you may think it a small fact in itself but it has I submit a pretty wide significance. We all know the climatic advantage which Lancashire is supposed to have in the cotton trade. But when I alluded to this Mr. Garnett said, "Never mind that, take something else that shows where the shoe really pinches German manufacturers ; think of the capital charges they have to face." He said a friend of his had lately been buying machinery in the Manchester district and sending it to Switzerland, and althongh the cost of this long transit was about 20 per cent. of the value of the machinery itself he was able to sell in Switzerland, at a fair proflt at 5 per cent. less than the price of German machinery which was so much nearer at hand. That gives one some idea of the way in which

div.head: MANUFACTURERS ARE HANDICAPPED
div.p: MANUFACTURERS ARE HANDICAPPED

in protected countries. In the cotton trade at present we dominate the great markets of Asia. Can we afford to jeopardise a trade like that by increasing the cost of manufacture all round? (Cries of No.") The margin ; of profit in this trade is often none too large. Corn- petition is fierce l enough as we all know in this great ' cotton industry which is second only to agriculture in ; the number of hands directly and indirectly I employed; because our cotton spinners have I not only rivals abroad, but local manufacturers to deal with on the spot where labour is terribly cheap. Well I suppose we take this reckless leap in the dark, and in the long run lose say 20 per cent of our trade is it only the cotton tra le which would suffer? That: would be serious enough because it is calculated that one-tenth or one-fifteenth of our population depend on it. But do you suppose that bad trade there would not affect other industries? Would there be no falling off in the demand for boots among workpeople, and machinery among employers—and the leather that goes to make the one and the metal the other? Would not the pinch- ing in food, and clothing, and little luxuries of all sorts affect other countries and other manufacturers all round? Don't forget,that big as your export trade is your home trade is six or eight times larger. (Applause.)Well that is a serious enough question for every man and woman, are we going to jeopardise this v astindustry of ours— the cotton trade—and our great position as shipbuilders for the world, at the same time that we indulge in what Lord Goschen has significantly and truly described as A GAMBLE IN THE PEOPLE'S _Poop?

I wonder -1;-ow that little jam; would have suited us during the recent hard times in Lancashire? Eineloyers and employed have stood manfully together during the bad times in the cotton trade, which are now happily over, but at such a time would not our peopls during the pincn of distress have felt a tax on food to be, as it has been called, a cursed tax like a blight on the weather or the barrennesof the soil. Is it in that way, ladies and gentlemen, we are going to knit closer the ties of blood and kinship and affection which bind our whole Empire together ? (Applause.) A cynical friend of mine said the other day. "One should never take politics seriously." Well, certainly, the present situation has its humorous side. It has I been amusing to watch our Premier's agility in his

div.head: DISTRICT NURSES.
div.p: THE DISTRICT NURSES.
THEIR WORK IN WARRINGTON REVIEWED.
Annual Meeting.
MORE HELP WANTED FROM THE CHURCHES.

How many Warrington people have cause to be grateful for the beneficent work carried on through the agency of the District Nursing Association it would be difficult to say. The institution has thoroughly justi- fied its existence, and as the end of each year comes a record of useful service has to be reviewed. At the Co-operative Hall. Sankey-street, on Tuesday evening, the seventh annual meeting was held,' and reports full of interest were presented. A good attendance was presided over by the Rector (Rev. Canon Willis), who was supported on the platform by the Rev. Father Wilson, Mr. F. Monks (hon. treasurer), Mr. John Fair- clough and Mr. J. Dutton Fairclough (one of the hon. secretaries).—The Chairman read a letter from the Rev. John Yonge regretting his inability to atteu'd, and testi- fying to the admirable and devoted work of the nurses. "I trust" he added "that the institution will receive in the future still wider and more generous support from the churches and people of our town." The Rev. Father Whittle sent a similar commulication. FORTHCOMING BAZAAR.

Mr. J. D. FAIRCLOUGM announced that several juvenile workers had decided to hold a small bazaar for the benefit of the Association and liberal support was appealed for. The arrangements were in the htolds of the Misses Baskerville and Whitney, Hanover-street. THE REPORTS.

In their annual report the committee emphasised the necessity for new and increased financial support,if the society is to continue a work commensurate with the needs of the town. The staff consisted of a Superin- tendent and five nurses, and the report of the Inspector after her annual visit was gratifying. The committee expressed their warmest thanks to the Superintendent and_ nurses and also to the subscribers,

The SUPERINTENDENT (Nriss Whitfield) reported that a comparison of the record of work done in the year just ended, with that of the previous year, showed an increase of 76 patients on the books, and of 51 to whom one or more visits had bean paid but whose names had not been entered; also of 1,124 visits paid. During the last few years there had been noticeable a gradual-and decided improvement in the sanitary condition of the homes of the people, proving in a most encouraging way that the efforts of the various agencies at work among the poor were not in vain. The kindly spirit which on all hands was extended to the nurses in their work was a source of help and cheer in the midst of much that is depressing and discouraging. Gifts of old linen were urgently needed, the demand at present being far in excess of the supply. In presenting the statement of accounts the treasurer called special attention to the need for new subscrip- tions. Deaths, removals, and lessened subscriptions accounted for more than the adverse balance with which they closed the financial year, and in addition they missed the handsome donation of .275 from the Cycle Parade Committee. He wished also to call attention to the falling off in congregational collections. Whether it arose from indifference to the work of the Associa- tion, or want of proper organization, he could not say, but the fact remained that not one third of the con- gregations of the town contributed to the funds of the Association. The subscriptions and dona- tions of workingmen from the Associations with which they were connected, showed a st3ady increase. The debt on the Nurses' Home remained the rime as last year,viz : £256 16s, 6d. the interest on this having been paid in place of rent.

div.head: RECTOR'S TESTIMONY.
div.p: THE RECTOR'S TESTIMONY.

The RECTOR commented upon several of the more important points mentioned in the report. The number of patients was about 500, and he found that out of that number about 400 had been sent in by medical men or through them. That was very satisfactory. It was sug- gested at first that it was possible there might be some disapproval on the part of medical men, but they had now a very strong testimony that they were thoroughly in accord with the institution. (Applause). Out of 500 cases there had been 400 recoveries, and that was in a great measure due to the skilful nursing. There were six nurses, who paid nearly 19,000 visits in the course of the year ; each nurse numbering 10 visits a day or 60 visits a week. It was a splendid record. He was delighted to see from the report that the nurses had found a gradual and decided improvement in the sanitary condition of the houses they entered./ He said at the beginning of the association that their skilful and tactful manner might help to induce some of the wives to be more careful in their homes and thus make them more attractive to the husbands. The institution was thoroughly appreciated by the workingmen who had contributed £6O. He was sorry to find that the congre- gational collections only amounted to about £3O, and that not one-third of the various places of worship contributed. He hoped many would see their way this year to contribute because there was a deficiency of £25 and it ought not to exist. There was a debt from last year which had not been lowered of £256 upon the Inurses's home. He hoped some rich friends would be I found to come forward and reduce, if not extinguish, the debt. (Applause).

div.head: FINANCIAL POSITION.
div.p: THE FINANCIAL POSITION.

Mr. F. MoNKs submitted a detailed financial state: ment dealing not only with the past year's work but with the operations of the Association since its formation. Commencing the year with a credit balance of £44 us. 9d., they had now a deficit of £25 10s. The total cost of the nurses' home, including furnishing was £1,317 19s. 11d. Towards that amount they received £9Bl 16s. 6d. (including a gift of £6OO from the late Mr. Robert Davies's sons), 'leaving a debt to be wiped oft of £336 3s. sd. The maintenance and salaries of nurses during the seven years had absorbed £2,657 13s. 7d., and rent, rates, coal etc., £616 13s. 7d.,making a total of £3,274 7s. 2d. Mr. Monks expressed regret

that the congregational collections on behalf of the Association were not at all satisfactory, some denomina- tions not having subscribed a penny. They were very much indebted to their Roman Catholic friends for the very handsome donations they had made through the St. Mary's Dramatic Society, total- ling £314 14s. 4d. (Applause). The treasurer also called special attention to the workingmen's donations amounting to £605 ss. 10d. and emphasised the pleasure it gave him to receive a cheque for £26—the proceeds of an angling contest. The balance on the current account was £53 16s. id. in favour of the institution which showed that for the seven years the•association had been self-supporting. (Applause.) Now as to the results of the work. When they started they had two nurses. Now they had six, and the total number of visits paid during the seven years was 93,699. The average cost of each visit was neatly eightpence. The total number of cases attended to was 2,621, and the average cost £1 55., the average number of visits to each being 37. They would agree that it was economical working. A great amount of suffering which would otherwise have been unattended to had been allayed. (Applause.) On the motion of the Rev. Father WILSON, seconded by Mr. J. RYMER YOUNG and supported by the Rev.W. BRACECAMP, the reports were adopted. Mr. YouNG remarked that at the outset there wasl tinge of disapprobation on the part of the medical pro- fession but he was delighted to know that it had long since disappeared. (Applause.) The Rev. W. BRA.CECAMP expressed the opinion a day should be specially set apart at the churches which collections could be made on behalf of the Association.
SEVEN XEARS' WORK REVIEWED. INTERE.STING PAPER BY THE SUPERINTENDENT.

In the course of a highly-interesting paper on "Seven years' work among the sick poor of the town," Miss Whitfield stated :—" The first intimation of the fact that you had agreed so celebrate the Diamond Jubilee of H.M. Queen Victoria's reign by establishing in your midst a band of trained nurses to care for and to attend to the sick poor of your town, reached me when WP3 completing my training in district nursing at the Central Training Home of the Queen Victoria Jubilee Institute, Bloomsbury-square, and the General Super- intendent informel me that after a fortnight's holiday I was to go to Warrington to start the work there. was to go as superintendent, for said she, "We expect great things of Warrington, and we .hope before long you will have six nurses at work there.' The change pleased me mucb in that I supposed Warrington tobe a manufacturing iown,and therefore abounding in work- ing people and people in humble circumstances, to whose service the Queen's Nurses are especially de- dicated. Accordingly I arrived, July Ist, 1897, full of enthusiasm and hope. My zeal in the cause of the sick poor, however, had perforce to be curbed for the space of three weeks, during which time our comfortable little hornet 41, Arpley-street, had 'Ai be furnished and prepared prior to our start in housekeeping. That accomplished, a call on the doctors to explain methods and to enlist co-operation seemed to, be the next move, and very kindly I was received. And so the association was floated, ar d when the first case came in it seemed to be fairly "under way." The first case,a good one from a professional point of view wes one of typhoid fever. This I took as a good omen. Then came a rush of - from all directions; Sankey Bridges, Bewsey-road, Winwick-road, Lythgoe's-lane, Thelwall-lane, all seemed to possess "sick poor " craving the attention of the new nurse. How to get round to them all and do what was necessary for them was often a problem, for in those days there were no trams, and I did not cycle. At last the work increased to such an extent that one pair of hands, however willing, could not compass it, and I was re-inforced August 30th, having been alone for two months. Cases continued to pour in, and soon the two of us were inundated with work. It was then that in sheer desperation we sought the aid of bicycles and were delighted to find that by the consequent economy of time as well as of physical energy formerly spent on walking and carrying a bag weighing 81b. or 91b., the increase in the amount of work we were enabled to do was enormous. (Applause.) Still the work grew and extended, becomine week by week better known and more highly appreciated, and in November of the same year, another nurse was added to the staff. By October of the second year, such rapid strides had been made that it was thought necessary to add one nurse more, and in February, 1900, still another, while our full growth seemed to be attained in February,l9ol, when the final addition was made by our staff being then made up to the present number, viz., a superintendent and five nurses. An epoch in the history of the associa- tion :was marked when, the accommodation at 41, Arpley-street; having for some time proved inadequate to meet the growing requirements of the staff, the larger premises at No. 21. wore taken, were altered and adapted for the purpose, and the nurses removed there in June, four years ago. Ido not propose to-night to enter into details of the daily work of the district nurses, as the majority preaent are already familiar with them. Some, indeed, know by their own experience the comfort that can be given by skilled handling in time of sickness others know the relief of having at their command the help and advice of one who, as they say, " knows her business," to assist in nursing their sick relatives, and ie intelligently carrying out the doctor's ()Hers. Nor do I purpose to harrow your feelings with thrilling accounts of dirty houses, unwashed patients, unsightly sores, pitiful weakness, or hopeless poverty. • All these are encountered daily by the nurses, and have been dwelt on at length on other occasions. The object of this paper is rather to trace the history of the move- ment from its beginning in 1897. And truly its history is a wonderful record of progress, such as fills one with humble thankfulness for the past and with firm hope for the future. Always remembering that "an Englishman's home is his castle,"be that home cottage or mansion,the freest possible entrance to the house has been given. Not often have we been repulsed, save in such cases as that of a child the other day, who knew that nurse's visit surely meant pain fort the moment, and who showed his disapproval by repeating again and again the fact that "he didn't want that girl with the big pinny on!" (Laughter.) Or perhaps in the case of a few stray aged Ipeople who have made no secret of the fact that they have not been thoroughly washed since infancy, and have no mind to undergo the process now in their declining days. (Laught 3r.) "One half the world does not know how the other half lives "—how true! Sad it is that a certain proportion neither know nor care—absorbed in self and their own comforts, they give little thought to their poorer and less fortunate brethren. Fortunately they are not in the majority and this association is a living witness that there are a goodly number who realize that they are "their brother's keeper," respon- sible for his wellbeing and welldoing. May we hope that in this audience there are more waiting to join this goodly number. The machinery is in order—it has been working for seven years. All it needs for its continued progress is oil for the wheels. Will you oil them ? (Applause.)

THANKS. MORE ABOUT CONGREGATIONAL COLLECTIONS Mr. JOHN FAIRCLOUGH prop"seda vote of thanks to Miss Whitfield and the nurses for their work during the past seven years. Mr. GEORGE THOMPSON seconded, and said it was a shame that the collections at places of worship should have decreased by £27 since 1901. He suggested that the Rector should approach the clergy and ministers of all denominations with the object of organizing a "Nurses Sunday." The motion was carried.

Two merabers of the audience having given personal testimony to the valuable work of the nurses, The CHAIRMAN proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Monks, the founder of the institution, who, he said, took the greatest interest in everything which con- cerned the welfare of the town. The motion was carried by acclamation. Mr. MONKS briefly replied. On the motion of Mr. THOMPSON, seconded by the Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON, the secretaries (Mrs. John Faircloigh, Mr. J. Dutton Fairclongh), and the Chair- man were thanked for their services.

div.head: BENEFITS OF SCIENCE.
div.p: THE BENEFITS OF SCIENCE.

Some of the greatest discoveries of the age, while they have proved directly beneficial to thousands, have also, at least for a time, injured other thousands. Even some of the best medi- cinal preparations, however much they may do to remove one class of disease, or suit some constitutions, at the same time either deepen the hold of another disease, or leave it entirely untouched, or if they benefit one class of patients, they may injure another. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. -- Warrington Borough Police Court.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. -- Warrington Borough Police Court.
Minor Cases.

SATeRDAY.—Before Mr.Birchall and other magistrates. SNI.A.RT CAPTURE.—John Green and Isabella Ban- croft, two strangers, were brought up on a charge of housebreaking in Manchester.Superintendeut Monaghan said he saw the male prisoner, who is a stranger in Warrington, and having his suspicions of the man's conduct, he oommunicated with the Manchester police, and ascertained that both the man and the woman who was with him were wanted there on a charge of house- breaking. Prisoners were ha.need over to two officers from Manchester. --•-- • • •
------- 310NDAY—Before the Mayor, Alderman Smethurst, Councillors Tinnion and Wilkinson, Messrs H. Thornton, J. W. Hayward, S. Wright, G. Piling and

W. Roberts. POCKET PICKING IN THE MARKET.—George Simpson. was charged with stealing a silver watch, guard and albert, of the value of £3, from the person of Michael Kerrigan, on Saturday night.—The Chief Constable said that for some time the market had been the chosen theatre'of operations of a number of thicYcs,tc the great discomfort of the tenants and loss to the general public. The prisoner, who was known far and wide as a pro- fessional pickpocket, was seen about the market, and Kerriga,n's watch and chain were dexterously removed and another mpn was relieved of his watch. Later the prisoner was caught by P.C. Lewis in the act of pawn- ing one of the watches in Winwick-road. He had pre- viously got rid of the other at another pawnshop. He was brought to the police station, and told the usual story about having bought the watches in a pdplichouse but did not know who from. They regarded the capture as an important one, and he asked for a remand that he could complete his inquiries.—The Fremand was granted.—On 'Friday, Simpson was again brought before -the magistrates, when an additional charge of stealing a watch, from the person of James Alliner was preferred against him.—He pleaded guilty to both charges and was sent to gaol for nine months with hard labour.

div.head: MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: MOTOR NOTES.

The Stanley Show at Islington has been a large and comprehensive one. The majority of the motor exhibits, however, owing to the agreement existing between Mr. Cordingley and the Stanley Show Committee, has been mostly limited to motor cycles and tri-cars, although, of course, some few vehicles have been also shewn.

Foremost among these must be mentioned the "Rover," which is a single cylinder car conducted upon lines that, are certainly unique, and the 8-10 h.p. Humber, a new four-cylinder light car which has created much interest. It is certainly a very well designed vehicle, whilst the three-seated body has many points to recommend it.

In the tri-cars displayed by the various firms throughout the building, many original and ingenious ideas were incorporated; but we doubt whether this form of motor vehicle will retain its present hold upon the affection of the public for very long. Even the cheapest types are, comparatively speaking, very expen- sive, and the aSerage motorist would rather pay the few extra pounds and become the possessor of a regular little voiturette. We were particularly taken with one machine of this class, however, which was provided with two bucket seats, placed side by side, and having quite the appearance of a miniature voiturette. These seats were quite separate, the space between them being occupied by the petrol tank which is of good capacity

Those firms which deal solely in motor clothing and accessories had gathered in great farce atlslington, and throughout the whole of the gallery the motorist was met with a bewildering array of lamps, goggles, horns, motor grease, chains, pumps, jacks, &c., and at intervals were suddenly confronted by various dummies correctly clad from head to foot in different styles of suitable clothing recommended for the use of practical motorist of both sexes.

Tt has been said that in all the works of nature the antidote for every poison is to be found close at hand. However this may be, we do not know; but upon ap- parently the same principle,we noticed that, in pleasing juxtaposition to several standr devoted to the exhibi- tion of pneumatic tyres, there were most appropriately located the venders of patent repairing outfits designed for use on tyres of cycles, motor cycles and cars as well. The well-known Patcho " firm has some new lines,in- eluding a quick vulcanising fluid and " patcho "solu- tion to be used in the ordinary way with prepared rubber patches, as well as the new famous " Patcho " cement whichacts practically as a puncture-stop.

Upon one stand, in addition to the generous display of motor clothing etc., with which it was adorned, we noticed rather a novelty in the way of a musical motor horn. This, however, did not appear to be worked upon at all the same lines as the " Tally Ho !" horn recently patented by Mr. Moffat Ford. which, giving a range of four clear and bell-like tones, closely resembles the post-horn in its cheery signalling.
• A.A.

div.head: OLD AGE PENSIONS
div.p: OLD AGE PENSIONS
Discussed by the Social Service League

Mr. E. OSBORNE presided at the weekly debate in connection with the Social Service League which was held in Golborne-street schoolroom on Thursday evening. There was a fair attendance.—lt was unanimously decided to hold all future debates on Thursday instead of Friday evening. The subject under discussion was "Old age pensions" and the Rev.. H. Dunnico introduced the debate with an interesting paper. He said that of the many schemes suggested for the amelioration of the condition of the poor there was none perhaps which appealed ,to the imagination as that which proposed 'to provide at the expense of the State, wholly or ' partially, a pension sufficient to enable the deserving aged man or woman to live out their days free from the horrors of poverty, and the prospect of the Work- house. The rev. gentleman proceeded to refer to various schemes which had been advanced in this country for providing pensions. He did not hesitate to say that it was distinctly annoying to find that any practical effort to test the possibilities of the best schemes had been checked by an attempt by both parties to make political capital out of the matter. In his opinion the idea was too noble to be made a eatch 'question by any party. (Hear, hear.) If we were to help the deserving poor we must not , pauperise them, and any scheme of old age pensions ' ought to stand at least the following tests: (1) It must aim at helping the deserving poor and them alone. , (2) It must encourage reasonable thrift. (3) It must be kept quite free from any taint of pauper relief. (4) , It must not be excessively expensive. (5) It must ' ultimately result in a reduction of poor law expendi- ture. He fully realized how hard it was to help others wisely. It was one thing to stand up at street corners and public meetings expounding Utopian schemes amidst the applause of a crowd. It was another thing to come and deal with men in the concrete. After criticising in detail various proposals, Mr. Dunnico said he granted that the case he had put before them was somewhat depressing and the pros- pect of solving the problem was not very hopeful. Still on the'other hand,old age*pension schemes were in vogue in other nations and if they had been able to grapple with the difficulties confronting them, we should not be true Britons if we were down in despair. New Zealand I had set us a brilliant example, but in his opinion it was to Denmark we must turn for guidance. There they had boldly taken the step of providing old age pensions for the deserving poor and were trusting to experience to suggest remedies. Under their scheme the peusions varied according to the locality. A higher pension was paid in the city where the cost of living was higher than in the village. The average pension for a man was about £6 to RS 10s. per annum and for man and wife £8 to RB.los. In addition there was a Government institution where men might do Fight work and receive their bed and lodgings as well as a small amount of pocket money. Two important aspects of the question to be considered were: "Would the establishment of old-age pensions encourage or dis- courage thrift. Would it adversely affect the working ' classes by lowering wages? An interesting discussion followernut the difficulties of establishing a practical scheme were freely recog- nized. It was suggested by Mr. Hawthorne that employers might adopt a system of deferred pay to be given to the men when they attained a certain age. There would, of cotarse, have to be a national system to deal with the workless classes. _

Mr. ENGLAND said crime and poverty were not altogether due to the individual but to the condition he had been forced into by the state of society. He would support a scheme to give to every person who required the money on reaching a certain age a pension. Mr. MORTON was of the opinion that pensions would adversely affect wages. - Unless certain economic diffi- culties were removed he did not see how any system could benefit the aged people without doing a great amount of evil in other directions. _ _
Mr. NIGFITING!LLE, Mr. TROW and others took part in the discussion.

- rbe Rev, H. Dowststp contended that the workingman himself was the greatest obstacle to formulating a scheme. No one would support a system of pensions more cordially than he (Mr; Dunnico) if they could help the deserving poor and refuse to help the undeserving. A separate 'system would have to be devised for the destitute but undesarving section. The On' trnm.ol recognized that the question was fraught with many difficulties. He did not see any reason why by individual contributions a sinking fund could not be created and pensions paid from it.

div.head: PEN KETH.
div.p: PEN KETH.

SOCIAL EY EN IN G . —Another of the pleasant social gatherings was held last Friday night in the St. Niary's Mission Room. The subject was "Farthest North," and the lantern slides showed scenes in the journey of Nansen in his recent research in the polar regions. Battle pictures illastrating the operations in the present war in the east, were shown, and the evening was a most successful one. No charge is made for admission at these functions, but a small collection is taken to defray expenses. The Rev. J. R. Jones, M.A. (Vicar), read the explanatory text, and the lantern was in charge of Mr. James Woodward.

A CHAT ABOUT BOOKS.—A very interesting paper was given at the weekly meeting of the Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Association on Wednesday night last. The Rev. R. Wilkins Rees was the essayist, and his subject was" A chat about books." The paper was much enjoyed, and an interesting discussion took place at the conclusion, and the rev. gentleman was cordially thanked for his efforts.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON. E
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON. E
SMALL CHANGE AND BIG ACTIONS.

_ On Saturday, Robert Worrall, moulder, Vulcan Village, Earlestown, sent his wife to get some beer for him, and on her return quarrelled with her as to the amount of change he had received. To lend force to his words, it is alleged, he struck her, kicked her, and rushed at her with an open knife, one of her fingers being badly cut. At the police court, on Monday, prisoner was remanded. NEWTON CRICKET, BOWLING AND TENNIS CLUB.' A most enjoyable social evening, which about 120 attended, was held in the Town Hall, Newton, on Wed- nesday evening to provide funds for the purchase of material to be made up by the ladies' sewing class,who are working most energetically for the bazaar to be held in May 1905. Refreshments were given by the Ladies' Committee and a few friends. Mr. Sudworth's band played for dlncing, and gave every satisfaction. The duties of M.C.'s were most ably carried out by Messrs. I'. Williams and R. Carson.

div.head: IRON AND STZL:i, TRADES.
div.p: THE IRON AND STZL:i, TRADES.
WARRINGTON WORKERS: AND THE
WAGES CRISIS.
Depression Not Due to Free Trade. SPEECHES BY MR. JAMES COMANr MR. A. H. CROSFIELD.
THE PREDOMINANT QUESTION

to be settled when the next election took place. They had heard that night a great many facts of paramount importance dealing with that enormous industry of the iron trade, and he was going to say a word or two about another industry which was equally mpfirtant Before doing so he would give them a bit of b. :personal experience in regard to an industry which was fa/ smaller than the one they had been considering but which certainly afforded a very striking example of the position that Britain held in the wor ls •scompetitionas influenced by our policy of free imports. When he went to business twenty-two years ago, he saw that their home trade, the old-fashioned cl of business which was established by his grand- father in the first instance, and developed largely by his uncle, George Crosfteld, and also by his father and his uncle Moreland Crosfleld, was, by reason of fluctuations in trade% and demand, dwindling and diminishing. It was, in fact, rapidly disappearing, and he had to buckle to, and from 1885 to 1895, with the assistance and co-operation of • other people, see that they replaced that class of trade with a totally different and more convenient style of modern production. It was not upon that that he wanted to dwell that night, because at the same time he was engaged in dealing with that alteration they had to face in trade, it struck him that they ought to develop pan i passzt with that home industry as good an export connection as they could. He could assure his hearers that from that time to the present day he had been most intimately asso- ciated with the

GRADUAL DEVELOPMENT OF THE EXPORT TRADE they now had, which extended to all the open markets of the world. It was that which had suggested to him an illustration which he thought was rather striking. While developing their own business abroad, the firm watched very closely what was being done by all their competitors in the United Kingdom and by their competitors in other markets. He had the figures constantly More him of exports from Germany, and the United States, and the amount of production in many of those open markets he was referrins to. It was perfectly true that there were prohibitive duties placed upon household soap which- prevented British firms shipping to markets like France, Germany, Russia, Spain, or the United States. But, let them consider the other side of the picture. They had, as in the cotton trade of Lancashire, an important demand from China. He did not know how far the cotton trade had made its way into China; but in the soap trade they had only as yet touched the fringe of that huge population of 400 millions. The merchants his firm dealt with informed him that their goods had not penetrated up country to an extent that would supply more than perhaps a fourth or fifth of the population. In addition they had India, the Straits Settlements, and the whole market of South Africa (which, for instance, took almost its entire supply of soap from England), the West Indies, Egypt, and many miaor markets he could name to them. All those markets were open to the free competition of the world. He had come across shipments from Ausz,ria, and he had seen many attempts made by German manufacturers to establish themselves in thosa markets. Above all the manufacturers of America, where the supply of raw materials was very convenient for the manufacture of soap, &c., had made a prolonged and determined effort to cat out the firms who were doing the business. The American manufacturer, protected in his home markets, had shipped his surplus products just as was done in other industries. Mr. Cox had spoken of the

div.head: LACK OF EMPLOYMENT IN AMERICA
div.p: LACK OF EMPLOYMENT IN AMERICA

and of the none too favourable condition of the steel trade. In the soap industry there was more lack of employmsnt and a less satisfactory condition of affairs in America at the present time than there was in this country. That had induced the manufacturers to try and secure outlets in many places abroad, and particu- larly to secure outlets where freights were in their favour. They got the New Orleans manufacturer coming into Demerara and others into Trinidad and Barbados where they were making a very prolonged effort to establish themselves. They had even gone as far as Ce.petnwn, and in that place for, about four years there was a very determined attempt made by one of the most powerful manufacturers in America. In the end all this effort had resulted in failure, and the American competitors had retired from those markets. He could show his hearers that except- ing trade which amounted to a mere bagatelle .the whole of the export soap trade of the world at the present time was being done in the main by the United Kingdom, and about nine-tenths of , the export trade of the United Kingdom was being done by three firms established here on the Mersey. (Hear, hear.) He thought that was a significant illustration of what advantage it VMS for British manufacturers to be able to buy their own raw material withont any let or hindrance, to have the command of all the markets of the world, and to know that, thanks to our Free Trade system, their cost of manu- facture was below the cost of manufacture of the most powerful firms in America or Germany. Consequently in the long run the foreign firms were unable to 'compete with us in those neutral markets wLich, important as they were now, as civilization made more and more progress would become of still greater importance in the future not only to our com- paratively small industries such as the soap trade but to the vast industry at our own doors which was the backbone of the whole life of Lancashire. (Applause.) Alluding to
THE COTTON TRADE

Mr. Crosfield pointed out that on returning from the great meeting at RaNyteustall he had the pleasure of a conversation with Mr. Tom Garnett who had had a wide experience in regard to that industry. Mr. Garnett mentioned that roughly speaking he thought we in Lancashire would be sending about £20,000,000 worth of cotton per year to India. On the other hand the stun total of what- the Germans were able to send to that great country was about a paltry £130,000 worth, and from America only about £150,000 worth of cotton goods were shipped —a mere drop in the bucket. Mr. Garnett also informed him that for every pound of cotton America sent us we sent her fifteen ponnds, while for every pound Germany sent us we exported to that country three pounds. Those were facts which it would be well for the politi- cal plunger of Birminghareto take into consideration —(hear, hear)—before he came down to Preston to talk to the Lancashire people about the cotton trade. He (Mr. Crosfield) had the pleasure of listening to the speech the Duke of Devonshire made at the Rawtenstall meeting. Although the Duke was by no means as ad- vanced as he (Mr. Crosfield) took it most of those present at the ironworkers' meeting and he himself were in general politics, still he (Mr. Crosfield) must say he thought it spoke well for British statesmanship to hear the Duke speak as he did on that matter of Protection. They might say the Duke was a very wealthy man and it did not matter to him if there was no protective duty put on, but all wealthy men were not, he (the speaker) was sorry to say as public spirited as the Duke on this great question. He (Mr, Crosfield) was very much impressed and he felt a great deal of admiration for the way in which the old Duke spoke with real earnestness and sincerity against

THE SHAMEFUL POLICY of taxing food and manufactures—(hear, hear)— although he knew that if a tax was put upon corn com- ing into the country it would eventually send up his own rents and put more money into his pocket. The Duke was far too public-spirited to endeavour to take advantage of the community at large in any such way. He (the speaker) was quite sure the Duke's speech was going to have very great weight throughoutlthe country with that large number of people who were not very strong partisans one way or the other. He wanted to give the meeting one other little illustration of what had occurred under the Protection regime while he (Mr. Crosfield) was in America. Mr. Cox hal told them that one of the inevitable results of Protection was the formation of cartels and trusts. While he was in America a dozen of the great sugar magnates met and arranged that they would put up the price of that commodity. The advance was made because there was no objectionable outside competition to prevent it.A nice little Protective duty kept all that out of the way and the result was that 80 millions of the American people had to pay so much a pound more for their sugar simply to enrich perhaps a dozen or I fifteen men. ("Shame.") The American trusts had got so i strong that they controlled everything and in many cases , not only the wholesale but the retail trade. He was assured on very good authority that four men in Chicago could alter the price of butcher's meat in every shop in the United States if they chose to do so —to such an extent had the system of trusts been carri ect on in the United States. As Sir Henry James put it at Rawtenstall and as so many people had put the case, it simply came to this : "If you are going in for Protection simply to serve the interests of a privileged few, you are going to make the rich richer and the poor poorer." (Applause.) They should set their faces absolutely against that. (Hear, hear.) Those who believed in progressive work in politics were not content to go into the next election merely on a negation, to fight solely on the question of Free Trade. It would be•a, big enough issue, but there were numerous issues of enormous consequence to everybody in this kingdom, and many of them were going to be planks in their platform. Before they could make progress in that direction, at least let them take care that they did not take a fatal retrogressive step. He was not one of those who thought they could equalise everything and put everyone on a level footing,' but he hoped gradually and by degrees to see Wore equal distribu- tion of wealth in the future, (Hear, hear). That, in a great measure, might be brought about through well- considered and reasonable reform in taxation. The .i. policy of Prote,.:tion would have the very opposite a effect. and they therefore absolutely ruled it out. At 1 the Rawtenstall meeting, which representatives from every part of Lancashire attended, he was struck by the feeling manifested which made it perfectly certain what

div.head: ANSWER LANCASHIRE WAS GOING TO GIVE
div.p: ANSWER LANCASHIRE WAS GOING TO GIVE

to this wild-cat and unscrupulous scheme. There was no doubt about Lancashire's answer. The question was what they in the old town of ‘Varrington, the half- way house between Liverpool and Manchester at the very gate of the county Palatine, were going to do. He hoped Mr. Cox's speech would be pondered by everyone in the iron trade and that no one would be led away by the specious and not altogether disinterested special pleading on the question which they had had in the town. He had given them a little illustration from his own business. That was the first time he had spoken on the question in that way for the very reason that other people were doing their utmost to make political capital out of their own businesses and any interests where they thought they might be specially favoured— (hear, hear)—and he thought it was quite time that those who believe I in Free Trade should not hesitate to speak out as regarded their own experiences. (Applause). They held very strong opinions on that matter and on many other questions. It was very kind of there to have asked him to address that meeting. There might be some present who differed from him politically—he had no doubt there were— but ho was sure they would forgive him for speaking quite plainly his own views. (Applause). Knowing how little they had to hope in this neighbourhood in the way of assistance from people of socal position and influence, they who were responsible for helping on the progressive cause in Warrington came to the conclusion that it would be better for them to make a straight appeal to the intelligent artisan classes of Warn ngton,and they were doing so. They asked for united support from the whole of the intelligent artizans of the town. He knew he was speaking to a trade union which had been the very back bone of the Liberal party. The members had stood by the party when the conditions were dull and depressing and black clouds were in the sky, with a faithfulness and fidelity which the workers of the party would never forget. Their appeal was made in a very special manner to that trade union; but he would like to say that they also appealed to all the other trade unions and to TUT WHOLE OF THE TABOUR PARTY of Warrington. At the head of the programme which he asked them to support came the defence of Free Trade. Mr. Crosfleld proceeded to enumer- ate the other objects of the Progressive Labour League as follows :—(2) resistance to Chinese or any other form of slave labour in any other part of the British dominions; (3) the establishment of a national education scheme; (4) defence of trade unions and the protection of their funds; (5) amending of the House of Lords ; (6) improved land laws and taxation of land values, especi- ally in and near cities and towns; (7) justice to Ireland; (8) improved liquor laws; (9) army reform. Nothing, he believed, was more urgent than that the taxation of land values should be dealt with. It had been very urgent fora long time and it was more urgent than ever now. They had had a policy which John Burns described as "plundering and blundering" going on for about eight years. They had had the savings of thirty or forty years of resourceful British statesmanship utterly squandered, and additions had beeil made to the national debt which would be a burden not only upon them but upon future generations. When we came to feel the real effect of competition in the days when they had got rid of protective duties over the water and America stepped in as a Free Trader we should begin to repent building up this mountain of debt like a millstone round our necks when we had to compete onan equal platform with our cousins aeross the wate-. People who had done lip service to peace had winked at Chitral: they had laughed at Thibet, and turned a blind eye to that mad business in Somaliland. He held the opinion more strongly now than ever that we 1 allowed ourselves to be

HOODWINKED AND MISLED in the most appalling and shameful manner over that South African war. (Hear, hear.) We spent 250 millions of money and he said distinctly—and he had good information from South Africa from men on the spot—that from the purely materialist point of view, if from no other, we were worse off to-day than we were before we fought the campaign. (Hear, hear.) Before the • war, there was no more loyal section of the community in any part of the Queen's dominions than we had amongst the Dutch of South Africa. But by the abominable machina- tions of those German Jews on the rand, controlling the correspondence of the London Press, nobbling Lord Milner, misleading Chamberlain--for he granted they had mlsle.4 him—we had been misled over the whole thing, and it was a sorry prospect indeed for British workingmen, who were told they were going to fight a miners' war, if they looked at the little game that was being played in Johannesburg just now. (Hear, hear.) The whole thing was perfectly disgusting, and apart from all the small wars on which we had wasted money, we had the enormous ex- penditure of 250 millions, and on the top of all that, without any adequate return, a vast increase in our normal annual expenditure amounting to 50 millions sterling. A splendid measure was passed by the late Sir William Harcourt in the death duties which were an admirable means of raising taxa- tion and placed the burden on the shoulders of those who could best afford to bear it (Hear, hear). If it had not been for that measure, he wondered how the Tories would have pulled through at all. They opposed it tooth and nail,but it had just saved them through these years of reckless expenditure. When they began to think of old age pensions and that kind of thing, the question arose "Where is the money to come from ? " Without going into detail he was sure, if they considered the state of the finances of the country and the expenditure which had got up to such enormous figures, they would agree that the taxation of land values was a measure for which they ought to fight very hard. (Applause.) He respectfully asked the work- ingmen of Warrington to back them up in carrying through the programme he had read. It had been said that when the Liberal party were returned to power—as they would be returned at the next election—they would not be able to do very much. He thought they ought all to realize the fear- ful obstacles which had been placed in their way by the kind of work which had been going on. It was no use returning the progressives to power for a short spell and then allowing that wire-puller, that American political "boss " of Birmingham— because that was really what he was—to step in and gull them with some other red herring drawn across the path. (Hear, hear.) They in War- rington made their appeal to the workingmen frankly and they hoped they might see their way to give them all the help they could. (Applause).

div.head: CONCLUDING SPEECHES.
div.p: CONCLUDING SPEECHES.

Councillor BURTON thought the ,iron and a steel workers could do a great deal by organizing deputations to continental firms to endeavour to get the same rate of wages paid to employes in those firms, as was paid in England. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded the chairman for his services and the meeting concluded.

Under the above title, Messrs. Hassard and Co., 180 Great Britain-street, Dublin, have issued a pamphlet which they offer free, as will be seen from our advertis- ing columns. It deals with a new method of treating many diseases, internally, by means of an embrocation and ointment called" Vita-Leo." The successes which have been achieved by means of their treatment cer- tainly seem marvellous. Yet in the light of latter-day discoveries, it is scareely surprising that such a panacea for human ills should be found, and Messrs. Hassard offer every guarantee as to the accuracy of their state- ments. Vita-Leo (embrocation) covers the ground from colds to rheumatism, pneumonia, fevers erysipelas, and many other complaints, while the ointment is a remedy for ulcers, bad legs, blood poison &c. The prices are small and these remedies are worth atrial.

A message from St. Louis reports that Prince Fusohimi has been robbed of three jewelled rings worth 5,00 dollars. They were taken from his rooms at the Buckingham Club whilst he was absent at the World's Fair.—The police have no clue to the thieves.—" Central News."

div.p: Two ri
Diagram 30 shows positions for the ordinary long run-through in-off from baulk. There are two distinct ways of playing this stroke. The first is by a strong slashing stroke with plenty

- of top and side—this is the way the stroke is played by most amateurs. The other and the MOTO scientific way is by a medium-pace stroke with plenty of drag and side—this is the way the stroke is generally played by all good class players. When the run-through with the object ball at A is played by a slashing stroke with top, little or no command can be had over the ball which will generally remain in baulk, whereas the medium-paced stroke with drag and side -Will always keep the ball in the 'field of play. Of the two ways, however, of playing the run-through with the object ball at A, the top speed stroke is undoubtedly the easier for all ordinary players, for the top and speed tend to keep the cue ball on the cushion and very little side is sufficient to carry it into the pocket, in fact the stroke can be got without any side at all. !All players, however, who occasionally make forties and fifties should discard the slash- ing strobe in favour of the aledium-pace stroke with drag. The reason that drag must be used with a comparatively slow stroke is because other- wise the side on the ball working in conjunction with the nap of the cloth (as explained in the chapter on "Side") would pull the cue ball out of its course before the object ball was reached. Also in slow strokes side is retained much longer when drag is used than when the cue ball is hit above the centre. When the object ball lies high up the side cushion as at B on, Diagram 30, the run-through should also be played by the medium-pace stroke, but in this position the top speed stroke is alsc a sound enough stroke, for it will always drive the object ball in and out of baulk. Iforeovez the top speed stroke is really quite easy. Played in this way, aim should be taken quite full on to the object ball and the cue ball should be hit well above the centre and without any side. Plenty of pace is required
GRAM 31
Bun-through in-offs that require running aid* owing to the cue ball having to travel against tilt nap of the cloth.

Diagram 31 shows a position {either side of the table) for a run-through in-off played from the spot end of the table, that is, against the nap of the cloth. Many very fair players would play such a stroke in exactly the same way as if playing from the baulk end of the table, viz., with check side, and repeated failures would never open their eyes to the real reason of their want of success.

If played with check side—right hand side in position A—the cue ball (presuming that the object ball has been truly struck) will after con- tact commence to run seemingly all right, but instead of clinging to the cushion it will, as it travels down the table, pull more and more away from it until by the , time the baulk cushion is reached the cue ball may easily be six inches or more away from the side cushion (as shown on the diagram) especially if it has travelled down the table rather slowly, and there is a good nap on the cloth. As explained very fully in the chapter on SIDE, side on a ball has just the reverse effect (as far as the running of the ball on the bed of the table is concerned) when a stroke is played against the nap of the cloth, of what it has when a stroke is played with the nap. Therefore in position A, check side, instead of causing the cue ball to cling to the cushion (or to pull it on to the cushion if at first it were travelling down the table just a little away from it), has the effect of pulling the ball away from the cushion. It may also be pointed out that side always takes the most effect after a very full contact with an object ball, for the full contact destroys the gaailer part of the momentum of the cue ball, thus giving much fuller play to any side or spin which it may carry. If this run-through against the nap be played with running side—right hand side in position B—the side will pull the cue ball to the cushion should it, after contact; be running down the table just a little away from the cushion. Once an the cushion it will hug it right down to the pocket.

- What makes this stroke very much more difficult than the correspolicling stroke up the table is the fact that this runnin,, side on the cue ball is the wrong side to take it into the pocket should the ball strike the oppesing angle, viz., the 'ankle of the baulk cushion. When a run-through in-off is played with check side, the side is always pocket side off the opposing angle, and the pccket is thus greatly enlarged. In the stroke under discussion, however, check side could never enlarge the pocket, for the simple reason that a cue ball carrying check side could never get near the pocket (on a cloth with a nap) no matter how often ;the stroke were played. Running side, therefore must be used, and a well played stroke will cause the cue ball to hug the cushion so closely that even though the opposing angle be struck it will be struck at a point inside the fall of the slate, and thus the ball will fall into the pockct in spite of the,side not being pocket side off the opposing angle.
(To be Continued.)

div.head: ROBERTS V. HARVERSON MATCH.
div.p: THE ROBERTS V. HARVERSON MATCH.

If any further proof was wanted that John Roberts can at least hold his own with any of the greatest players in the laud, his play last week when conceding Harverson 2,750 in 9,000 furnished it. It was not so much that he won the game by over 500 as the way he played. He gave the spectators the idea that he always had the game in hand, notwithstanding that Harverson played consistently well, and one afternoon quite brilliantly, making 248 and 271 in rapid succession. The large Billiard Hall at Messrs. Orme and Sons was crowded every af terno on and eveningnotwithstanding that Roberts had been playing all the previous week. Roberts' play is however, always so fascinating to watch even though he may be only making sixties and seventies, that the same people go time after time to watch him. Many of the leading Manchester amateur cueists were there daily, in fact the week was a billiard feast to local players. Roberts's biggest breaks during the match were 344 and 381 and the manner in which these breaks were compiled makes it pretty safe to say that it will not be long before a 500 break will have to be recorded to the King of billiard players. Next week some notes will be given on the match now in progress between Roberts and Inman. Owing to pressure of space, answers to correspond- ents are unavoidably left over till next week. NORTHERN LEAGUE.
First Division. NORTHERN RUGBY LEAGUE. FIRST DIVISION. G. T. P. G. T. P. Leeds 3 3 15 Rtincona

Salford 3 2 12 Hunslet 3 0 6 Oldham 1 1 5 Bradford Hull Warrington Br'ghton Rangers 2 1 7 Widnes 0 2 6 Wakefield Trinity 1 2 8 Hull Kingston R 0 0 0 Leigh 1 414 St Helens 1 1 5 Halifax WARRINGTON v. BATtEY.

There was a gate of about 4,000 at Warrington on Saturday when Batley, the present wooden-spoonists of the League, paid their annual visit. Warrington were still without Hockenhall and Boardman, the two Davies's playing together at half back for the first time. Fine weather again favoured the game. The teams and officials were : Warrington—Hallam, back; Fish, Isherwood, Dicken- son, and Harris, three-quarter backs; Jack Davies and Di Davies, half backs; Thomas, Shugars, Belton, Cook, Jolley, Naylor, Preston, and Morrison, forwards. Batley—O'Brien, back; W. Davies, Turton, Goodall and Johnson, three-quarter backs; Robinson and Bogg half backs; Tebbutt, Fozzard, Shackleton, Wade,Settle, Judge, Kidson, and Hodgson, forwards. Referee, Mr. G. F. Dickenson. Touch judges,Messrs. W. Mainwaring, Salford, and L. Lee, Leigh. Play opened directly in Warrington's favour and some fine kicking was witnessed. Preston had a lengthy penalty shot, which just failed, but Fish made amends a few minutes later with a similar opportunity. Then I for a time Batley made a better show, Robinson and Turton putting in good work. J. Davies started ai brilliant movement in the centre, and the ball travelled rapidly across to Harris who rushed over at the corner but lost the ball. Warrington maintained the pressure and Di Davies cleverly bluffed Robinson in order to run over behind the posts. Fish landed a second goal. The visitors were quite unable to cope with the strong scrummaging and speedy pacing of the Warrington men and before half time J. Davies completed a fine effort by dashing over in good position. Fish hit the cross bar wi th his kick at goal. The scorer was injured as he fell over the line by Hodgson, who was sent , off by the referee. Half time: Warrington 10 points; Batley nil.

Turning round, Warrington forced the game in the Batley quarters, and futile efforts to score were made by Preston, Dickenson, and Isherwood. Play degener- ated considerably, though Batley made a better show. From some exciting play at the Batley end Wattle Davies intercepted a pass, and kicked over Hallam's head, but the visitor was robbed of possession a yard from the line. Batley's hard luck did not end here, for Johnson missed a try with the line at his mercy, and following this let off Warrington took the game to the opposite end, and Di Davies scored an unimproved try. Result :—Warrington 2 goals 3 tries (13 points), Batley nil.

div.head: CHESHIRE JUNIOR LEAGUE.
div.p: CHESHIRE JUNIOR LEAGUE.

ROBERTSON'S V. WIDNES ROVERS.-At Widnes on Saturday. The home team won the toss and the visitors kicked off before a strong breeze. Robertson's attacked but were driven into their own half,They were thenpena- lised and Noon from a good shot scored a goal. Resuming, play went into the home 25. Bailey making a good attempt to break through. From a long kick the home team found touch, and play again came into Robertson's 25, when Burns receiving evaded all opposition and scored an unconverted try. At half-tune Widnes Rovers led by 51points to Robertson's nil. Resuming the visitots had the best of it, and play kept in the local 25, when following up a long kick Jones rushed up and caught the ball and dashed over. The same player failed at goal. Resuming, Robertson's kept play well up the field, and from two penalties .unsuccessful attempts at goal were made. Ashton kicked well in touch, but owing to the very soft state of the ground, which was entirely void of grass, the fine passing tactics of the visiting backs were spoiled. Result—Widnes Rovesr 5 points, Robertson's 3 points.
