div.head: LIBERALISM IN THE KNUTSFORD
div.p: LIBERALISM IN THE KNUTSFORD
DIVISION. Meeting at _ 6-Inpenhall.

Owing to the wretched state -of the weather on Mondaynight there was only a meagre attendance at a meeting which was held in the Large Room, Grappenhall, under the auspices of the Knutsford Division Liberall Association. Mr. C. Jackson Holmes presided, and was supported by Mr. A. J. King, vice-president of the Association, and the prospective Liberal candidate at the next Parliamentary election in the Division, Mr. Wm. Long, Mr. J. Middleton, of !the National Reform I Union, and Mr. J. Smith, Liberal agent. The CHAIRMAN remarked that when he last took the chair in that room a good many people thought the general election was close upon us, but we now heard very little of that subject. He supposed it was because those members already in the House of Commons— especially Conservative members—were anxious to retain their seats as long as possible, because it seemed to be taken for granted that at the next general election there would be a great change in the constitution of the House, with a result that a great many of the Conserva- , tiva gentlemen were in fear and trembling of losing their seats. It was now generally expected that the general election would be at the end of next year, though one great statesman, the Duke of Devon- shire, had stated that Parliament would dissolve at a much earlier date than was probably contemplated. The Duke of Devonshire foreshadowed a dissolution after the next Parliamentary• session, but though we might have longer of the present government than we anticipated, and had had to swallow their retrograde measures, it was perhaps not a bad thing as they were given time in which to enligten their constituents—if they requiredenlightening—upon the fallacy of the pro- ' tection cry—a redicuious cry—which at one time ap- peared to be assuming a somewhat serious aspect. Mr. Chamberlain was a man who seemed to have speeches read to suit all classes as was shown by recent speeches made by him. Iu one he said his proposals would encourage British farming and would bring into cultivation thou- sands of acres of derelict land. In another speech be said his proposals would encourage wheat growing in the colonies and would therefore increase the amount of wheat in the world with the result that with an in- creased supply there would be a falling in price which would benefit the workingman. If his proposals would lead to an increased supply and a consequent falling in price, he (the speaker) did not see how the British farmer was to be benefitted.especially when he found it hard enough to grow wheat at a profit at present prices. He hoped the farmers in that district would think over that point. He believed the country would do well and would act most wisely in returning to power that party which trusted the people and whose motto was Government by the people and for the people. Mr. Chamberlain wished to legislate avowedly for one class at the expense of every other class and to the detriment of the community as a whole. The object of the Liberal party on the other hand was to pass laws for the benefit of the whole community and when the general election came he hoped they would do all that lay in their power to see that Mr. King was returned as their representative. (Applause.) Mr. King said that during the last 12 months we had had another session of Parliament which had been barren and weary. During the whole of that period practically only two acts had been passed. One of these was with the object of forcing upon Wales an educational system which she did not want and which she repudiated. The other act passed during the past year by the present Government was the " Endowment of Brewers Act" more commonly known as the Licensing Act, which became law because during the last year or two the magistrates of the country wakened up to the fact that they had it in their power to deal with appli- cation for the renewal of licenses in a manner similar to that in which they dealt with applications for new licenses on the merits of the case. That power they commenced to exercise to a limited extent and as soon as they did so the brewers went to Mr. Balfour and threatened to put him out of office unless he did something for them. Mr. Balfour promised to help them and lectured the magistrates for their conduct and even went to advise Quarter Sessions toreverse the decisions come.to in the lower courts,advice which was hardly in accordance with the constitution of this country. When he did introduce his Bill for the relief of brewers be applied the closure so vigorously that the Bill was rushed through the House of Commons without being discussed or express( d. Mr. Balfour described that Act as a measure for temperance reform though it was a singular fact that temperance reformers —men who had spent their lives studying the question- did not agree with Mr. Balfour, but regarded the Act a retrograde and destructive measure, over which the only people who rejoiced were the brewers. He would not go into details with regard to that Act, but would content himself with saying that it was the object of the Liberal party not to wipe that Act off the Statute Book, but as shey recognised there were some good points contained in it to amend its worst features. The Member for the Division had been showing unwonted activity of late and had been telling his constituents some nice fairy tales. He had told a meeting at Bollington that a bounty upon exported cotton goods granted by the Government in 1873, had given such an impetus to the cotton trade that the exports went up 2,000 per cent, though he altogether failed to take into account in his speech the tremendous impetus give to the trade by reason of the mechanical inventions which were brought out about that time, and which gave to Lancashire the proud position she occupied to-day in the cotton trade. Mr. Egerton also omitted to mention that prior to that year it was illegal for people in this country to wear British made cotton goods. Mr. Egerton went on to illustrate how, to his mind, our cotton trade was going down under a system of Free Trade, by comparing the number of people employed in that trade in 1891 with the number employed in 1901. Looked at broadly those figures did appear to imply that our trade was decreasing, but analysed they showed that while the number of children employed had decreased by over 43,000, as a result of educational enactments the number of adults employed had gone up by over 19,000 during the last year or two. Owing to a scarcity of raw material times had been very bad in the cotton ' taade,put those times had been passed through largely owineto the fortitude displayed by the cotton opera- tives. At the present time there was a prospect of the cotton trade being as good as it had been at any period during the last 40 years, manufacturers being air eady booked up until next August,

THE FISCAL QUESTION. Mr. King .proceeded to deal with the question of tariff reform. With regard to the promise which was made that if Mr. Chamberlain's fiscal proposals were adopted the price of food would not go up. he .would

point out that the same promise was made two years ago at the sugar convention. It was then stated that the price of sugar would not go up, but in spite of that sugar was dearer by ss. per hundred weight than it was at the time of the convention. That increase meant that the people of this country had to face an extra expenditure of £8,000,000 per annum, and that all the businesses which were built up when sugar was cheap had been severely hit. In face of the effect of the sugar convention he thought they had no reason to believe that a tax upon food stuffs would not increase the price of food (hear, hear). Mr. Chamberlain further argued that when his scheme was adopted, even if food were dearer, wages would go up. That argument was con- trary to all results which had been arrived at so far. From the year 1880 to the year 1900 the price of food had fallen 30 per cent, rents had been reduced by 25 per cent, whilst wages had risen by 9 per cent. That he thought rather lisproved the theory that a rise in the price of food meant a rise in wages (hear, hear). He hoped that at the next election they would by an over- whelming majority show their adherance to our free trade policy. (Applause),

ONE GREAT DANGER with which we were taxed at the present time was the enormous accumulation of capital underlthe controll of a few persons. To illustrate the danger of that he would take the example afforded by the brewers. They made no mistake but said without hesitation that their trade was their politics, and that at election times they would devote the whole of their energy in support of the man who would do the most for their trade. When other trades reached the power held by the brewers their cry would he the same, and if we had protection we should 'see every powerful trade working, not for the man who had at heart the interests of the community, but for the man who would promote the interests of their particular trade. (Hear, hear.) When the present Government came into office in 1895 it pledged itself to a course of social legislation but they had practically done nothing *for the working- men, though they had carried out

LEGISLATION FOR PRIVILEGED CLASSES and for the stimulation of certain industries. He moved "that the meeting condemns this Government for its Protectionist propaganda, for its financial wastefulness and its passing of the Education and Licensing Acts against the will of the people." (Applause.) With regard to the financial wastefulness pf the Government he thought the fact that our expenditure was now R 50,000,900 a year more than it was in 1895 would speak for itself. (Applause.) Mr. Middleton s.oonded. He thought the Govern- ment was being condemned, not alone by the Liberals, but by its own supporters.'The member for the division speaking at a recent meeting said he thought it would be a good thing if Parliament was not &ailed together for two or three years as we had had enough

GRANDMOTHERLY LEGISLATION. He would remind Mr. Egerton that he belonged to that party which he accused of giving grandmotherly legis- lation to the country. (Applause.) If the Government had only been guilty of the charge •made against it by Mr. Egerton no serious complaints could be made but what they did complain of was the mischievous legislation passed by the Government. (Hear, hear,) They had passed Acts which would not work as witness the Housing Act. That Act provided that every agri- cultural labourer should live in a house of his own upon his fulfilling certain conditions. The first was that he must. possess one-fifth of the amount of the cost of the house,and'as no respectable cottage could be built for less than £lOO that meant the labourer must have £2O. The labourer must then go to his landlord and induce that gentleman to let him have the land upon which to build his house. Having done this he had then to go to his local authority which might give him the remaining four-fifths of his purchase money, though they were under no compulsion to do so. He thought they would agree with him that that was a most ridicu ions method of attempting to solve the housing problem. (Applans.) If they wanted that question solving they would havtto go to the party which would legislate for them—the Liberal party. (Applause.) He would like to know exactly what Mr. Egerton's attitude was upon the fiscal question. Mr. Egerton had said he supported Mr. Balfour in the first instance but he thought Mr. Chamberlain's proposals commended them- selves more to the country. (Laughter.) What were Mr. Chamberlain's proposals? Mr. Chamberlain pro- posed that we should tax all corn except maize and all meat except bacon. As compensation he would reduce the taxes upon tea and tobacco. He (the speaker) would point out that the taxes which Mr. Chamberlain pro- posed to reduce were partly temporazy, and would be reduced as soon as the financial condition of the country warranted it, to a greater extent thanrwas proposed by Mr. Chamberlain. The tea duty would serve to prove the incorrectness of Mr. Chamberlain's statement that the foreigner and not the Englishman would pay the tax upon food, as they all knew that when the war tax was put upon tea, that article we nt up in price to the extent of 2d. per pound. In that case the consumer paid the tax, and in every case the consumer would .have to pay the tax. (Applause.) The resolution was carried amid applause. Mr. LONG proposed a vote of thanks to the speakers and chairman. Referrinc, to his own political career, he said it was nearly 20 years since, from motives of conscience on the Irish question, he left his party, and from that time he had taken no active part in political life. But now the big question of taxing the food of the people had brought him out from his retirement. (Hear, hear.) In three days of selfish legislation, such as they had gone through during the last few years, it behoved them more than ever to consider what course they should take to safeguard themselves and their wives and families. Let them go and hear both sides of the political questions of the day and then judge for themselves. They were not all political men, in a sense, and many of them did not, perhaps, read the papers much, but to his mind the best criterion for a working man to take was to look at the characters of the men on each side who spoke up and down the country. One of these was'the Duke of Devonshire, a man who, in his opinion, stood head and shoulders above anybody else as the trusted leader of the thoughtful people of this country. The Duke was also one of those who left his ; party in 1886 as he (Alr. Long) did,and became a Liberal , Unionist; By the excesses of that other leader of ; Liberal Unionists, Mr. Chamberlain, in the way of hav- • • ing introduced his fiscal question, a split had been ' caused in the party. But the Free Traders were united, and he thought the next election would see Free. Trade i still held aloft as the policy of the nation. Once let us ; begin on the slope of Protection, and they never knew ; how it would end. The workers of this country were ; quite able to see that no good would come to them by ' a tax on their fooci,and they would not, he trusted, give jup the substance for the shadow in the way of more wages promised by Mr. Chamberlain (Applause.) Mr. Chamberlain had made a speech in which he argued his proposals would ! result in an increase in the wages of the farm labourer In another speech he aagued that his proposals would result in an increase in the world's supply of wheat and a consequent cheapening of price, which would not I make the living of the workingman ally more costly. I How Mr. Chamberlain reconciled the two statements and thought that with a reduced selling price wages would be raised, he, the speaker, did not know. He asked them all to think out the question and give their verdict accordingly. (Applause.) The vote of thanks was heartily accorded, and the j Vicar haying been thanked for the use of the room the I meeting ended.

div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. CHIT FtC fi rho subject seems to us hardly worth -pursuing any further.—ED. "Ex."] National Service. Sir,—Referring to the letters from my friend Major Roome and my brother, Captain Crosfield, which appeared in the "Examiner," lam unable at the moment to continue the discussion which forms the subject of this correipondence, but with your permission I will make few further observations in the course of ainother week or so.—Yours &c., A. 11. CROSFIELD.
November 24th, 1901.

• The Workhouse Extension. Sir.—l have been instructed by the Warrington Branch of the Independent Labour Party to forward to you copy of a resolution which was unanimously carried at our last meeting, and to ask if you will kindly publish it in your next issue.—Sincerely yours, EDWARD LEES, (Assistant Secretary). [Co ['Y.] "That this branch of the Independent Labour Party protests against the proposed extention of the Workhouse, believing that the circumstances can be better overcome by a reasonable extension of outdoor relief, instead of by the spending of a large amount of money upon a new building, with the additional expenditure in furnishing and pro- viding an addition to the permanent staff and we trust that the board will reconsider the whole question."

Councillor Ellison Corrects Rev. H. Dunnico. Sir,—l take exception to a paragraph contained in a letter to Mr. Dodds dated May 25th, 1901, wherein the Rev. H. Dunnico states that it was owing to his keen resentment of the action of the temperance party in Latchford thatiCouncillor Ellison was compelled to make an apology before the Temperance Federation. Why the temperance party should be brought into this controversy, or why my nameshould be made use of so often in public and private letters, is beyond my corn; prehension. The fact is, I never was compelled to do anything by Mr amnia° or any other member of the Fed- eration. A committee meeting was held on Nov. 25th,1902, at which a discussion took place with regard to my attitude at the November election in 1902, after which I made a plain straightforward statement of facts in connection with the Liberal Ward Committee meeting over which I presided, which was the cause of much misunderstanding for which Mr. Dunnico was respon- sible through a letter of his which appeared in the papers denouncing the temperance and Liberal parties in strong terms. After having made my statement it was resolved "that having heard the statement, the Federation accept the same and express renewed confidence in Counciller Ellison.' I was afterwards elected 'chairman of the Federation. This speaks for itself. I have also the satisfaction of knowing that my friends in Latchford Ward, who are best able to judge of my work and con- duct, have so much confidence in me that they have just elected me for the fourth time to represent them in the Council by the largest majority ever given to a conn- cillir in this ward and so long as I retain the confid- ence of the electors of a largo and intelligent ward like Latchford I can afford to disregard all attempts to draw my name through the mud of discord.—Yours &c.,
LUKE ELLISON, CBl, Knutsford-road, Latchford. November 24th, 1901.

div.head: Mr. A. H. Crosfield and the "Observer."
div.p: Mr. A. H. Crosfield and the "Observer."

November 23rd, 1904. Mr. A. H. Crosfield has this week addressed the following letter to the editor of the "Observer." Sir,—My attention has just been drawn to the letter written by "Loyalist" published in the "Observer" of November 19th. In this letter it is stated that "During the course of the war I proved myself to be entirely out of sympathy with those engaged in it"; and further on it is insinuated that I either lost no opportunity of casting reflections on our troops in the field, accusing them of methods of barbarism and all sorts of brutality, or connived at charges of this kind. The statement I have just quoted, and these insinua- tions are equally untrue. I have condemned in very strong language the new methods of diplomacy adopted in the summer of 1899 which, as Sir Edward Grey has stated were in fact not diplomacy at all; and without going over the old ground in detail I may just say that am certain that if those who were responsible for that reckless work in 1899 could recall events they would act very differently. While I condemned, and condemn still as emphatically as ever their action, I never said or felt inclined to say, one word against our soldiers in the field. On tho contrary, I have always held that the tighter the place we found ourselves in during the war, the greater the honour to our soldiers, both of the regular and auxiliary forces, who helped us to get out of it. I endeavoured daring the war to prove my sympathies with our forces in such practical Ways as were open to one, and in reply to "Loyalist's" state- ment that I proved myself entirely out of sympathy" I may again repeat that this is absolutely contrary to fact. I may just further add that as regards the volun- teers who went from Warrington, I thoroughly respec- ted their public spirit and patriotism as I have had an opportunity of t,estifying on more than one occasion ; and I may add in passing that there is no one in the town more keenly anxious to see our auxiliary forces encouraged, helped and strengthened than I am. Very well sir, these are the facts. It is only charit- able to assume that "Loyalist "was ignorant of them, but I am afraid we cannot give you the benefit of that assumption. And wh.t can one say then of your conduct in publishing a letter of this kind, the object of which can only be either some wretched attempt at party capital, or,as the concluding portion of the letter seems to show, to alienate public sympathy from a cause which surely might appeal to every one? If the former were "Loyalist's " object he ought to be ashamed of himself, if the latter then the next time this self-styled patriot writes to you I advise him to sign his letter Disloyal,"—that will bo a good deal nearer the mark. As for yourself, yen have already received one digni- fied rebuke from a contemporary who, although opposed to me in politics,appreciates,as an English gentleman,at their true value these palpable attempts to" -i it below the Belt." Is that not sufficient to teach you that these efforts of yours to vulgarise our local politics are not Appreciated in a town where political controversy has, so far as my recollection of it goes been conducted with good temper and good taste.—Yours Scc.. A. H. CROSFIELD. P.S. Another wretched insinuation in " Loyalist's" letter is disposed of in a short reply by the Secretary of our Footblall Club of which a copy has just been sent to me from Bank Quay, and whick I presume will appear in your issue of to-day.

Sir,—This is my last letter on this subject as far as newspaper discussion is concerned. I had hoped that some slight interest would have been moused and that solely on account of nublic opinion some steps would have been taken in the matter. Apparently, however, the public do not care a fig for the health of our children, but prefer to waste their time listening to Parr Hall discourses on impracticable things, absurd dogmas of religion, non- trading personalities and such like. While blaming the public,l ought not perhaps to over- look our friend the fighting Parr Hall parson. I would suggest in all sincerity that our friend turns his atten- tion from the palaces above to the slums and market halls below. Nor will our friend do much good by telling his congregation that if there are any friends of Mr. Bracecamp or Mr. Dodds present will they kindly inform those gentlemen of his most warlike and bombastic utterances and challenges. Such proceedings at a" Divine Service "are to say the least, quite out of place and are ungentlemanly. While millions are starving in this life and are living under the most degrading conditions—conditions that almost make life not worth the living—our friend calm- ly sermonizes and guesses on a Sunday night as to whether the grave ends all and if not, what is beyond. He does this serenely unconscious, it would appear, that many thousands of poor under-fed children prowl round the markets and other such places lf our large towns seeking luxuries in the shape of rotten and decayed fruit,ithis being the nearest approach to the desired luxury of good fruit. About 400 years B.C. one might almost have been tempted to believe that a Christian Minister would have been the first to have helped in doing some good prac- tical work. Weare told there are souls to save for God. If this is so I should like to know why our friends at Parr Hall and all other Christian workers and ministers do not press this matter of our markets and have something done with regard to the storage of rotten fruit. and the emptying of fish bins Sm. The souls of those children who frequent our markets and who eat all descriptions of filthy fruit, cannot be particularly clean. Neither can they be particularly pure in heart. "Blessed are the pure in heart for they shall see God." Are our Christian friends attempting in any way to make this possible for these young children. Christians have a very bad habit of wonder- ing why there are so many atheists, infidels, etc. Just look at the colossal success of Christianity and you have before you the most eloquent of reasons, the poor children I have spoken of for instance. They live in slums and eat rotten fruit. Are they likely then to appreciate the inestimable advantages of Christianity and to praise God for living in such a beautiful and Christian country where slums and rotten food, etc., aboun

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, November 26, 1904.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, November 26, 1904.
ALFRED HULME. Latchford, November 25th, 1904.

Rev. H. Dunnico and Mr. Dodds. An Extraordinary Letter. Sir.—ln the "Examiner" of Saturday last I replied ; in a mild form to certain criticisms passed upon me by ! Mr. James Dodds. These criticisms were in the first !place uncalled for and extremely childish. By some occult process your correspondent was able to divine ' the contents of my letter and in the same issue contri- buted what purported to be a reply. Along with that I letter he also published without even asking permission ; certain correspondence which had passed between ,us I including one private letter. So far as the question at issue is concerned, he could not have done me a greater I favour. The correspondence verifies in every detail (1), the contents of my letter (2) my utterances upon Parr ! Hall platform. That however does not minimise the "dirtiness" of sending for publication a private letter. Those who II know Mr* Dodds intimately assure me that such an action is quite in harmony with all that he does. If it is I very sincerely regret it. Men who do such things are destitute of all those qualities which have made !English public life the purest in the world. So far as I am concerned I can only say that such a letter the publication of which (so many months after it was written) may give unintentional pain to some, would not have been written if I had not firmly believed that I was writinc, to an honourable and trustworthy man. With regard to several points touched upon in the correspondence I desire to say that neither,Mr. James Dodds nor anyone else has ever subscribed a single penny to the funds of our church during the whole of my ministry. That the two appeals made on the occa- sion of our Sunday School Anniversary have been made on behalf of work distinct and separate from the work of the church. Moreover the second appeal was based upon the fact that both the church and myself had made sacrifices in order to carry on such work. I also beg to state that one year before Mr. Dodds received the circular with the postscript "I shall be pleased to wait upon you personally if you desire it." 'I received both a verbal and a written message from Mr. Dodds expressing a desire to see rue at Penketh House and "hoping soon to to have the pleasure of making my acquaintance." There are several other discrepancies which I might point out were I so disposed, all of which prove that either Mr. Dodds' veracity or memory is a doubtful quality. I commend to him the motto which occupies so conspicuous a position on his own note paper viz., "Magna est Veritas" I also beg to state, that I have never made one single reference to Mn, Dodds in any sermon I have ever preached apart from the one published verbatim in your columns and even in that one I did not mention his name. I have referred to him on two occasions since then at an interval in the service. In doing so I have only done what has been my custom ever since I commenced my ministry. That is of replying one Sunday to criticisms passed upon my utterances of the ' previous Sunday. Thousands of ' people can testify to the accuracy of this statement. Mr. Dodds states that he has uttered his last word i, "an unsought wrangle." That it is a wrangle I admit that it was unsought I deny. He deliberately stepped out of his way to attack me. A more uncalled for attack has never been made upon any man. But it is only another glaring specimen of that debased kind of opportunism which has unfortunately been the out- standing characteristic of his political career. His criticisms however do not trouble me, water does not run more easily off the back of a duck than the criticisms of Mr. Dodds off the back of an honest man. He may adopt his hyper-critical air and accuse me of being inconsistent but I beg leave to doubt whether he is a good judge upon such matters. It is a quality in which he has proved himself so conspicuously deficient that the absence of such in himself renders him incapable of detecting it in other people. He is so fond of telling us what he is not that some of us are at a loss to know what he is. He has repeatedly told us that he is not a teetotaller, but surely there is no necessity to labour that point; that is taken for granted. There was a time however when even he moved in temperance circles. He then says he is not an official of the Liberal party, but that is a well-known fact. Still he would have been if it had been possible to have captured it for his own purposes. Then he informs us that he is not an official of the Wesleyan Church but I do not hear that they seriously deplore this. Still why did be leave it? Then we learn that he is not even a member of the " Non-trading Party." Surely be is, whatever he is not, eligible for the society of " Nothing arians." It is not long since he was publicly condemning the parsons and ministers for not identifying themselves with the last party he has thought fit to repudiate. Such condemnations were but the rediculous creations of a disordered and dissipated imagination. It never seemed to dawn across his mind that a campaign of boisterous jeers. exuberant ridicule, giddy Taiety, and in some cases vile slanders was not one likely to enlist the co-operation of thoughtful men. Mr. Dodds then proceeds to throw a stigma and a slur upon my church and congregation, but I hurl it back with contempt Last Sunday was the thirtieth service I have heldlwith an aggregate attendance of 45,009 people and they will keep his insult in mind. On not more than three occasions has there been even an attempt at. applause and last Sunday was the first occa- sion on which there has been deliberate applause. Whether they are justified in applauding at divine ser- vice is a matter upon which Mr. Dodds is not an authority but right or wrong I would rather they assemble there and applaud than sit at home in self righteous pha raism. In conclusion I would simnly point out that 11111903 Mr. Dodds informed me by letter that in his opinion "there was nothing Warr,ington more needed than a strong and active Baptist Church " now he is " much concerned "that such a church is inlexistence. Happily our strength and activity is not dependent upon his paltry donations. But why this change of front? Tell it not in gath. The minister has had the audacity to criticise the Non- Traders' methods. In conclusion I would advise Mr. Dodds not to be so " killingly in,liscreet." I would warn him that the robe of purity with which he and some of his confeder- ates have clothed their questionable tactics is even now being torn asunder by an intelligent public and for a time deceived. The public is beginning to realize that however worthy the Non-Trading ideal may be it will never be established by savage animosity or Bull dog ferocity but by those who have "clean hands" and " pure hearts."—Yours truly HERBERT DUNNICO. '

P.S.—I am informed that the private letter published by Mr. Dodds has given rise to some misunderstanding. I therefore desire tn say that I did not support the can- didature of Mr. Councillor Pemberton, and desire neither the credit nor discredit of his return as the case may be. I simply condemned the action of teetotallers supporting a brewer, and it has been publicly stated that my condemnations set on foot certain forces which brought about Mr. Pemberton 's return. This is the sum and substance of what was written in confidence.. I also desire to express my regret for having used the word " compelled " with regard to Councillor Ellison's apology. I now substitute the word "induced." Coun-
Author of "Search Lights oa Land, Labour and Social Problems."

thing from the heel pad on your boot to the tyre of your I bike. It has a type foundry, where they cast all kinds of metal type, and this employs a number of men and boys. It has a hosiery factory that is supplied with some of the latost and best machines for making stock- ings, and finds employment for a large number of work- people. It has a coffee mill and a pea flour mill, fitted with modern machinery for working out some patents of a special kind in these two industries. It has a tannery, and a brewery, and a glue factory, and Heaven knows what beside, for cheap land ;and cheap labour are attracting fresh industries continually. I have been greatly impressed by the number of healthy, strong, well-fed, well-nourished people I have met in my rambles. I have been five weeks among them and have never seen a drunken man,or a beggar,or a ragged hungry-looking child since I came. They breathe some of the purest air in the world, and they do not live on the offal of the towns, for their gardens supply them with the best vegetables for next to nothing, land they raise their own eggs, and poultry, and pigs into the bargain. For country-bred men and women, who take life by the smooth handle, and live wisely, this is an ideal place, and for the man who owns a bike there are some glorious rides through half a dozen shires. For .the town-bred man, who cannot live without his theatre or his music hall, or his club, or his nub or his wild round of excitement, this place has no attractions, and he had better give it a wide berth. I shall be heartily sorry when my time is up, and I have to leave it, for T have made many friends, and I have fallen in love with he place.

Paris to discuss the Dogger Bank outrage perpetrated by Russia on our innocent fishermen, was a welcome mark of progress following on the lines of the Hague Convention. President Rooseveldt had just lately promised to try and arrange with other countries that another large Peace Confer- ence should meet at the Hague. It was only to be expec- ted that much time and patience would be required before they could expect all nations of the world to follow in our footsteps, but England must continue to lead the way, and do her best to show that war was absolute folly and savagery, and merely belonged to heathen times. With regard to the subject of the address, a meeting was held at her (Mrs. Holmes's) house last, week when Miss Calthrop, of the London Society, ad- dressed them and la Women's Suffrage Society for War- ringtonlwas formed, of which Mrs. Monro had con- sented to be secretary., (Applause). It must be under- stood that they only aimed for the Parliamentary vote for!women ratepayers and did not wish for women to st in Parliament. (Applause).

div.head: INDUSTRIAL PROBLEMS AT MARKET HARBOROUGH.
div.p: INDUSTRIAL PROBLEMS AT MARKET HARBOROUGH.

" New occasions teach new duties, Time makes ancient good uncouth; He must still be up and onward Who would keep abreast of Trath."— EMERSON. trket Ilarborough is a quiet little old-fashioned market town, in the very heart of England. It is mid- way between Leicester, Rugby, and Northampton, and it is built on the banks of the river Welland, which separates the county of Leicester from Northampton- shire. _

EL:PbR MANY CENTURIES IT HAS BEEN AN UNPROGRESSIVE TOWN. Its rivals built factories and workshops, and opened quarries and mines, and found employment for thousands of poople, but it was content with its three staple industries—coaching, hunting, and farming. So they grew into large towns, while its population was either stationary or declining all the time. In the old coaching days it was a place of some importance, because it stands on the great highway to the north of England, and it is about eighty-two miles from London. If you want to know what that means, you had better count up the number of large, roomy. comfortable hotels in the place, with a score or more of bedrooms, and stables to match. These hotels used to tap the traffic on the turnpike road, and find comfort- eble lodgings for man and beast, and a large portion of the inhabitants of Harborough made a verylcomfortable living by catering for the wants of the passengers who travelled through the town. You need not wonder that these people regarded all railways as their natural enemies and when the Midland and London and North-Western . _ _ .

Railways proposed to lay down lines through Market Harborough they resisted them to the death and com- pelled them to build their station nearly a mile away from the centre of the town. Time and experience have taught them that this was a mistake, but the mischief is done now, and they cheerfully pay sixpence for a ride in a bone-shaking 'bus from the town to the station. The advent of railways destroyed the chief industry of the town, and ruined many innkeepers, and cast adrift hundreds of coachmen, and stableboys and ser- vants, who reaped a rich harvest from travellers. Then the little town was left with only two strings to its bow—hunting and agriculture—and though it had but a handful of people, it had to solve the problem of the

unemployed. - The hunting season begins on the first Monday in November, and lasts till March, and five or six different packs of hounds are kept within a radius of twenty miles from Market Harborough. So the nobility and gentry who keep hunters and follow the hounds are attracted to the town because it is a convenient centre for a winter's sport. Fox-hunting has always been an aristocratic pastime, and the subscribers and members of each hunt are not only rich, and titled people, as a rule, but they are exclusive and clannish, and they can snub any humble follower of the hounds who does not belong to the "county famines." The late John Leech, in his "Hunting sketches" for "Punch," hits this off remarkably well. He pictures a largo field of horsemen clearing a hedge and ditch in fine style, but one of their number has come to grief, and gone head first into the ditch. "Who is that gone down?" asks the master of the hunt. "It is the parson, sir," was the reply. "Oh, never mind him; ha will not be needed till Sunday," said the master, so they rode on, and left him to his fate. Need I tell you that scores of these artistocratic fox- hunters, with their families, and servants, and horses, make a wonderful difference to a little country town when they settle in it for five months out of each .year. The best is good enough for them, and money Is no object. They rent the biggest houses in the district, and they try to outstrip each other in their handsome turn-outs, and their luxurious style of living. Ido not blame them for this, for the possession of money gives them all the influence they have got in this world, and if they spend their money freely, other people will reap some profit out of it. When fox-hunting was in all its glory towns like Market Harborough and Melton Mowbray, and all the great hunting centres, reaped a rich harvest from the aristocrats who followed the hounds. But even this source of income is declining. So much damage is done to crops and hedges by reckless riders, and the foxes make such daring raids on poultry pens and farm yards, that the farmers, like the publi- cans, are insisting on compensation. and they are getting it. The result is that fox-hunting is becoming a very costly amusement indeed, and only very rich people can afford to keep big establishments, and stand the racket from all quarters. Now, I have shown you how Market Harborough lost its coaching and posting industries by the introduction of railways, and how its hunting has suffered from the altered circumstances of the time. If you take these two sources of income away, it has nothing left but its agriculture to keep it alive. Fortunately it has some of the richest soil in England and its green pastures are among the best in the world, and its shrewd farmers have more wit than to grow wheat at a loss,when they canigrow beef and 'mutton at a profit. I have spent five or six weeks lately in Market Harborough and the surrounding villages, using my two eyes and ears to some purpose. Agriculture is not a decaying industry in that district and I have met with many farmers and market gardeners who are well satis- fied with their lot in life. Those rich pastures are particularly suited to the rearing og young cattle. I have seen Herefords, and frish, and Scotch young bullocks turned loose when they had hardly an ounce of fat on them. They were a sorry collection of bones, and hides, and horns, and hoofs, but they had the making in them of the finest cattle in the country, and it is from those green fields and well wooded pastures that we get some of the best beef that the world can produce. But cattle rearing does not solve the problem of the unemployed, and there came a day in the history of Market Harborough when the people had to wake up and bestir themselves, and look out for neW industries to keep the town alive. Their cottages were fast degenerating into slums, and their children had to emigrate to the large towns in search of employment, while the population at each cenaus was either stationary or declining. When things get to the worst they are usually either ended' or mended and there came a turning point in the history of Market Harborough. About a generation ago, a few clear headed, shrewd business men agreed that they would make some effort to stem the tide of migration to other towns, by finding employment for the people nearer home. They decided to pull down some of the vile rookeries and slums, and to build some neat attractive cottages at reasonable rents. It was a bold ambitious scheme, but it has been more than justified by its success, and the story of this enterprise may encourage other people to follow their example. IT. THEY BEGAN LIKE WISE MEN BY SOLVING THE LAND PROBLEM.

A comn—anv was formed that purchased about sixty acres of land, and turned it into building sites, and allotments, and cottage gardens. This land is not in one plot, but it consists of several very convenient lots all around the centre of the town. Among the treasures they found on this land was a.valuable bed of clay. and this found employment for the brick-makers. When they had made plenty of good cheap bricks they began building houses for working men, and it is astonishing what yott can do in that direction if you get plenty of cheap land, and cheap building materials, and you happen to know your way about. The Market Harborough Land Company, from first-to last, has built about five hundred neat, attractive, and substantial houses, and in nearly every case there .is

_ land enough for a very profitable kitchen garden adjoin- ing. These houses let from four shillings per week, to six shillings and sixpence per week, according to the size of the building, and the area of the garden. I only wish I could get a house equal to the best'of them at Southport, at !anything like the price. I do not wonder that so many of the tenents have bought their houses and gardens out and out, for they evidently know a good and cheap thing when they see it. This land company began its operations about twenty years ago, and with commendable worldly wisdom it tempted manufacturers of all kind:, to build factories, and 'workshops on its estate, by the offer of cheap land. These new ventures sprang up like mushrooms in all directions, and to-day it would be difficult to find in all England another town of its size, that has so many strings to its bow, or that can boast so many industries. Some of these factories and workshops are owned by manufacturers who have similar concerns in other towns, and they were'attracted toMarket Tfarborough'by cheaper labour,"and 'timer rent, and rates,and working expenses. The workmen admit that they receive lower wages than they'would get for similar work in some large towns,but they tell me that they would not change places with a town workman if you offered them twenty-five per cent more wages than they are getting now. The increased rent and rates they would have to pay, and the doctor's bills, and loss of work through ill-health,,would more ; than swallow that up every year. have been trying to find out how many new indus- tries Market Tiarborough has attracted to itself since it turned over a new leaf, and made a bold bid for its share of industrial prosperity. It has a large corset factory. employing many women and girls as machinists,and nutting considerable sums of money into circulation every week. It has a workshop for bending timber, and mv,king carriage shafts, and harness, and wheels, and its reputation has spread far and wide. It has:a rubber factor,wherethey make any-

div.head: WOMEN LIBERALS.
div.p: WOMEN LIBERALS.
ANNUAL MEETING OF THE WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION. Address on Women's Suffrage.

The gratifyingly large attendance at the annual meeting of the Warrington Women's Liberal Associa- tion held at the Liberal Club on Monday evening was a striking evidence of the vitality of the organization. The annual report too showed that the past year has been one of particular activity, and the members of the Association have cause to congratulate themselves upon the success of their efforts in connection with the big Liberal bazaar. Prior to the annual meeting tea was served to a good company. The meeting was presided over by Mrs. Ziba Armitage (president of the Association) and amongst those present were :—Mrs. Jackson Holmes (hon. secretary), Mrs. Walker (hon treasurer), Miss Crosfield, Miss Wyse of Birkenhead, and Mrs. Osborne. Mrs. ARMITA.GE expressed the pleasure it afforded her to attend and to see such a large gathering. Perhaps the recent bazaar had helped to bring them together. They had not made quite as much money by it as the gentlemen expected they would have done, but they certainly worked hard and they realized a fair amount. (Hear, hear.) The ladies enjoyed the bazaar in a way. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) She thought it would be better for all women to know how the country was to be governed, and with that object in view they must arrange for some good lectures and discussions and thus educate themselves. Miss Crosfield would have some- thing to say about that matter later on. ADDRESS ON WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.

Miss WYSE than delivered an interesting address on " Women's Suffrage." She said the question far from being a modern innovation and merely the desire of the new woman, so called, dated from the feudal ages. In the olden times women had a right to elect members to Parliament. The Magna Charta, written in Latin, made the word" bomo "stand for both sexes and it was not until some centuries later that the quibblings of the lawyers gave a different meaning to the word. They believed that the word" bemo " referred to men when privileges, such as voting, were concerned, but when it came to responsibilities such as tax paying, the term included both men and women. Ancient records told them that women had the privilege of voting for members of Parliament, and that con- tinued until about the seventeenth century when their liberties began to be curtailed. It was not the law of England which decided that women should not have the franchise but the lawyers of that day. It was not until the passing of the Second Refor.n Act, when women were still further deprived of their privileges, that organised efforts were made to reinstate woman in her ancient position of elector. Since then petition after petition had been sent to the House of Commons and Bill afterl Bill had been presented but all of no avail. It was not that women had no champions of their causelin thelfioae. In the early seventies they had John Stewart Mill, John Bright, Henry Fawcett and others who worked strongly for that cause of justice. Their efforts were unsuccessful, for prejudice died hard, and a great deal of ridicule was heaped upon the movement. The very fact that women were not represented in Parliament was in itself a bar to further ptogress. Was it right that in the struggle for existence women should be fettered by laws with the making of whi.3ll they had nothing to do? She instanced the restriction of hours of employ- ment and pointed out that employers were prevented from employing females during the night even on special classes of work. Miss Wyse referred to several Acts which she contended wereone-sided—and described the Divorce Act as the most cruel Act on the Statute Book. People were apt to say "Women have gained so much. What more do they want ?" Not one single advantage was secured to them unless they got the fran- chise. At any day it fmight be taken from them, and further restrictions imposed. The only public positions left to women were seats on the Boards of Guardians, and of those they might be deprived at any time, because there was a move- ment on foot to bring Boards of Guardians under the control of county and municipalauthorities. Women's suffrage was a question which appealed to both parties. They had friends on both sides of the Hpuse. Very probably if women's suffrage had been a party measure they would have gained it long ago. Therein lay their weakness and their strength. The nearest approach they had to victory was in 1897. They got a majority of 71 for a Bill for women's franchise on the second reading and they were in great hopes that it would pass the third reading. They were, however, doomed to disappointment as when the measure again came up for consideration a section of the House deliberately talked for hours on insignificant matters. in February of this year Sir Charles McLaren brought forward a resolution to the effect that the time had now arrived when the women's suffrage question ought to be taken up in the House. Thal resolution was passed by a majority of 114, and Sir Charles said it was owing to the efforts of women throughout the country that the members who were in favour of it kept their pledges and voted accordingly. As late as August 3rd a Bill was read for the first time to grant the franchise to women. They hoped to be successful in the ballot at the beginning of next session. It had been said that women did not wa ,t the franchise, but to that she could give a flat contradiction. The women engaged in cotton weaving in Lancashire were most anxious ta have votes and they were working enthusiastically to attain their desire. Sixty per cent of the money raised in support of Mr. Shackleton's candidature at Clitheroe was subscribed by women members of the trade union. (Applause.) In being deprived of votes women were placed in the same class as paupers, children, idiots, and criminals. Even the pauper might improve his position and obtain the voting qualification; the idiot might have a sane moment and might be allowed to vote ; and the criminal, when he had served his term, could also exercise the privileges of the ballot. But the woman had no chance. She was debarred from voting simply and solely by her sex. Very soon the country would be called upon to settle ono of the most momentous questions in its history—. the fiscal proposals. %Vas it just that lthat question should be decided without the opinion of the women being taken. It was a subject that concerned women equally as much as men. but their legislators did not seem to think so. She maintained that women ought to have the franchise accorded to them before the fiscal question was settled. She asked her hearers to refuse to work for any Parliamentary candidate unless he would promise to support women's suffrage in the House. The gentleman they had chosen to represent them in Warrington as their candidate was very sensible on the point—by that she meant he was in favour of it. (Applause.) Miss %Vyse alluded to the formation of a committee in Warrington to press the subject, and wished it every success. The greatest bene- fit that would be obtained from the suffrage was the widening of woman's mental horizon which would accrue. She would have 3 greater incentive for study- ing the questions of the elev. (Applause.) THE ANNUAL REPORT.

In her annual report Mrs. HOLMES stated that the committee had met when occasion required. Mrs. Clay and Mrs. Osborne attended the federation meetings in London this year. They spent a very interesting and profitable time there and had the good fortune of finding hospitality at Doills Hill. where Mr. Gladstone so often stayed, and where the Countess of Carlisle and Lady Aberdeen were also guests. The association's picnic came off in July, and was a huge success, a most enjoy- able time being spent at Eaton Hall and surroundings, 700 partaking simultaneously of an excellent tea at Eccleston Ferry. The large bazaar at the Parr Hall, which entailed so much work, was a thing of the past, and was pronounced by those who were able to gauge the state of trade generally a success, £7OO being realised. The best thanks of the Liberal party were due to those who sn willingly devoted their time and morey to this en 11. It was very satisfactory to be able to state since the last report was written two more ladies had come forward and had been accepted as guardians and an additional sanitary inspectress had been appointed. The recent municipal elections had proved very satisfactory to the Liberal party- Perhaps a little credit for that might be given to four members of the committee is ho helped with the canvassing, more especially in the Howley I Ward. A letter of acknowledg- ment had been received from Mr. Clegg asking her to express his deep appreciation of their services. They were very glad to see the efforts which were being put forth from time to time by the King and President Roosveldt in the interests of peace. Only that morn- ing appeared in one of. the papers a picture of King Edward putting an arbitration muzzle on a large dog which was being held by a Spaniard. The arbitration treaty between Britain and Portugal had just been signed at Windsor. The settlement of the constitution of the Commission which was to assemble in

div.head: FEDERATION MEETINGS.
div.p: THE FEDERATION MEETINGS.

An interesting report on the meetings of the Women's Liberal Federation held on the 31st May, and the Ist and 2nd of June in London was presented by Mrs. Osborne who along with Nlrs. Clay, represented the Warrington Association. The Countess of Aberdeen, she stated, in addressing the delegates said the past year would be marked as one in which the recognize.- tion of the justice of women's suffrage had been parti- cularly emnhasised. It was decided to welcome re- union with the Women's National Liberal Association provided that it could be effected without fundamentally altering the constitution of the Women's Liberal , Federation, and that the policy of the Federation with regard to women's suffrage and the State regulation of , vice was upheld. A resolution was passed urging the 'Liberal party to recognize the rights of women to the Parliamentary franchise, and calling upon Liberal leaders to place women', .suff rage among those reforms which the party pledged itself to promote. The Federa- tion also declared itself in favour of Free Trade principles and condemned the Licensing Bill. In regard to the Macedonian atrocities, a resolution was passed calling upon the Govern- ment to use all possible efforts to secure the execution of the Treaty of Berlin. Parliament was also urged "in the interests of womanhood, sobriety, and good morals" to pass a law by which the future employment of women in bars on licensed premises should be prohibited, but the opinion was expressed that any such law should not apply to women at present engaged in the calling. A motion in favour of the amendment of the Education Act was carried and the meeting expressed itself in favour of the Land Values (Assessment and Rating Bill). The moral degradation and suffering caused by the increase of gambling and betting was alulded to in forcible terms. While recognizing that the evil could be checked chiefly by moral means, the Council ex- pressed the opinion that good might be done by more vigorously enforcing the existing laws and by extend- ing legislation, and therefore cordially welcomed the Street Betting Bill as a step in the right direction. In conclusion Mrs. 05130EtNE stated that there were upwards of 600 delegates from all parts of the country present at the meetings of the Council. The total number of affiliated associations was 496 with an approximate total membership of 61,900. The subjects under discussion were exceedingly interesting and instructive, and the debates were entered into with much earnestness and enthusiasm, all of which proved that Liberal women were not less competent than Liberal men to form a right judgment on the burning questions of the day. Mrs. Clay and she were the guests during their visit to London of Sir Hugo Gilbzean Reid, at Dellis Hill House, the house made so interesting on account of its associations with the late Mr. Gladstone. They were entertained right nobly, and the pleasure of their stay in the metropolis was further enhanced by the receptions given to the delegates by the Countess of Aberdeen, Lady Pearson and Lady Denman. (Applause.)

div.head: NEW DEPARTURE.
div.p: A NEW DEPARTURE.

Miss CROSFIELD moved a resolution'to the effect that during the winter months the members of the associa- tion should meet occasionally for the purpose of self- education. Nothing, she said, broadened the mind so much as discussion,and if they could meet for that pur- pose in a friendly way two, three or four times during the winter months—without any intimidation from the presence of the men and their superior knowledge of things—(laughter)—thy would not only get to know each other better, but have a bettlr idea of the great Liberal principles for which the party was fighting. (Hear, hear and applause.) They could discuss any topic that might interest them. Suggestions for the meetings were advanced, and it was decided that the first one should be held on the evening of December 12th from 7.30 to 8.30 at the Liberal Club.

During the evening violin solos were rendered with taste and skill by Miss Bouchier, the pianoforte accom- paniment being supplied by Mrs. Holmes. The usual votes of thanks concluded a successful meeting.

div.head: WAGES IN THE IRON TRADE.
div.p: WAGES IN THE IRON TRADE.
How 0,000 was Lost in Wages

A good deal of feeling has been aroused in Midland iron-making circles during the last few days over the loss of a big order for iron by the Patent Shaft and Axletree Co., Wednesbuty. The firra have received an order in connection with the building of some South American Docks. A large number of 1-inch plates were needed for the execution of the contract, and the firm were very anxious to roll these themselves. They were however confronted by the fact that by purchasing the plates !in South Wales they would effect a very considerable saving, they accordingly approached their workmen and asked them to accept such a reduction as would enable them to roll the plates themselves. It was pointed out that this would mean the payment to them of some £5OOO in wages. The men declined to consider the matter, and the order has now gone to. Wales. The matter has caused a good deal of vexation in the town, which is suffering severely from the general depression. Mr. J. P. Lacy, the Chairman of the firm assured our Birmingham representative that the men would have been the gainers, inasmuch as the regularity of employ- ment would have more than recouped them for the slight loss. On the other hand, Mr. W. Aucott the men's secretary on the Wages Board asserts that an im- portant principle was involved, and that if such an arrangement were assented to there would be an end of the Board's authority as a wage regulator. There was a lonz conference on Thursday of the Wages Board Sub-Committee concerning the Wednes - bury difficulty but no communication of importance was made. The sub-committee referred the matter to the parties directly concerned for conference and up to the present there has been no formal report by them as to the result.

div.head: KATE OF THE MARKET.
div.p: THE KATE OF THE MARKET.

The iron trade in Birmingham yesterday showed a further gain in strength in raw material, and in this respect showed a marked contrast with the conditions prevailing this time last year. In steel, continental firms were unable to quote a lower price than English manufacturers who have had business pretty much in their own hands of late, and having made good contracts their quotations have tended firmer, with the result that an advance of 2s. 6d. is quoted for delivering next year. So far inquiries for the first quarter of next year hesve been good, and there is every promise of a stealy improvement and more lucrative business.

In pig iron there are plenty of inquiries, and business is fairly good. In finished iron the only improvement to be noted is in black sheets, and makers are fully occupied and in some cases there is a decided pressure for delivering. In these instances as much as £7 is being asked for next year's delivering. On the whole there is a very buoyant tune in this, branch and the future holds out more promise than has been experienced for some time. There continues to be a steady inquiry for marked bars and makers of crown bars, who are quoting £5 15s. are now well occupied, though the figure is not largely remunerative.

div.head: Cairo-street Literary and Debating Society.
div.p: Cairo-street Literary and Debating Society.

On Tuesday evening, the members of the above society were favoured with a visit from tht Rev. J. F. Matthews, of Latchford, who gave an interesting and instructive address on " passive resistance." The chair was taken by the Rev. C. Harvey Cook, and there was a large attendance of both ladies and gentle- men. In explaining his reasons for being a passive resister, Mr. Matthews said that his objection to pay- ing the present education rate was neither political nor social, but was essentially religious. He held that rate-aided education ought to be unsectarian, and maintaine4 that if the Bible was to be made use of in day schools, it ought to be studied merely as a literary work. There was, he said, a prevalent notion that passive resisters were estab- lishing a bad precedent, but to this view of their attitude he strongly demurred. Nor were they guilty of breaking the law, as some people supposed. He did not in any way object to educa- tion at the ratepayers' expense, and, for his own part, would willingly pay a rate much higher than the pre- sent one, if only it were imposed for the purpose of providing a national system of unsectarian education. Several members spoke on the subject, some expressing themselves in favour of passive resistance, others arguing against it. Throughout his discourse, Mr. Matthews commanded the closest attention of his hearers, and. before the close of the meeting was accorded a very hearty vote of thanks for his kindness n attending.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
(By " Ovalist.",

So far have Batley fallen that they never put up any very serious opposition to Warrington winning on Saturday. With only two victories to their credit out of .eleven games they could hardly hope to obtain points at Wilderspool. Time was when they would have disputed every inch of the ground but even in their palmy days they never succeeded on Warring- ton soil. The game was one of those moral certainties for the home club, and if there is anything I hate, it is 3 contest where the odds are overwhelming on one side. Poor sport is almost invariably the result,and there could hardly have been worse football than that served up for the Warrington enthusiasts in the second half of the game on Saturday.

The initial moiety was bright and attractive, for until they had put some points on the board Warring- ton could not very well win. And to score points they set about in grim earnest right away. Batley for a while held out manfully, but they were over- played by the home backs, and Dai Davies opened the score with a clever individual effort which Fish augmented with a goal. Warrington continued to apply high pressure and another piece of speedy com- bined play saw J. Davies record his initial try for the Warrington senior team. By a carelessness which he has manifested on three occasions, Fish missed the place kick in front of goal.

A regrettable incident occurred at this point. While Davies was lying on the ball in the act of scoring Hodgson, a Batley forward deliberately kicked him,so lam told. Though I saw the try scored I did not see the foul act take place, but the Referee at once gave the offender marching orders. Very shamefacedly he walked up the touch-line to the accompaniment of a chorus of hoots;troans, and yells of" Coward." One can allow something for the exasperation of a partizan crowd, but it struck me as being very poor sportsman- ship, especially on the part of some occupants of the hon. members' stand, who ought to behave better.

By the way, there are one or two individuals rejoic- ing in the description of honorary members who rarely fail to create some sort of disturbance on the stand by their partizanship and unmannerly behaviour. It has been, suggested in several quarters that the Club should return the subscriptions of these men, and I hope the committee will not hesitate to use drastic measures in dealing with people who make themselves habitually obnoxious.

To return to the game, however, Warrington were a comfortable ten points to the good on chang- ing ends, and. as Batley were a man short in addition, there was some obvious slicking in the second half. Play rapidly degenerated into little better than a scramble and Batley held their ONVII more evenly than at any part of the day. Wattie Davies had hard luck in not scoring after a fine individual effort, while Johnson, on the other wing, made a bloomer of the easiest of chances. Then Warrington asserted themselves once more and show- ing a little genuine determination they drove the gallant youths before them and Dai Davies notched his second try. The whistle then brought hostilities to a close, with Warrington easy winners by 2 goals 3 tries to nil.

The only interesting feature of the game was the experiment of playing. the two Davies's at half-back. Seeing that both are individualists they combined in creditable fashion, and the younger man did much to open out the game in the first half. He is very smart at handling the ball, but sent several bad passes through recklessness. Com- pared with Brooks he is much the better man for the half back vacancy caused by Hoskenhall's injury. The Warrington threequarterrs were poor, except on the defence, and neither Isherwood nor Dickenson seems to have got into proper attacking form. I have no doubt that they will come" again, just as they did in last season's cup-ties. Naylor and Preston were very prominent among the forwards. On the Batley side, only Wattie Davies and Turton showed any pretensions to class, and the team is a long way from being equal to the cup-winning side of a few seasons back. Even Mark Shackleton , has been resuscitated, and his piano-playing in the rear of the " serum" was laughtable. I don't think he was ever fairly down in a single "scrim," and if Batley cannot get along without a rank spoiler of his stamp they must be in parlous plight.

Far and away the best performance of the day on Saturday was Oldham's win at Bradford. It was quite unexpected, particularly in the neighbourhood of Park Avenue, and gave Oldham a useful lead in the League tournament.

The Leigh notns in the Chronicle on Saturday aired this kind of opinion and remarked that Warrington were the only team Leigh had lost to in the competition but he failed to add that Warrington would probably repeat the dose on December 31st. The sad news was received at Warrington just prior to the Batley match, of the death Of Joe Richardson, !Runcorn's smart, half back. He had been ill from pleurisy for a fortnight, but a fatal termination was not expected so 'soon. The loss is a very severe one to come on top of the many troubles which the "Linnets " bare to face just now. Richardson was in his .?7th year, and he was fast earninglfor himself a great reputation at half back. I can honestly tender Warrington's sympathy with his relatives and his club.

To-day, Warrington are due at Hunslet, but unless the ground has been protected there is not much likelihood of play. A. strong fifteen has been chosen and if the match takes place, I hope .Warrington will for once in a way do themselves justice on Yorkshire soil. With the exception of Hockenhall, the best side the club can muster is taking the field and it ought to be good erough to beat the Parksiders, who are not a very clever organisation. The Goldthorpes are the greatest danger, and if they can be prevented from putting on goals Warrington will stand a big chance. Boardman and Cook have recovered from their injuries and once more come into the forward division.

The full side is : Hallam, full back; Fish, Isherwood, Dickinson and Harris, threequarters ; D. Davies and J. Davies, half backs ; Boardman, Thomas, Preston, Shugars, Belton, Jolley, Naylor and Cooke forwards.

The "A " team will entertain and put through its paces a new team from the Wigan district called Whelley. At half back, Duckworth and Jordan will officiate while the threequarters will be Brooks, Berry, Roberts and Short.
Hockey. [BY R.G.P.]

Last week the Stockton Heath first eleven easily overcame Eccles by 6-0. This defeat although heavy, would have been much more decisive, had the ground been anything like level, but to say the least of it, the Eccles ground is positively dangerous to play upon.

W. Longdin, who turned out in place of R. Pierpoint played a fine game, and obtained the first three goals; then W. Richardson obtained the fourth, and C. H. Bond finished up by scoring two beautiful goals after characteristic runs half the length of the field.

R. Fairclough seems fated not to score this season. On Saturday after running round both backs and trick- ing the goalkeeper, he was just about to shoot through the open goal, when the whistle sounded for half time. (Hard cheese!)

The second eleven were defeated by Salemoor, the score being no less than 6-0, but it should be noted that they only had nine men up to half-time. If there was a little more keenness about the players,the second would have more victories to their credit, than is at present the case.

The following teams are selected to represent the club against Sefton this afternoon :—First (home) : R. G. Pierpoint, goal ; E. E. Woods and L. Fairclough, backs; J. Richardson, Eric Fairclough and G. Hatton, halves; C. H. Bond, S. Baiter, R.Pierpuint, W.Richard- son and R. Fairclough, forwards. Bully off 2.45. Second (away) : J. Gray, goal; P. B. Hawtin and E. Fairclough, backs ; W.Tinnel,H.Smith and J.Houghton, halves; A. Ferguson, W. Howatd, W. Longdin, A. Hodgkinson and D. Skelton, forwards. Train leaves Central Station 1.50.
Although the match is not yet (Friday) officially cancelled, yet under any circumstances it will be almost impossible to play.

div.head: WORKHOUSE INNOVATION. Warrington Inmates Presented with a Piano.
div.p: WORKHOUSE INNOVATION. Warrington Inmates Presented with a Piano.

Under ordinary circumstances, the lives of those unfortunates condemned by stress of circumstances to end their days in the workhouse, are apt to become monotonous, and even at times cheerless. The inmates of the Warrington Workhouse are no exception to the general rule, and it was with a view to doing something to brighten what must naturally become a hum-drum existence, that the members of the Warring- ton Co-operative Society on Saturday presented a piano to the workhouse. As was stated when the instrument was formally handed over to the custody of the officials of the Union,the absence of a piano has been a long felt want, and persons pro- jecting the holding of concerts have hesitated before carrying out their ideas, on account of being faced with the initial expense of hiring a musical instrument upon which to provide the necessary accompaniment!, and also because of the fact that pianos procured lU this way do not always come up to expectations. The Tembers of the Board of Guardians and the committee of the Co-operative Society mustered strongly at the workhouse on Saturday night,and there was also a large attendance in the dining hall at that institution of aged poor. Mr. T. BIR.CHALL, chairman of the Co-operative Stores Committee,remarked upon the extreme cordiality with which the suggestion, made by grs. Clay, that the society should provide a piano was received. They felt, ho said, that there they had an opportunity pre- sented of doing some real good, and in some measure brightening and cheering the lives of those unfortunate people who had to spend their days in the workhouse. Fortunately there were in England wealthy individuals who devoted a portion of their wealth to the ameliora- tion of the lot of their fellow-men. That was one of the things for which we had every reason to be satisfied. In the case of that presentation the circumstances were different. The contribltors to that gift were in many cases themselves poor but who by reason of eareful organization were able out of their savings to make the presentation without any perceptible sacrifice. In that presentation they recognized the valuable services of the guardians of the poor in Warrington. They had a great responsibility placed upon them both to the community at large and to those entrusted to their care. They were part of that vast army of unpaid workers in this country who were continually doing something for their fellow men, and without whom, he often wondered what would become of the country. Mr. Birchall pointed out that the Co-operative Society existed for the purpose of teaching its members to be thrifty by enabling them to save in their ordinary expenditure, and thereby did something towards keeping people out of the Workhouse. The members and committee of the Society wished the poor law guardians and the officials of the union every' success in their efforts to brighten the lives of the people committed to their care, and in that work they hoped the instrument, of which he asked their acceptance would be helpful. (Applause). Mr. BROOKS said that on behalf of the Board of Guar- dians he had very great pleasure in accepting so hand- some a gift. He did not think there was a single in- strument which would do so much for the advancement of the interests of that institution as that very hand- some piano which he hoped would tend to sooth, elinate, and rejuvenate those committed to the care of the Board. The piano moreover, would be a great help to the officials whose work vv.'s of a depressing nature and who required a little relaxation such as the instru- ment would afford. He thanked the me nbers of the. Co-operative Society most cordially for their generosity' and for the suitability of their gift. (Applause.) Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said it was many years since he became a member of the Board of Guardians and from the very outset it had been his desire and his strensous efforts had always been in the direction of doing all that lay in his power to improve the administration of the poor law in that institution. Other members of the Board had not always seen eye to eye with him but he was sure they would all give him credit for having tried to administer the poor law in Warrington on humane, Christian and scientific lines, and in a manner which was in the interests of the community as a whole, and which was marked with an absence of all methods savouring of Bumbledon. (Hear, hear.) 3/r• Birchall had always taken a great interest in the welfare of the inmates of the workhouse. He hoped the gift would be helpful and useful in the working of the insti- tution and that it would counteract the unhappiness which some of the inmates experienced from time to time. (Applause.) Mr. AWBAIRY (workhouse master) said that on behalf of the officers he could say they were most cordially thankful for the magnificent gift. The officers always endeavoured to do their best for those committed to their care. Occasionally discipline had to be enforced but no real disagreeableness arose which was not easily' overcome. (Applause.) Under him he had a good set of officers whose endeavour it was to treat the inmates in as humane a way as was possible, and he was sure that in the discharge of their duties they were guilty of nothing which could be characterized as the conduct of a bully. (Hear, hear:) In the long winter evenings both officials and inmates were in need of considerable enlightenment such as would be provided by the use o f that pia,no,and on their behalf he thanked them mos t heartily for the consideration whiehhad promoted that gift. (Applause.) Mr. S. DAviEs remarked that for the past 15 years the need of a piano had been a seriously felt want,though the Board had never felt justified in spending the rate- payers' money in that direction. Mr. THOMPSON and Mr. HicKsiAxalso expressed their thanks for the gift. Mr. PEMBERTON, an aged inmate, said he felt con- vinced that the piano would prove a very Nvelconle addition to the institution. The capabilities of the instrument—which has been made by Russel, of Liverpool—were then demonstrated by Mr. W. H. Payton, mus., bac.,who gave an excellent interpretation of "The flarmonious Blacksmith." The inmates were then entertained to an excellent concert arranged by the Warrington Male Voice Choir. In addition to the silos given by the choir, items w!re contributed-by Miss P. Houghton, Mr. J. Hannan, -gist Lucy Davies, Mr. J. Broadhurs t. Mr. A. 0. Clay, and Messrs. Hassan, Taylor, Gough, Spruce, Ryder, D. 13' Dunn, D. Dunn, and J. Broadhurst
