INQUESTS AT WARRINGTON. _ kiScratch Which Resulted in Death. Whilst following his employment with Messrs. Peter -Walker and Sons, at Dallam Brewery; on Wednesday of last week, Gannet Bruin (45), who lodged with Mrs. S tarkey at 2, Academy place, scratched his right hand on the hoop of a barrel. The wound was an insigni- ficant one to all appearances and Bruin took no notice of it at the time. He continued his work throughout the week baton Monday of this week he complained of feeling unwell and Dr. Liston was sent for. On arrival that gentleman found Bruin was suffering from septic blood-poisoning caused by the scratch. Bruin died within a couple of hours from the visit of Dr. Liston. At the inquest which was conducted on Wednesday by Mr. F. A. Jones a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence was returned. Mr. Steel attended at the inquest on behalf of Messrs P. Walker and Sons. WORKMAN'S TERRIBLE FALL. • Richard Lawson (35), of 37, Glasshouse-row, met with a fatal accident whilst following his work on Sunday night. Deceased was employed as a labourer at Messrs. Crosfield's works and shortly after ten o'clock on themight in question had been examining two elevated caustic settling tanks. He was about to descend the ladder leading to the tanks when he missed his footing and fell head foremost on to an iron platform fifteen feet below. A fellow workman named Ernest Carter heard the fall and at once sent for Dr. Liston, who on arrival pronounced life extinct. Mr. Jones, deputy cnroner, conducted the inquest on Wednesday. Mr. F. R. Roberts appeared on behalf of Messrs. Crosfield, Mr. T. S. Steel on behalf of the relatives of the deceased, whilst Mr. Clarke, H.M. inspector of factories was also present. In the evidence which was given it was stated that the ladder was only a temporary means of access, the structure as yet being incomplete. At the top of the ladder there was nothing for a workman to catch hold of to assist him when getting on to the ladder, though a rope had been placed for that purpose since the accident. It was further stated that the ladder had been used regularly by the men engaged in placing two more tanks in position. The jury returned a verdict of" Accidental death s and expressed the opinion that until the structure wa' complete some protection should be placed at the top of the ladder to prevent such accidents happening. Mr. F. R. Roberts on behalf of the firm expressed their sympathy with the relatives of the deceased. It had, he said, always been the first consideration of the firm to protect their workpeople.and they were exceed ngly sorry the accident had happened.

Padgate followed up smartly and play settled in the visitors' 25. St. George's pressed and gained considerable ground. Padgate got possession and Furness receiving a pass from Astley scored an unconverted try at the corner. Give and take play then followed for a short time. The home backs again got going and Bell receiving the ball beat all opposition and scored a fine try. No goal m- alted. Close on half time Furness added two tries. Half- time :—Padgate 11 points, St. George's nil. Padgate were the first again to make progress and good passing enabled Furness to score under the posts. The same player kicked the goal. After another splendid run Furness again scored under the posts and missed the goal. Towser made a fine breakaway for St. George's but was well brought down by Ashton. Furness added four good tries in quick succession. Tries were scored for Padgate blr Wallace, Deeley, Hughes and Cottam, but were all disallowed by the referee for some reason only known to himself. E. to-morrow under similar circumstances. Mr. Henry Roberts and "Trading." fALL RIGHTS RESERVEDI. Sir,—Mr. Henry Roberts on the "trickery of the c; SOCIAL SERMONETTES Non-Traders" is decidedly rich, but is it wise of him when his indignant objection to "trickery "has scarcely FOR disappeared from the hoardings to write such a letter as appeared over his signature in last Saturday's papers? WORKING MEN. In his statement of the issue between himself and the Non-Traders he alludes to the objection of the latter to local limited companies exercising their "legal right" BY JOHN TAYLOR to compete for Corporation requirements. The way he puts it suits his case very nicely, but had ho stated the position faithfully, the usefulness of the point would have been sadly impaired. Of course he knows, as all Warrington knows, that what the Non-Traders object to is not local firms competing for and securing orders from the Corporation, but rather to local firms having large shareholders representing them on the Council, with a possibility of those representa- tives opening tenders and making use of the early infor- mation thus gained to secure business for themselves, and with a possibility also of their influencing (inten- tionally or otherwise) the oMcials who have to pass the materials supplied by the firms they represent. Mr. Roberts will recognize, I hope, that these are not "precisely the same conditions as firms from outside the town " enjoy. Subject to these dangers being safe- guarded against, the non-traders have always supported local firms. Mr. Roberts also refers to the "mischief" which has resulted from agitating. Of course, it. is a slip on his part substituting the effect for the cause, and he no doubt knows that the mischief lies at the door of the men who wanted to ba sellers and buyers at the same time, their own interests being on one side and these of the town on the other. I would remind Mr. Roberts of the Parliamentary Committee before which he gave evidence on this point. I would alsoifoint out to Mr. Roberts that he is the only man who is keeping the Non-trading agitation in full vigour now. According to him, it has been a 'dying agitation" from the day of its birth, and now that its work of stopping the "trading" is done' its members are quite willing that it should drop its individual existence. but as Mr. Henry Roberts threatens to return to the Council and re-introduce the " trading " that has caused all the mischief, he compels the Non-Traders to put off the day of their voluntary demise indefinitely. If he will go into the Council pledged to that old determination of his to take no profits from Corporation contracts, and will show his good faith by stopping all trading (indirect as well as direct) between his company and the Corporation,. the Non-Traders would be the first to welcome him back If, however, his intention is to sell as a merchant, to himself, as a representative of the town in the old way, I believe the majority in Warrington will oppose him, and when he tries his fortune at the polls, he will learn that the Non-Traders are still to be reckoned with, and ' that their" last legs " have a good kick left in them.— Yours B:c.,
